wear it like she does - buckled around her thigh - but it’ll at least hold a fair amount of stuff.
He loops the two straps over his shoulders so the bag hangs sideways on his back, and makes
his way to the dock.

It’s easy enough to stay in the shadows - there aren’t many people moving around right now.
Their armory will be guarded, but a lot of these merchant-type numbskulls don’t think to
guard their own stash very rigidly when they’re not at a port, so he heads to where he expects
to find the cargo hold.

He has a master’s intuition for ship layouts, so it’s easy to find an access point to the holds.
He sprints through an underpopulated, too-fancy central chamber, dodging between ornate
statues and shelves, and then down a few more corridors before he finds them. The massive
doors to each bay slide upward, so he’s able to just lift each one a few inches and squeeze
under into a hold. Once inside, he takes his time, meandering between crates of furs - morbid,
he thinks - and various other trade goods. Then he’s out and moving onto the next one,
mentally logging the contents of each chamber as he goes. There’s one full of Atraxian
lumber that he doesn’t care about - the stuff is pricey but too big for him to carry by himself
without attracting attention - and another full of Sovereign booze that he’ll probably come
back to. He hasn’t tried their liquor yet, but he imagines it has to be strong if it’s gonna
intoxicate one of those genetic nightmares.

He hits the mother lode in Hold Nine. Padded crates full of datapads, electroscreens, comms,
batteries, projectors. More boxes and cases are carrying medical equipment: medpacks,
needles, bioscanners, nanite reserves, surgical glasses. And then, far in the back: a treasury of
prosthetics. He prefers to get them from people who are already using them - there's
something that feels a little like payback, and a little like nostalgia - but they’re still just as
useful in mint condition, even if they’re not as fun. He reads the labels, then opens a few.
Nanotech tentacles. Robotic arms. Some kind of enormous insectile leg, segmented and
manipulated via a network of hydraulics. The way it reminds him of Floor makes his chest
clench.

He distracts himself by wishing he had more time and a bigger bag.

He works fast, humming under his breath to one of the songs they’d listened to on their way
from the Splinter. He can manufacture his own tools out of the needles and magnets and clips
available, and then use those tools to dismantle everything else. He throws a few things,
whole, into the bag and stuffs others into his pockets: two pairs of surgical glasses, a couple
medpacks, reams of laser scalpels, a few tubes of nanites, as many batteries as he can get.
Everything else, he strips down to circuitry and parts. The hydraulic system from the
segmented prosthesis is removed, bundled, and tucked away. Countless datapads are reduced
to tiny circuit boards, and bioscanners are pared down to just their coin-sized cameras. Into
the bag they go.

Finally, there is nothing else he can fit in it. When he looks around, he chuckles. It looks like
a Praxius IX windstorm blew through.

“Glad I’m not the jackass who has to report this,” he mutters under his breath, and snickers.

He bundles up the bag tightly to prevent any jostling and clinking from within, then slings it
onto his back and loops the straps over his shoulders. He sniffs the corridor cautiously before
hoisting the door up - higher now, to accommodate his haul of treasures - and exiting, darting
from bay to bay in the shadows.

On second thought...

He pauses. Because he really wants to try that Sovereign liquor.

He’s backtracking to Hold Six when he hears a few sets of footsteps approaching from
around the corner. Tucked into the shadows by the door, he holds his breath while they pass.

That’s when the Hold Six door slides up and open behind him, and he almost stumbles.

For a second, he blinks up at the Centaurian towering over him, and the Centaurian blinks
back.

“Well, shit,” Rocket deadpans.

The Centaurian lunges, but Rocket’s already pulled Jolie's electric-bola cannon and blasted it
in his direction. Quicker than Rocket's sharp eyes can follow, the blue-skinned man is on the
ground: wrapped in a line of red electricity, anchored by two sharp metal hooks that have
embedded themselves in the skin of his hand and the clothing over his bicep. Rocket tips his
head consideringly. The Centaurian is already trying to tear the bola from around his torso,
and it’s not going to hold him for long - especially once he thinks to open his mouth and call
for help.

Luckily, it’s not a single-shot: Rocket figures there’s at least a few rounds left. He pulls the
trigger another four times, and in seconds, the Centaurian is jittering uncontrollably in the
crackling red coils wrapping tight around his body.

“Yeah, that’s fun,” Rocket says, looking from the Centaurian to the bola cannon and back.
His lip curls in a sneer. “Writhe, little man.”

He looks around, spies an open crate stamped Sovereign Spiced Rum, and leaps up so he can
peer inside. Nestled in between shreds of gold paper are six wide-bottomed bottles, sealed
with gold wax. When Rocket pulls one out and holds it to the light, he can see that the dark
amber liquid inside shimmering with metallic flecks. He rolls his eyes.

“These guys are so over-the-top, you know?” he offers up conversationally to his victim.

The Centaurian just continues to thrash, semi-conscious against the tight electric binding.

“Rude,” Rocket mutters, and hops back down before heading to the open door. His ears
swivel just a second too late.

“Did you hear something?” someone says down the corridor, and Rocket freezes in the bay.
He’s not sure how many there are, or how many shots are left in the bola cannon. He’s fast
and agile and good with a knife, so he can probably still take them, but who knows how
many will come next?

“I think Hold Six is open,” another voice says, and it’s only gonna be a minute before they
see Big Blue here on the floor, writhing in a wreathe of electricity. Rocket hesitates, wishing
again he had one of his actual guns, and then he lunges through the door, making a break for
the other end of the corridor. He hears some surprised exclamations, and then someone yells
out, “I think it electrocuted Farthu!”

The shooting starts and he’s scrambling. Run, he thinks. And: protect the booze.

He dodges blast after blast and veers around the corner, coming face-to-face with three
Krylorians and an Atraxian. They catch sight of him, mouths dropping in shock, and then
they’re pulling their guns too and he’s so mad that he doesn’t have any heavy artillery on
him.

He lunges upward: slamming into the first Krylorian’s chest, propelling himself over the
man’s face with a swipe of his claws, and launching off his head onto the next. He’s slicing
their foreheads as he goes, letting the blood pour into their eyes because headwounds bleed
like a bitch, and then he lands in the corridor just past them and half-spins to watch as they
stumble, blood-blinded and frantic.

He practically cackles, and it feels good.
Then he turns and books it down the corridors, moving from floor to wall as needed, slicing
tendons here and fully barrelling between legs there. The wide open central chamber passes
in a blur as he ricochets off railings and bodies and statues and hanging lights. He’s knocking
over whatever he can - using any passing item as a projectile - and he’s loving it as he
watches these idiots stagger around, tripping over themselves and rippling into a small tidal
wave of Faraday crew. Unfortunately, without a real gun, he can’t do much to fight off all of
them, and he knows it’s going to become a problem soon. There are bullets and blasts
everywhere and he’s dodging, darting.

He slides half-past the corridor to the docking bays, his momentum carrying him a meter too
far and his claws skittering on the tile. He scrambles back to his feet, spins, and shoots the
bola cannon again - once, twice. It flares and fizzles on the third charge, so he turns and
throws himself down the corridor, breathing hard.

The airlock of the Gemma Lynn is open and he’s not sure how he’s going to be able to make
it inside and seal it closed before they flood in; he’ll have to get in, get to the panel, lock in
the command - and never mind getting it undocked without taking damage. The feet are right
behind him -

He hurtles through the doorway and something slides next to him, behind him.

The sound of boots squeaking on tile, bodies slamming into each other. He whirls.

It’s the Terran girl. Jolie. Because of course it is.

She’s standing between him and this small mob of angry merchants or crew or - well,
whatever they are, they’re not good at it - and she has both arms extended. In one hand, she
grips the laser pistol and points it at the small cluster of people halted halfway into the
corridor. With the other, she’s lodged the upper barrel of her quadblaster squarely into the
lead pursuer’s mouth.

“Hello, yes, what the fuck do you think you are doing?” she says sweetly to the wide-eyed
man whose mouth is gaping around the blaster barrel. Rocket’s lungs are heaving as he
watches. They’ve all raised their hands, weapons discarded now if they hadn’t been before.
She steps forward, pushing the blaster toward the back of the man’s throat. His teeth click
against the housing - he’s choking, and his eyes are streaming. He staggers back a step to
keep from gagging, and she moves forward; the modest crowd of crewmembers at the edge
of the airlock stumble back a step too.

A pause, and then she steps again, very deliberately. The quadblaster clinks against his
pursuer's teeth once more. Again, the collective shrinks back.

And again.

It’s…kinda hot, actually.

These few crewmembers of the Faraday - all except the leader, who’s still gaping around the
barrel Jolie’s blaster in the airlock - are all in the corridor now. She’s got that satin hair
everywhere, the too-big black tunic sloping off one shoulder, showing one strap of a tank top
or bra. Her stance is wide but casual, and only the tense muscles beneath her leggings give
away that she's feeling any misgivings are worries at all. The black bags of tools are buckled
around her waist and both thighs like gun holsters.

“I asked what you’re doing,” she says pleasantly to the crew of the Faraday, and then her
voice grows flat and very, very dark. “On my ship.” Another step forward. “To my friend.”

One of the people in the corridor speaks up nervously. “It was stealing - “

She fires the laser pistol and it whiffs the speaker’s pointed ear. Blood spatters and the
crewmember shrieks, clamping both hands to the wounded side of their head.

“He,” Jolie enunciates clearly. “You mean he.”

Something inside Rocket sparks and flickers.

Jolie pauses, and her eyes flicker back to the man currently drooling all over her quad blaster.
“You know I get a haul as part of my price,” she says. Her voice is placid and polite, but her
eyes are flat and dead. She waits a moment, then lifts her chin. The man takes it as some kind
of signal and this time, when he steps back, she doesn’t keep pace with him.

He flexes his jaw, cautiously wiping at his spit-covered lips with the back of one hand, the
other still raised in surrender. “You usually only take art -“

“And that’s my prerogative. Today it’s -” she pauses, a flicks a glance over to Rocket “-
whatever he’s got in that bag, and the illuminated manuscript you promised me.”

“But the bottle of Sovereign rum is worth more than three times your agreed-upon fee!”

The smile she’s wearing now is very different than the ones she’s given Rocket over plates of
scrambled eggs and map screens. It’s all sharpness and danger and satisfaction, and yeah, it is
hot.

“Then we can consider it the cost of your brutality toward my copilot,” she says evenly. “I’ll
make sure the other assessors and restorers in the guild know what kind of hospitality - or
lack thereof - the Faraday offers its contractors.”

The man’s jaw drops. Jolie slides her eyes briefly over to Rocket again, then back to her
employers, or hostages, or whatever they are at this point.

“Can you get us away from this trash heap, please?” she asks him mildly.

He doesn’t want to, actually. Not now.

He wants to stay and watch.

But she’s backing up through the airlock, weapons still extended, and soon she’ll have to
close the double doors between them and the Faraday. Timing is of the essence. They need to
be ready to get out of here as soon as the airlock prevents her from shooting them. Never
mind that technically, she doesn’t know he can fly. Some dim part of him registers that she’s
taking a gamble on him, but he kicks that thought aside and goes: darting through the
common area of the ship and sliding over the bridge and into the cockpit, flicking on the
flight engines and checking the airlock.

As soon as it’s sealed, he’s undocking and pushing up into the thruster, practically tearing the
docking port off the Faraday and singeing it in the process. He maneuvers the ship as
skillfully as he can, as swiftly as the Gemma Lynn can manage - which, all told, is pretty
swiftly.

Oh, it feels good to have a yoke in his hands again. The Gemma Lynn flies smooth and sweet.
And she handles so easily, like she was made for him.

A moment passes, then two. The Terran girl hasn’t come up to the cockpit yet but on the off-
chance that the Faraday is gonna pursue them, he keeps the ship at full-throttle, hitting a
nearby and totally-unnecessary jump, and then a few more, just to make sure they’re good.

By the time Jolie’s sliding into the other seat, he’s entering coordinates for the Achaemenid
system and checking their flight path. She’s not looking at him, and he’s fine with that. His
brain is currently comfortably wrapped in the instinct and euphoria of flight.

But later, he knows he’s going to remember the way she looked: blaster barrel planted in that
moron’s mouth, glossy hair streaming around her like it had a life of its own, the only sign of
her tension in the tight muscles beneath the packs strapped to her thighs.

It’s an hour at least before she speaks. She’s not looking at him, but she extends one arm,
pointing at him across the cockpit.

“If you drink all that booze without sharing this time, I’ll kill you.”

++++

That night, with the Gemma Lynn tucked safely into an abandoned pocket in the Achaemenid
system, they tuck into the kitchenette and dining nook. The common area is useless, he
thinks, but when he makes the ship his own, he’ll turn it into a giant workroom.

Aside from the incident on the Faraday with the quadblaster, he knows the Terran girl is a
soft-touch. He’s beginning to think he could probably just ask her for the Gemma Lynn, and
she’d give it to him. He might have to convince her that he needed it, but that wouldn’t be
hard. She’d be the type to fall for a sob story quick enough. And maybe that means he can
forgo stunning her.

Not that it bothers him either way, of course. Of course it doesn't.

He waits and watches as she cleans out the glass from the night before and pulls another out
of the dishware locker. When she sets the glasses on the bar between them, he peels the
golden wax off the mouth of the Sovereign bottle and pours a generous portion of rum into
each. The liquid is bright amber, swirling with that metallic and shimmery nonsense, and it
flashes gold as he pours.
It tastes even better than it looks - spiced, and it reminds him of some kind of autumnal
syrup. It packs a punch too: warm on the inside, as silky as heated Atraxian marble. He can
already feel his limbs going loose and his eyelids heavy.

The silence feels companionable for exactly as long as he lets it. As the liquor melts his
insides, he starts to think maybe he should say something. He’s not even sure why he’s
continued with this masquerade of silence for so long. At this point, it has to be clear to her
that she’s not dealing with some kind of dumb animal, right? With a pet? He’d intended to
leave her in the dark as long as possible, but at some point in these last few days, he’d given
up on hiding anything but his capacity for speech. So why not take the next step and actually
say something?

Of course, if he opens his big mouth now, he’s just as likely to say something he’ll regret.
The thought makes him morose, and bitter, and sad. He takes another swallow of the warm
rum, trying to wash it away.

When he glances up, she’s leaning her back against the sink, sipping her rum and gazing at
him absently. It makes him itch with sudden, familiar irritation - What’re you lookin’ at? he
wants to growl, though not quite as rudely as he might’ve yesterday. She shakes herself when
his lip curls, and she looks bemused.

“Your face is really expressive,” she confesses, dropping her eyes to her glass with a hesitant
little smile, “but I wish I knew what you were thinking sometimes.”

Doubtful, he thinks with an audible snort, and her gaze snaps upward at the sound, big eyes
wide and mouth forming a little o.

Then her smile hits like an Indigarran sunrise and that tension inside seizes him, full-force.
He feels his shoulders tighten and rise.

“It’s nice to hear you make some noise, even if it’s just complete derision,” she says, fully
laughing now, and his hackles are suddenly all the way up. He feels himself glower, and
flashes a tooth at the corner of his mouth for good measure.

“There he is,” she teases - mocks, he thinks. “There’s the guy I’ve come to know and love.”

Oh, he’s going to kill her after all. Toss her ass right out of the airlock halfway to
Conjunction.

He bares all his teeth and she chuckles softly, raising her hands in surrender. “Okay, okay,”
she says. “You try being less likable for like, five minutes, and I’ll stop telling you how much
you’re growing on me.” She tosses back the last drops of her rum and sets the glass in the
sink, pauses, and then tilts her head consideringly. “If we leave early, we’ll get to
Conjunction tomorrow around mid-morning. I’ll head to my gig and you can do….whatever
it is you need to do? Will you need anything from me while we’re there?”

He’s sure she means units, and part of him thinks venomously: take her for all she’s worth -
but he just stares at her with his eyes half-lidded, flat and expressionless. All that
companionable silence last night, that absolutely unexpected and sexy stunt on the Faraday,
and he’d been thinking maybe she was all right. Tolerable, even.

But now here they are, and she’s back to laughing at him.

The bola canon might be out of hooks and line, but there’s still the stun feature on her
quadblaster. That’ll do it. He’s looking forward to seeing her flail.

He’s glad she’s reminded him of how much he hates her.

Her brow furrows as she considers him. She’s eyeing him searchingly, trying to read
something on his face. “Well,” she says after a moment, her voice reluctant, “good night, I
guess.” A pause. “Rest well.”

She starts to move around him toward the ladder, and then pauses behind him. When she
speaks, he can tell she’s turned to face him again.

“Hey,” she says softly, hesitantly. “I’m not sure if I’m getting this right, but it feels like the
vibe just changed. Like, a lot. All of a sudden.” Silence. She swallows and for maybe the first
time since he’s met her, she sounds nervous. He sneers silently into his glass.

“If I said something that hurt you, I’m really sorry.”

Boo frickin’ hoo, sweetheart, he wants to say. It’s only sheer stubbornness that keeps his jaw
locked tight.

And then he thinks again: why not?

“Hurt me?” He mimics, and then bursts into a full-throated laugh that’s rife with
condescension and contempt. He swivels on the stool so he can look her in the eye, one paw
gripped tight on his glass as he leans back lazily against the bar countertop. “Don’t make me
laugh, doll.” His eyes narrow and he makes sure his voice drips with poison. “The vibe only
changed because I suddenly remembered that I’m sharing my priceless hard-won booze with
an entitled, spoiled brat who kept me up all night, sniveling and snotting and whining like an
actual damn infant.” He snorts. “What a waste of good rum.”

She’s gone completely pale - starting right around the time he’d called her spoiled, and
growing whiter and whiter straight through the word whining. His stomach sinks, but he
shoves the feeling aside and raises a brow at her, sneering with a mouthful of teeth.

Always go for the throat.

The silence is long. He takes another sip of his rum like he couldn’t care less, watching her
coldly through scornful, half-lowered lids.

“Oh,” she says at last. Then again, “Oh.” She chews her lip and gives a tight little nod: face
still ashen, eyes still wide. “Okay.”

And she turns and heads down the ladder.
  So she can dish it out, but she can’t take it.

  It should make him smug. Satisfied. But seeing that pale, drawn face in his mind’s eye only
  makes his sternum ache. He’s kidding himself, isn’t he? As much as he might hate her, he’s
  giving up on the idea of abandoning her on Conjunction.

  She’s too frickin’ soft.

  He’s going to have to find some place safer to dump her. Xandar, maybe. If he can tolerate
  her that long.

  Unless she wants to be left sooner. Which, after this night, might actually be the case.

  He turns back to the bar, and leans his head down onto the countertop, and curls himself
  miserably around his glass.

                                       Chapter 4: Got There First.
Chapter Summary



      in which our heroes obtain an arsenal and street food.



Chapter Notes
See the end of the chapter for notes



   Jolie is grateful when she’s able to make it down the ladder without reacting too much. She’s
   had a lot of practice at anchoring her pain inside, after all. So she holds herself very tight and
   very tall, careful not to let anything beyond her initial hurt show in her face or body as she
   collects her night shirt and heads to the shower stalls.



   As soon as she steps inside and adjusts the sound waves, her hands start shaking.



   What was that?



   She’d been wondering since that very first day on the Eclector if he was hiding what he was
   capable of, and every moment since she has been proven right. He can understand her words.
   He can fly like a dream. He can, apparently, dismantle any wayward machine he is able to
   find, and reduce it to parts.



   So the talking isn’t that surprising.



   His voice had been deeper than she might have expected, but she hadn’t been able to really
   focus on it once her brain registered what he was saying.



   Oh.
She hadn’t expected him to find her the other night, and certainly hadn’t expected him to
share those quiet sad moments with her. It had been, she’d thought, an actually beautiful
moment of connection and understanding, in a bittersweet way. He’d seemed to have been
having a rough night too, and it had been clear from the first moment she saw him that he’d
lost far more than she ever had, through no fault of his own. She had tried to be careful, to
not let her grief spill onto him too much - but apparently, she’d failed.



But it isn’t her fault he’d decided to sit with her in the dark. She hadn’t asked him to stay.



It doesn’t make her feel any better, or any less vaguely, hauntingly guilty.



She scrubs at her skin half-heartedly before giving up and just letting the compressed sound
waves beat against her with thudding pressure. She is wrung-out, and so exhausted. Hadn’t
they had a good day, by most accounts? Hadn’t they had a pleasant flight, and shared a
delicious drink, and enjoyed a near-escape that had given them a good shot of adrenaline
without anyone dying? Hadn’t they felt like friends for just a moment?



Or were years of relative solitude warping her mind?



Had she said or done something unkind? She can’t think of anything, but she only just met
him. Maybe she’d pressed some button she didn’t know existed. And what he’d said - well, it
was hurtful, but she supposes it’s better to know how much he dislikes her than to keep…
keep bothering him. Or whatever.



She estimates an hour or more has passed when she steps out of the shower, pats herself off
more out of habit than need, and wraps herself in the old Terran button-down she wears to
sleep most nights.



When she gets to her bunk, she lets herself crumple into bed.



She barely sleeps, but she doesn’t move all night.
++++



In the morning, she finds him still at the bar. It looks like he hasn’t moved all night either,
and sure enough, the Sovereign rum is gone. She says nothing - just quietly drops the bottle
into the recycling compressor in the cabinet, and begins making breakfast.



When he looks up blearily from where his head has been resting on the countertop, she eyes
him consideringly, and pulls out a pan. She’s not hungry herself - nerves have murdered her
appetite in the street - so she just cubes and pan-fries some yaro root, then adds rehydrated
egg-mix and cheese, making a passable skillet: hangover food, or at least the next best thing
with what they have. She washes and fills the two glasses of water and slides both to him,
then pulls a bottle of anti-inflammatories from the cabinet, pops two herself, and casually
leaves the bottle within his reach on the counter.



Tea and coffee are out of the question due to his recent dismantling of the electric kettle - not
unless she wants to force them to spend more time in the tiny kitchen together while she boils
water on the stove - so she grabs a mug of sourberry juice for herself. Through all of it, he
says nothing, and for just a moment she lets herself fantasize that last night was just an
unfortunate dream.



“Let’s head out,” she says mildly. “We can get to Conjunction in a few hours.”



Then she’s moving back to the cockpit, letting him do - well, whatever he wants.



They’re halfway through their abbreviated flight before he joins her, but he’s still not saying a
word and it crushes her up just a little. She reminds herself that, based on his first and only
words to her, she probably shouldn’t expect anything else.



She still doesn’t even know his name.



When they dock at Conjunction, she pulls both the quadblaster and the laser pistol out of the
drawer in the console, where she tends to stash everything she needs for a day’s off-ship gig.
The bola canon is gone - she suspects he took it to his bunk to dismantle it at some point after
their adventure on the Faraday. She also suspects it’s out of ammo.
She turns in her seat to look him in the eye. For a minute, she thinks he’ll refuse even this
acknowledgment, but then he sighs noisily and faces her.



“Whaddaya want?” he asks flatly.



She holds out both hands, one firearm in each. “Take your pick for the day,” she says quietly,
and his eyes flick up at hers before he snags the quadblaster so quickly that it’s clear he
thinks she’s gonna snatch it back. It’s a good choice - the area she’s heading to is pretty
financially distressed, but it’ll probably be safe as long as she looks like she knows what
she’s doing. She suspects he’ll be in the market, where conflict is more likely to happen.



Of course, at this point, she wouldn’t expect anything less of him.



“I’ll need to be here the rest of today, and then probably another rotation and a half - but we
can stay longer if you want.”



“That’s fine,” he says tightly.



“Okay,” she agrees, chewing her lip. She hesitates. “Be careful.”



“Be careful,” he mimics nastily, and she just looks at him tiredly. How did everything get so
fucked, so quickly?



For a second, she thinks he flinches, but then he’s scowling again and heading toward the
airlock. She waits till he leaves before scrubbing her hands over her face, sweeping her hair
into a messy ponytail high on top of her head, and buckling on her supply bags. Normally she
hides her holsters under the baggy, oversized Terran sweatshirts she’s managed to scavenge
in various hauls and markets during her travels - but this is Conjunction, so she makes sure
her firearm is visible.
She places an order for the ship to be refueled while it’s docked, and then she’s heading out,
locking down the Gemma Lynn behind her. She suspects her copilot has already hacked in
and added his own biometrics to the key, but she’s not too worried he’ll return before her
anyway. She can do her best work on this project here on the ship, where she has more room
and more screens and projectors - so she’ll be bringing the job home, so to speak.



It doesn’t take long to get to the residential area where she’s been hired. It’s definitely not one
of the rare, wealthy areas of Conjunction - but that’s part of why she took the job. She can
make a decent amount of units off whatever haul she takes from the Ravager ships and
smugglers, and the commissions she takes from merchants, high-end dealers, smugglers, and
rich people. She tries to operate on a sliding scale whenever she can. As far as Jolie is
concerned, everyone deserves art, and the ability to hold onto someone they love.



The family who accepted her bid is sweet - so sweet. The parents insist on offering Jolie
food, and she doesn’t want to be rude, so she accepts a plum-like stonefruit that she doesn’t
recognize and a breakfast-cup of some kind of sweet lilac-colored tea. They bring out the
remains of the old family holovids they’d been able to keep, and Jolie asks if they want to
join her while she pulls the information she needs.



“It’s not an exact replication,” she says. “When I do this…it’ll be like an electronic painting.
It’s just a representation - it won’t be completely realistic.” She smiles lopsidedly. “But it
always seems like the image is truer if I get to know the people I’m trying to reflect.”



They agree, and soon they are laughing and telling stories about each brief clip she’s able to
capture and clone on her palm-sized data disk. The kids - one almost an adult, and two that
are quite a bit younger - look, at turns, fond and somber. She laughs with them and asks
questions of her own to prompt more of their warm memories, and if at some points things
get a little sad and quiet, that’s okay too.



She’s used to sadness. She’s sorry for what they’ve gone through - what they continue to go
through - but she’s grateful she can be with them in it.



Maybe it was worth coming out to far edges of this stupid galaxy after all.



It only takes maybe half the remaining day before she has everything she needs. The family
tries to offer her a baked orloni-and-yaro dish, but she smiles and waves them off. “I’m
having dinner with a friend,” she laughs, and of course it’s a lie. Unless she counts the
holovid clips in her data disk as friends.



“A rotation and a half,” she promises, and now one of the parents pulls her into an impulsive
embrace, and the older kid is trying to act tough but they keep having to scrub at their eyes.
“A rotation and a half,” she repeats, her heart aching a little bit with fullness.



She leaves the neighborhood and weaves through the outskirts of the market, stopping at a
street food stall to try some kind of grain wrap, stuffed with ground orloni and a cabbage-like
slaw she’s never had before. The spices are delicious. When she gets back to the Gemma
Lynn, she sees it’s already been refueled, and she sets up shop in the common area, dimming
the lights.



Six projectors on the floor in a crescent. She parks herself in its arms and slides her palm-
sized disc into a datapad, opening a holovid multiplayer and selecting the clips she wants to
use as reference for now. The two furthest projectors on each side suddenly shoot up with
columns of pale, flickering light.



A Luphomoid child, maybe just on the verge of adolescence, smiles out of all of them.
They’re all different moments, just one- and two-second clips, caught stuttering over and
forever.



Then she opens the damaged file. It’s only five minutes long, but it’s five minutes more than
they currently have.



Jolie begins her work.



++++



When she finally wraps up for the night, she realizes that time has gotten away from her - as
it often does when she’s doing this kind of thing. It’s grueling labor and her spine snaps like
bubble wrap when she stretches back against the edge of the sofa from her place on the floor.
Her fingers ache when she eases the stylus out of them, and the insides of her eyelids feel
fuzzy.
It’s deep into the dark hours of morning, and she realizes her copilot isn’t back yet.



Jolie frowns.



He might be regularly plotting her murder - especially since last night - but she’s pretty sure
he was planning on coming back to the ship to sleep. She doesn’t think he plans to stay on
Conjunction any longer than he needs to. When he’s been in the cockpit, she’s seen his eyes
on the stars, searching the sky for forever, and she doesn’t think he could possibly mean to
stay planetside for long. Maybe that means he’s bought himself a ride somewhere, or met up
with people he actually wants to travel with. Or maybe he was just planning to stay out for
the next few rotations, till it’s time to leave.



She’s not trying to dwell on how much he hates her company, but she’d be lying if she said it
didn’t sting.



Her initial assessment of him - as extremely likable - hasn’t changed. He’s probably the
smartest person she’s ever met: clever, creative, brilliant. She’d already have wagered he’s
witty as hell, even before she’d learned firsthand how quick and biting his commentary could
be. And almost every expression she’s seen on his face since she met him - mostly variations
on annoyed and outraged - has been a fucking vibe.



She tells herself there is no rational, logical reason she should go look for him. He’ll probably
only be more irritated if she does stumble across him somewhere.



But.



She doesn’t know what kind of funds he has, and as far as she can be certain, he only has the
quadblaster on him. After catching the final seconds of his grand exit from the Faraday , it
seems likely that he can hold his own in some level of combat - or at least get away - but
obviously, he’s been caught before. By the Yondu clan - or whoever brought him to them -
and by whatever evil monster had enacted that brutal surgery on him. The High Evolutionary
Hisself, Taserface had said.
If someone on Conjunction knows or finds out about the bounty on his head…



“I’m just going for a walk,” she murmurs to the empty room. “Just…to stretch my legs.”



She’s not even bothering to really try and convince herself.



Despite the hour, the streets of the market are still loud and boisterous and questionable.
Everything is shady as hell, but that doesn’t particularly bother her. She’s no warrior, but
she’s held her own before.



And it’s all still very pretty. And alive. There are strings of lights winging between buildings,
making bright canopies and flying buttresses over the streets. There are lanterns made from
paper and wire that are too complex for her eyes to follow - though she’d love to get her
hands on one and admire the craftsmanship up close - and bright neon signs reflecting in
puddles of forgotten booze and oil. The bricks in the pavement are patterns of six
interlocking hexagons, and she hasn’t seen that kind of masonry anywhere else - frankly, she
loves it. They remind her of jump-points, honeycombing across space and time.



A couple times, someone tries to stop and sell her some black market hallucinogens, but she’s
able to brush them off with a vapid smile and a steady pace. The more dangerous characters
won’t be so obvious out here, and they’re more likely to be meeting someone specific than
looking for random prey.



Mostly, she reminds herself, and lets her forearm press against her holster just to remind
herself that the pistol and dagger are still there.



She’s starting to get anxious, even though she knows - she knows - he’s probably fine.



He may not want to be landlocked for long, but that doesn’t mean he wants to spend the next
two days with you, she reminds herself again.



But even if it’s true - and it probably is - she just needs to make sure that he’s okay.
There’s the sudden, muffled sound of an explosion - just a few haphazard blocks away, if you
can measure the rambling patterns of the Conjunction black market in blocks - and a few
shrill screams and angry yells. It startles her, and she pauses, trying to pinpoint the noise -
because she doesn’t know how, but she just knows he’s involved.



A flurry of activity spills from an alley a few streets down, and she runs toward it like an
idiot. There’s a cloud of smoke or dust in the air, billowing up and out, and as she gets closer,
her progress is momentarily buffeted by a small stream of people fleeing.



When she breaks into a ring of gathered spectators, she finds an open-air bar that looks like
the scene of a brawl. Part of the canopy has collapsed; the masonry of the wall is crumbled
and glowing, like it’s been hit by a meteor. The ground is littered with broken bottles and
booze and chunks of slag-glass and burning brick, and in the center of it all is her dear
copilot, brandishing a firearm that’s easily as big as he is.



Where the fuck did he get a laser cannon?



She blinks, trying to process everything. And she realizes that, holy hell, he is yelling.



She hadn’t heard a peep out of him in the first few days of their time together, but right now,
he is yelling very furious words, in the harshest and deepest and angriest voice she’s ever
heard.



And he is violently drunk.



“Keep callin' me rodent, tough guy!” God, his throat must be raw with the force of his
bellowing. How does such a small body have such a lung capacity?



Whoever he’s yelling at must have fled by now, or is hiding in the tattered crowd. Jolie
pushes her way to the edge of the circle, one hand reaching out, palm up. “Hey,” she says, her
voice as low and gentle as she can make it. “Hey. It’s me. Are you okay?” It’s a stupid
question, but she doesn’t know what else to say.
He half-spins toward her, his eyes flaring in the hanging streetlights. His lips have peeled
back from his teeth and she thinks,



oh, this is when he rips my throat out.



He doesn’t seem to register her presence though, in spite of the fact that she’s eased her way
into the open ring, almost crouching. He wheels around and for a moment, she thinks he’s
going to clock her in the head with the side of the cannon, purely by accident.



“I’m not gonna let you all sit here and make fun of me!” he roars into the crowd.



“Hey,” she murmurs softly, still half-crouching and cautiously edging closer. “Hey. Nobody’s
making fun of you.”



Now he does see her. “He called me rodent! And the bartender called me a rat! And a thing,
and an it!” His eyes go narrow, and his ears are flat to his skull. He bares his teeth, snapping
his jaws in her general direction - so hard and fast she has to fight herself not to flinch. “And
you!” He sounds betrayed. “You think I’m just some stupid joke too!”



“What?” she whispers, feeling her eyes widen with shock.



“You do!” He brandishes the enormous firearm. She’s not sure how he gets louder, but he
does. “You called me love and darling and handsome and friend - “ each word is dripping in
sarcasm, in high-pitched mockery “ - like you think I don’t know you’re laughing at me!” His
voice cracks.



Oh.



She’s even more of an idiot than she’d already realized.
“Well, I didn't ask to be made!” he rages, and his voice starts to wobble and then goes fully
ragged, like he’s torn the inside of his throat. “I didn't ask to be ripped apart and put back
together over and over and over and over and - and turned into some - some kind of freakish
little monster for you to buy as a pet!”



Jolie feels like she’s been cracked right through the sternum. She takes the last two steps
toward him. Her knees hit the broken brick road hard but she barely notices.



The fur on his face is damp.



“Hey,” she says softly. “I don’t think you’re a monster. Or a joke. Or a pet. I swear I don’t. I
swear I don’t. I’m so sorry I made you think that.”



For a second, his eyes focus on hers - really focus - and it looks like maybe she’s getting
through. But then someone from the crowd mutters something - she can’t even hear what it is
- and someone else snickers, and that’s it.



“Let's see if any of you losers laugh after five or six good shots in your frickin’ faces!” he
roars, swinging the laser cannon around and taking aim.



Jolie can no longer see the wetness in his fur because she is staring right into the quadruple-
barrel cannon, and it is only inches from her nose.



Someone gasps in the crowd and the remaining people around them scatter. It’s all fun and
games until someone gets brain matter on their clothes, Jolie thinks from a great distance,
and all she can hear is the thud of her own heartbeat.



The silence is long. The bar has completely cleared out, and of course no-one else is coming.
People stay away from this kind of scene on Conjunction.



She holds very still, staring into the four barrels. She can hear him breathing, and she sees the
cannon shift - just a little - like he’s suddenly uncertain.
Very slowly, she lifts her right hand, lightly touching her fingertips to the side of the firearm.
It’s still warm from the blast that hit the building, but it doesn’t burn, so she gently guides its
aim away from her face.



He lets her.



When she can see him again, he looks so miserable it breaks her heart all over again. His eyes
are downcast and his shoulders are heaving with the force of his breathing. He looks
exhausted and inconsolable, and he smells like too many kinds of booze to name.



She wants to wrap her arms around him. She wants to tell him she can’t remember ever really
thinking of him as an animal, not since those very first few seconds on the Eclector - and
certainly never ever a monster. She wants to say that she’s meant every nice thing she’s said
to him. She wants to scoop him up and carry his sad, drunken ass to his bunk, and stroke his
fur till he sleeps.



Instead, she stays on her knees in the street, the broken glass digging into her skin and the
spilled booze soaking into her leggings.



And she waits.



Finally, he lifts his gaze and looks at her, eyes bleary and ears drooping.



“Hey,” she says again, her voice as soft as the shadows around them in the alleyway. “I came
looking for you. I was worried.”



He doesn’t say anything, but the laser cannon lowers, aimed at nothing but the hexagonal
pavers for now.



“Do you want to come home?” she asks gently, and he nods.
“Then let’s go together,” she offers simply, trying to make her voice into a balm. It takes
another long moment of stillness between them, but then he reaches back and clicks the laser
cannon into some kind of magnetic holster on his back that she hadn’t even registered was
there until now.



It only takes a few steps to realize he’s not going to make it. Between the alcohol and the
abrupt departure of what she’d imagine was a lot of adrenaline, he’s lurching. She pauses,
and then kneels again in the street.



“Okay, dude,” she says tenderly, and taps her fingers to her opposite shoulder. “Hop on.”



He stares at her for a minute, drained and confused and forlorn, until she taps her shoulder
again. For a moment, he stares at her like he’s trying to parse through some very complex
equation, but then he gives up and climbs up onto her back.



She lifts herself to her feet and leans forward a bit at the waist so he can lay along her
backbone - as if she were giving him a piggy-back ride. He’s heavier than she expected - the
laser cannon, she figures, and maybe all the metal she’d glimpsed on his body that first day -
but he isn’t so heavy that she can’t make this work. She locks her hands in at her hips to give
him a little more leverage with her forearms, and tries to adjust herself under him in a way
that will make his weight more bearable. His clawed toes prickle into the leather waistband of
her holster and the flesh of her hip, through her sweatshirt. It almost tickles, and she shivers a
little. His hands grip her shoulders: one fisting in the fabric of her sweatshirt, and the other
wrapping around her bare upper arm.



They walk for a long time, and she thinks he might be sobering up, just a little. Eventually, he
leans into her, easing his weight evenly along her spine. His long nose buries slowly into the
crook of her shoulder. She feels his breath stir the strands of hair that have escaped her sloppy
ponytail, and she is suddenly very aware of his sharp teeth next to her bare throat.



She suspects that - even drunk - he is aware of it too.



He tilts his head and lays his cheek against the nape of her neck instead. His hand in her
sweatshirt grips a little more tightly, and the other one disappears from her bare shoulder. A
second later, she feels the sharp little claw trace the skin next to the exposed strap of her
sports bra, where it curves over her shoulder. A soft huff of breath skates over the flesh of her
back.



She might blame it on the void left behind from her own adrenaline rush, but the light touch
makes her shiver again.



“Thanks for not shooting me in the face,” she says at last, softly, partly to distract herself. He
grumbles something indecipherable into her skin and hair, but she knows he’s heard her.



When they get back to the Gemma Lynn, she considers setting him down. She’d bet he’s
steadier on his feet now. But he hasn’t said anything and she’s not going to bring it up, so she
just carefully climbs down the ladder with him still on her back.



She opens the door to his bunk, and it’s her first time seeing what he’s made of the room. It’s
currently only illuminated by the half-dimmed corridor lights, but she can see countless
electrical and mechanical bits and pieces, everywhere she turns. Contraptions - no, treasures
he’s been making.



Well. She’d figured he was something of a genius. Everything in her somehow goes even
softer, and she crouches next to the shelf bed so he can climb onto it without ever even
touching the ground.



As soon as he’s sitting, he begins the lengthy process of disarming himself. She hadn’t
thought beyond the laser cannon, but it becomes exceedingly clear that he’s packing an entire
arsenal now. He lines each piece up at the head of the bed, within arm’s reach: the quad
blaster she’d given him this morning is now joined by two more; there’s a couple of
electroshock batons, two ion cannons, a few daggers she’d noticed were missing, and a
handful of grenades. He unlocks his armored chestplate and removes his belt, which is heavy
with pouches of items she can’t even guess at. He starts to slide out of his jumpsuit before
thinking better of it, and rolls fully-clothed into the nest of blankets he’s made for himself.



She moves to stand up, and he says, “Wait.”
She looks down at him, eyes soft. “I’m just going to get you some water,” she says gently,
then tilts her head thoughtfully. “And maybe some painkillers. I’ll be right back.”



“Wait,” he repeats, doggedly, his back still to her. And then: “You said you’d stay with me.
You said, f’I wanted you to return the favor.”



Christ.



If she’d thought she was going to escape this night with any of her heart left intact, that hope
is fucked. She swallows and nods. “Okay,” she says tenderly, for what must be the hundredth
time in the last day, and sinks down to the floor beside the bunk. “Okay. I’m not going
anywhere.”



And that’s the end, as far as she’s concerned. She’s already thought the sentiment at least a
dozen times since the Eclector but now, whispering the words to his back like a vow, it might
as well be carved into her bones.



And she’s fine with that.



She perches her chin on the edge of the thin mattress, watching him, and then hesitantly
reaches out. Gently, gently, she massages his head at the base of his ear.



He recoils from her fingers, holding himself tense, but she doesn’t pull back - she just stills,
and waits.



“Is this okay?” she asks softly, and circles her fingertips tentatively through the surprisingly
silky fur there in small, careful strokes.



The silence is long enough that she starts to pull away, but then he whuffs out a muffled
“yeah” and just…melts into the bed. It’s only a few moments before he’s breathing in quiet,
purring little snores.
His fur is softer than she would have ever imagined.



She leaves her hand on his head even after she’s sure he’s asleep, and she turns sideways,
propping her other forearm up on the mattress and resting her head in the crook of her arm.



She has no plans to move until morning.



++++



The first time Rocket wakes up, he sees that the door of his bunk is still open. The corridor
lights are fully bright, leaking in to slick the floor with a pale trapezoid - which means the
Gemma Lynn is on its wake rotation.



He ain’t ready to be awake though.



He can see the crown of Jolie’s head, pillowed on her elbow, and streamers of glossy hair
puddled on his mattress. Is she sleeping on the frickin’ floor?



Her other arm is outstretched toward him, hand curled - palm up - next to his chest. He drags
himself around it, to the edge of the bed. He can see her legs curled beneath her, crumbles of
gravel and glittering glass clinging to her knees. Still fuzzy-headed and itchy-eyed, he
hesitates - and then reaches out to stroke the top of her head, just once.



The second time he wakes up, she’s gone. There are two glasses of water waiting for him on
the edge of his desk-become-workbench, and a bottle of inflammation-reducers. When he
looks down, there’s not a trace of glass or grit, and he just knows she meticulously collected
every bit of it out of some misguided desire to protect his feet.



Shit, he thinks flatly.
He remembers most of last night, for better or worse. He remembers stocking up on about
half the firearms and supplies he wanted - today is supposed to be the day for big artillery. He
remembers how pissed off he was, and he remembers the jackass bartender. Normally he
would’ve just been a jackass right back, maybe robbed the cash register when the dickhead
wasn’t looking - but he’d already been screwed up since the weird awful half-fight with Jolie
the night before. Too many drinks and too much bullshit from strangers and too much hating
himself and -



He’s pretty sure he’d blown a hole in a building.



Well. It wouldn’t be the first time.



At some point in all that, she’d found him, her stupid eyes all big and soft and - worried. He
was pretty sure he’d heard her knees hit the brick road - she’s gotta be bruised - but the order
of things gets pretty mushy after that.



I don’t think you’re a monster, she’d said. I came looking for you. I was worried. Do you want
to come home?



Thanks for not shooting me in the face.



He groans. He had, after all, nearly shot her in the face. Maybe he wouldn’t have pulled the
triggers - he likes to think he wouldn’t have - but it doesn’t matter. Because all she could’ve
known in the moment was that he’d had a face-melting laser cannon leveled square to her
head, and she’d had no reason to trust that he wouldn’t mow her down.



And in spite of that, he’s pretty sure she let him ride her shoulders back to the ship anyway,
nose buried into the side of her neck and tangled hair, teeth not an inch from her pretty throat.
He thinks he remembers that she let him trace a line over her bare skin with his grotesque,
mangled fingers.



He’s also pretty sure he repaid her by making her sleep on the floor to keep him company.
Okay, she’d said readily. I’m not going anywhere.



“Shit,” he says, out loud this time.



He’s overwhelmed by the idea that he’s doomed to fuck this up, but what is this anyway?
There is no this, not that he can think of. Everything feels like it’s slipping through his
fingers, faster than he can even pick it up. His head is killing him, but he’s not sure how
much of it is actually because of the alcohol. He takes the painkillers and drinks the water,
grabs a clean jumpsuit that he’d stuffed in his pocket at the market the day before, and heads
to the showers.



“Get a grip,” he mutters to himself as the sound waves hum around him. He touches the back
of his skull behind one ear, where he thinks she had gently rolled her fingertips against his fur
till he fell asleep.



Is this okay?



What had he called her the other night? An entitled, spoiled brat?



He hates everything right now, but himself most of all.



When he finally drums up the bravado to climb the ladder, she’s just finishing making
breakfast. She looks up at him with an uncertain, lopsided smile, and he frickin’ hates himself
all over again, which makes him want to get mean.



He strangles that impulse, but he doesn’t know what else to do instead, so he just stands there
at the edge of the common room, looking anywhere but in her direction.



“We’re running out of food,” is all she says. “I’m going to need to pick some up before we
leave tomorrow, after I drop off my work.” And she slides out a plate of rehydrated orloni
strips, fresh and crisp. Eggs as usual, and some kind of rehydrated roll she’s smothered in
seasoned gravy and chunks of yaro. She must be really worried about his hangover.
He rubs the back of his neck self-consciously, not moving.



“Hey,” she says softly, and waits till he finally looks up. He’s already wincing, and he hates
himself for that too, but he deserves anything she has to say this morning and he knows it.



But she’s just holding a fork out toward him with one hand, wrist and palm skyward, almost
like it’s an offering. Her voice is gentle, light, and even; each sentence is complete and
distinct.



“Good morning. Today is new. I’m following your lead.”



His eyes skim the line of her inner forearm, the sleeve of her too-big black tunic - a different
one, he realizes, which reads if no one else got me, i know the infinite void of space got me -
up to her shoulder, chin, eyes. He hesitates.



“Call me Rocket,” he says at last.



++++



Some fourteen or more hours later and he’s still remembering the way her smile had lit up her
frickin’ face. She’d tried to hide it but she couldn’t, and it had taken him about fifteen slow
and painful minutes over their shared breakfast plate - watching her try not to show too much
happiness over him just giving her his name, like she’d won something - before he’d realized
that she’d probably never been laughing at him at all over these past days.



Which makes him feel like even more of a jackass. And that really shouldn’t be possible at
this point.



He distracts himself by thinking about how lucrative today has been. He’d snagged a datapad
from the console before he left and, pulling up the tab he’d programmed into her map
screens, he’d been able to snag not one, not two, but three local bounties, all reasonably
priced. The combat goggles he’d swiped yesterday had helped considerably.



He’d visited a few more firearms dealers and scrappers afterward, and soon was carrying a
pretty decent-sized bundle of ion, laser, and electric charge generators, along with plenty of
spare cannon parts. He’d found a malfunctioning directed-energy particle rifle of Chitauri
design, and a necro-blaster that was still in pretty decent condition, though the moron selling
it had no idea what a treasure it was. He’d haggled, stolen, and threatened, and overall, he's
very pleased with the armory he's amassing. He has some designs in mind for a collapsible
blaster rifle and if it works, he's gonna make sure Jo has one, because she can’t just be
rambling around the galaxy like an idiot and not be better-armed than she is.



Not that he’s really letting himself consider how easily his plans have shifted from
abandoning her on Conjunction to dropping her off safely in Xandar to making sure she’s
fully armed before he leaves her behind. And not that he’s let himself consider for more than
a second that he could maybe let her stay. If he thinks about it at all, he knows that keeping
her is going to be more work than it’s worth. He’ll have to spend way too much time looking
after her.



Never mind that she’s the one who’d intervened on the Eclector. And the Faraday. And last
night.



Okay, so maybe she’s done just fine with everything they’d encountered so far.



Of course, the other alternative is that she won’t want to stick around. He’s been even more
of a jackass than usual these past two days.



He’s had to go back-and-forth from the market to the Gemma Lynn a few times to drop off his
goods, and each time, he’s found Jolie, barely budged from where she’d stationed herself on
the common room floor, working with her columns of light. He’d caught a few glimpses of a
Luphomoid kid when he passed, but he’d been careful not to disturb her - she’d seemed so
intent. He’d thought she was some kind of art dealer or smuggler, but whatever she’s working
on now, it’s not that. Forgery, maybe?



It’s late when he makes his last purchase and picks his last pocket - not bad, he thinks
smugly, stuffing the little pistol that throws exploding darts into one of his many pouches.
Content, he stops at an open-air street vendor and orders some zargnut-crusted moonfish. It’s
decent: crispy, warm, a little spicy. The fish is flaky and sweet. He starts to walk away as he
finishes it, but for some reason, the image of Jolie sitting on the common room floor flickers
into his brain. He pauses, hesitates, and then turns back on impulse and orders a second.



As soon as the paper-wrapped fish is in his hands, he stares at it for a full minute, uncertain.



“You good, mister?” the vendor asks. “You’re holdin’ up the line.”



Rocket rolls his eyes and steps aside. “What, you’ve got a raving customer base?” he jeers.
“There’s like two people waiting.” He elbows the big lumpy green guy behind him, voice
crackling with sarcasm. “Get ready for this menu, buddy. It’s five-star quality.”



The vendor glares at him, but Rocket’s used to that - prefers that - so he just sneers back and
spins on his heel, hoisting his bundle up higher on his back and starting the trek back to the
Gemma Lynn.



The broad’s probably not even still up, he reasons, glancing down at the fish again. But
maybe it’ll hold till breakfast, and they can split it with eggs.



It’s a perfectly rational, normal thought, but it makes him flinch away for a second, and he
almost throws the second moonfish to the curb on impulse. He stops himself at the last
second, hating how conflicted he feels about a frickin’ fish.



“Screw it,” he mutters at last, and continues making his way back to the Gemma Lynn, street-
food in hand like a half-assed peace offering he kind of loathes himself for.



When he gets there, he’s glad he didn’t ditch the second order after all.



“Have you even moved today?” he asks, and she honest-to-fuck jumps like she didn’t just
actually see him walk in the airlock four feet away from the holovids she’s staring at.
She hums distractedly. “Sorry, what? No. What?”



“Have you eaten?”



Another hum, and she’s shaking her head distractedly. She’s no longer using the stylus - now
she’s zoomed in close on something blue, adding just the faintest touch of lilac with light
brushes of her sensored glove on the datapad.



“Sorry,” she apologizes again, not looking up. “I’m really close to getting this right and if I
do, I can be finished early tomorrow and we can go -” now her eyes focus, and she does look
at him, that still-hesitant smile creeping back over her face. “Well, we can go wherever you
want.” She turns back to her blue beam of light. “Sky’s the limit.”



Today is new, she’d said, and she’d seemingly meant it. He knows there’s no frickin’ way
she’s actually forgotten the way he’d spoken to her two nights ago - but apparently, all he has
to do is not be a complete asshole, and she’ll act like the slate has been wiped clean. I’m
following your lead.



It makes the back of his neck prickle with unease.



He hesitates, then sets down his roll of goods - possibly slightly larger than he is himself -
and hops up on the couch and over to her, fish in hand.



“Eat,” he says, his voice sounding more annoyed than he’d meant it to.



She pauses again, looks down at the moonfish and then up at him. Her gaze has gone all
shimmery.



He rolls his eyes so hard that his whole head rolls with them. “Yeah yeah.” He pitches his
voice high and breathy. “‘Oh Rocket, you do care.’”
She bursts out laughing, so hard that it almost startles him. “Is that how I sound?” she asks,
snickering, and slips off her glove to accept the food he’s offering.



“You sound worse,” he informs her rudely, and she practically cackles. He tilts his head and
considers her. He knows he’s frickin’ hilarious, of course, but most people don’t appreciate
his refined sense of humor. Especially when they’re the target.



She inhales the crusted moonfish though - even though it’s probably gone cold now - and
utters a moan around the crispy meat.



Rocket swallows.



“This is good,” she’s telling him between bites. “I didn’t realize how hungry I was. Thank
you - seriously. You’re a lifesaver, Rocket.”



Who frickin’ knew that buying someone a shitty bite of street-food could be so damn
gratifying?



He shifts a little uncomfortably, then leans back on the sofa behind her. “So what is this?” he
asks, nodding to the column of blue light. He doesn’t really care, but it distracts him and
gives him an excuse to avert his eyes as she sucks the last bit of crushed zargnut off her
fingers.



“Hmm,” she hums, agreeable and maybe a little excited, picking up the stylus. “This is good,
actually. You can tell me what you think.” She cocks an eyebrow at him playfully. “I trust
you not to try and spare my feelings.”



He snorts. “Not really a risk.”



She has the audacity to wink at him again, but it’s not pissing him off nearly as much today.
Tapping a few buttons on the data pad, she zooms out on the four peripheral holovids and
pulls up a new one spanning the center two projections. The vid in the center looks corrupted
somehow, but not in the way he usually associates with screwed-up holos. It’s kind of painful
on the eyes to watch, jittering sharply in some places and seemingly completely absent in
others. He can just see the top left part of a blue-skinned head with shaggy black hair, and a
crown of copper candles on top of it. Occasionally, different parts of the kid’s face flicker into
view, but it’s erratic and incoherent.



“So this is where we start,” she says with a nod.



When he glances at the other holovids, they all show the one kid from different angles, and
he’s able to put two-and-two together.



“You’re patchin’ it up,” he says curiously.



“Eh,” she shrugs. “Not exactly - this data’s fucked. But here’s how far we’ve come.”



Now he really is intrigued.



She brings back up her blue column in the middle, and zooms out.



It’s the kid. It’s clearly the kid. He’s laughing, and there are other Luphomoids - his family,
Rocket suspects - all around him. It’s some kind of celebration, and he’s at the center of it.



“Holy shit,” says Rocket, and whistles. The holovid keeps running - she’s somehow
recovered an unbelievable portion of the sequence. A parent cuts in front of the frame at one
point - the other drops a kiss on the kid’s head, behind the wreath of candles. A toddler
invades the scene, demanding into his brother’s lap. “How did - “
But then he pauses and peers closer, because there’s something a little off, a little softer than a
real holovid. The edges look more dreamlike, and the shadows are somehow more
comforting than dark. Colors blur together in some places, like one thought folding into the
next.



His eyes snap to her. “You made this from scratch,” he says, startled. “You…painted this.”



She’s not looking at him though. She’s watching the Luphomoid family, chewing her lip,
brow furrowed. “It’s not quite right,” she confesses after a moment. “Here - “ and she
rewinds the vid a few seconds.



Rocket stares. He can’t see a thing wrong with it.



“It’s the hair,” she frets. “Right? There should be a sort of -” she makes a weird, sort of
fluttery gesture with her free hand “-movement to it, when he turns - like these strands here
should just be…I can’t quite…” she’s trailed off, distracting herself, studying the sequence
again.



“You’re insane,” he tells her flatly. “How much are you getting paid for this?”



She cringes a little, and his eyes narrow.



“How much are you getting paid for this?” he repeats.



Then she’s smiling at him radiantly, like she thinks she can distract him with that stupid,
sunshine-grin. “Two hundred units?”



His jaw literally, actually fuckin’ drops. He’s not sure that’s ever happened to him before.



“It’s only five minutes of footage,” she says quickly, like she hasn’t just spent at least an
entire day pouring over it. He bets she was doing this all yesterday before she came looking
for him, too.



He wonders if she skipped eating last night, too. And he bets her fingers are cramped and
aching from gripping the stylus for too long. He’s experienced something like that when he’s
gotten caught up in some delicate circuitry for too long, hands curled around a soldergun or
light-cutter until they’ve molded to its shape.



She must see something grim in his face because she’s already making more excuses. “It’s
just - they can’t afford anything else.”



He’s shaking his head, pinching the bridge of his nose between his eyes. “You’re an idiot,” he
says forlornly. “You’re all I have in the frickin’ galaxy right now, and you’re an idiot.”



“But you do have me,” she reminds him, her voice light - almost playful, though he thinks he
can hear a thread of uncertainty in it.



He narrows his eyes. “I’m kickin’ you out of the airlock right after we leave.”



She’s already waving him off like she knows it’s an empty threat. “Between this and the last
two jobs, it’ll keep us in food and fuel till I can hit up a Ravager ship, or another merchant
conglomerate.”



“Why are you doing this?” he laments.



She pauses then, eyes searching his in a way that almost makes him sink back into the couch.
She tilts her head and he can tell she’s debating what to say to him.



Without responding, she turns back to the five minute vid, which is cycling through a second
time. The kid laughs, one parent gets in the way, the other kisses his head, the baby wants to
be picked up. Five minutes of unfettered joy. Even he can feel it creeping in.
It makes him feel queasy.



You could charge tens of thousands for this, he thinks. Maybe hundreds. It’s like a drug.



She pauses the vid, zooms into the kid’s frickin’ hair, and shifts a strand, curling it out a little
at the end. She’s chewing her lip again, pensive. “Do you remember hearing about that
genocidal Titan that ripped through Luphom like, thirteen or fourteen years ago?”



She shifts another strand of hair.



He nods slowly, putting the pieces together. “Yeah. Thanos and the Black Order. They've
massacred a bunch of planets.” He cocks his head at the holovids. “You’re sayin’ they’re
refugees.”



She looks up at the vid, plays this half-second again, and adds a broken thread of copper. Sets
some kind of vector, then another. When she plays the sequence again, it ripples through his
hair, transformed into a glimmer of candlelight.



She hums, zooms out, and stares at the laughing kid. Rocket thinks he might be losing his
mind, because it does somehow look more playful. Happier.



What the hell, he thinks blankly.



She gnaws her lip, still dissatisfied, her eyes studiously on the screen. When she speaks,
there’s something tired in her voice. “They lost him. When they were running. He was
crushed in the streets by one of the Order while their family was trying to flee. His parents
tried to carry his body with them, but...” Her voice trails off, crackling into loss. Then she
absently taps the datapad with the oval nail of her index finger. “These clips are the only
thing they have left of him.” She shrugs, and even though she’s got her eyes on the holovid,
he can feel something inside her shift again.



“People deserve their memories,” she says quietly.
He feels himself go still. Shit.



There’s no point to trying to talk her out of it after she’s reconstructed the whole thing, and he
probably wouldn’t be able to if he tried. He can tell that by her voice. He closes his eyes and
pinches the bridge of his narrow nose once more, because he can already tell she’s going to
be even more of a headache than he’d originally thought.



He sighs. “Two hundred units?” He’s almost pleading.



She casts a little, apologetic, sideways glance up at him. “The next take will be bigger,” she
promises, and tilts her head consideringly. “I can ask for a job with the Collector if I need to.
He always has something for me to do. He pays well and the tasks are…interesting.”



His eyes narrow. He’s heard questionable shit about that guy. “Pays more than two hundred
units at least, I’m hoping.”



She snorts. “With those hazards? He’d better.”



Well. He definitely doesn’t like the sound of that, for reasons he’ll examine later. Maybe.
Probably not.



“You do gotta sleep though,” he tells her irritably, and now she looks back at him, curious.



“Already?” she asks. “What time is it?”



He nearly chokes. “Maybe three hours till morning,” he tells her, and she grimaces, eyes
flicking back to the columns of light.
  “Save it,” he orders. “It’ll still be there in a few hours. And this is already - look, I can tell
  you’re some kind of perfectionalist, but this family ain’t gonna be disappointed, probably not
  even if you’d stopped working on it hours ago.”



  She’s still hesitating.



  “Jo,” he says warningly, and her eyes blink over to his, startled, before she gives up that
  stupid sunshine-smile.



  “Pet names?” she teases. “Are we approved to use those now? Because I am in.”



  He growls, but she only looks more delighted.



  “Bed,” he grinds out, but she’s already chuckling and shaking her head, clicking a few things
  on her datapad and powering down the projectors and multiplayer.



  Then she stands, dips her head in a little acknowledgement, and winks again. “Yes, sir,” she
  says lightly, and heads to the hatch.



  He grabs his roll of gun parts and combat goggles and incendiary devices, and follows her
  down the ladder.



  Yeah. She’s still a moron. But so is he, because he’s pretty sure he’s just screwed himself.
