Chapter Summary



      in which one hero refuses to babysit and the other refuses to leave.



Chapter Notes
See the end of the chapter for notes



   Jolie sleeps in late - more than she means to. Once her eyes flicker open and she realizes,
   she’s rolling out of the shelf-bed, cursing, still barefoot and wriggling into her sportsbra when
   she stumbles out of her bunk. She’s halfway through the hatch before she gets the shirt over
   herself like a hood, blinded by fabric and still clutching her socks and boots with one hand.

   When she manages to emerge - from both the hatch and the collar of the sweatshirt - she sees
   Rocket already sitting at the bar, half-turned to watch her with one brow raised sardonically.

   It also looks like he already has half a plate of eggs and a few round pats of sea-owl sausage
   waiting for her. She freezes, sure she looks like a deer in headlights, before blinking
   cautiously and tugging the hem of her shirt past her midriff.

   “I knew this was gonna happen,” Rocket says, somehow managing to sound both annoyed
   and smug as hell at the same time. He nudges the plate in front of the empty barstool beside
   him, then slides a fork over too.

   She approaches slowly, like it might be a trick, then buys time by adjusting her sweatshirt and
   raking her fingers through her hair. She knows her tendency to both express endearment and
   hide anxiety through the same teasing tone is going to eventually be her downfall, but before
   she can stop herself, she’s echoing his words from the night before.

   “Oh Rocket, you do care.”

   He glowers - but not, she thinks, like he actually wants to kill her this time, and that’s a first.
   The relief cracks open inside her and she grins recklessly, trying to pour all her fondness and
   gratitude into him through her eyes.

   “Thank you,” she adds softly, and takes the plate. She hums in surprise at the first bite, closes
   her eyes, and swallows. “Delicious. You better be careful or I’m going to let you do all the
   cooking.”

   “Not a chance, sweetheart,” he growls, and now she is staring again, frozen with the fork
   half-raised to her mouth, surprisingly-fluffy egg forgotten. Because she knows he’s being
   sarcastic, but the term still takes her by surprise.
And sarcasm or not, she kinda likes it.

He stares back like he can’t figure out why she’s making that face, but she can tell exactly
when he connects the dots, because his brow drops in a scowl and he brandishes one clawed
finger at her.

“Don’t.”

“Okay,” she promises meekly. Wide eyes not leaving his, she finishes transporting the fork to
her mouth. “It is good though,” she adds as soon as she swallows. When she tries the
sausage, she almost moans. He’s seasoned them with something godlike, and they’re
perfectly juicy. “Holy shit, though. You’re like - a really good cook.”

He grunts but doesn’t respond, watching her as she slides onto the barstool. His eyes are
hooded, and she has no idea what he’s thinking now.

“I need to put some finishing touches on the holovid,” she says between bites. “I think maybe
you were right though, and I was getting too lost in the minutiae.”

“‘Course I was right,” he states with a sort of snarky matter-of-factness that makes her smile.
She tries to hide it behind another mouthful of breakfast, but she’s pretty sure his sharp eyes
pick up everything.

Instead, she hums. “It’s my downfall. Twenty hours without food and I get extra-stupid.
Thanks for saving me.” Something flickers in his eyes, and she ignores it in favor of not
annoying him. “So…I’ll try to drop the data disk off in the next - three hours, maybe? And
then I should pick up food and supplies. Any requests?”

“I got it,” he says, and she blinks again.

“Okay,” she says blankly. “Okay.” She tilts her head, studying him. She’s already figured out
that he must have more units available to him than she’d realized, but she hasn’t expected…
well, generosity. “Thank you. Yet again.”

He crosses his arms, almost defensively, like he’s waiting for something. She racks her brain
for what it could be, and comes up empty, so she just focuses on her food for a minute. She
can feel his eyes on her: still calculating, still a little suspicious.

To distract them both, she asks, “Where do you want to go after I get back?” She pauses
consideringly. “Or do you need more time here?”

She glances toward him and - oh, there it is. His whole body has tightened: shoulders raising,
folded arms tensing, teeth gritting.

“I gotta go to the Kyln.”

She pauses. Full of surprises. “Excuse me?”

He sighs, but it sounds equal parts ragged and annoyed. “I got a friend. He’s waiting for me
and I’m not leaving him.” His voice hardens. “I can drop you off in Xandar. Or you can stay
here and find your own way off Conjunction.”

Jolie curls her bare feet against the base of the barstool. He’s serious - she knows that
instinctively. She’s not surprised, though, or particularly worried. She’d wondered if he’d
been planning to take off in the Gemma Lynn and leave her behind for a hot minute now -
though she also suspects that it wouldn’t be quite as cold of an abandonment as he’s trying to
make it sound.

But it doesn’t matter - not really, anyway. If anything, she’s just a little sorry he hasn’t
already anticipated her response. She finishes the food he’s made her, puts her fork down, and
looks at him consideringly, head cocked to one side.

“You know,” she says at last, her voice slow and thoughtful, “I think a lot about what I
would’ve done if we hadn’t been able to get you off the Eclector. “

He stiffens. “I had a plan.” Then he pauses, curiosity clearly warring with impatience on his
face, and every muscle in his shoulders tense. “What would you ‘a done?”

She leans in, dangerously close, her nose maybe a couple inches from his own. His eyes go a
little bigger and she holds his gaze very, very seriously.

“Died trying.”

His eyes get just a little wider, looking up at her, and his ears go down - not angry, she thinks,
but maybe a little alarmed, or confused. She retreats: pulls back, shrugs, stands, and collects
the dirty dish and fork to throw them in the sink, dusting her hands off.

“So, yeah, dude. Let’s go get your friend.”

++++

Jolie can tell that he’s not entirely sure what to make of her words, so she does her best over
the next few days to make it clear that she’s not leaving him. Rocket will have to abandon her
somewhere - or jettison her - if he wants to get rid of her so badly.

He still intends to head to Xandar first, and it’ll be nearly two cycles’ worth of flying to get
there. At first, all of his glances are every shade of suspicious, but she’s pretty sure that over
the quiet span of rotations, they’ve become…almost speculative, instead. Reluctantly
reconsidering.

They settle into a routine - taking turns flying, sleeping. He makes their meals at least as
often as she does, depending on who’s awake first and who’s flying. Most times, they eat
together, hunched over the same plate in the kitchenette or the cockpit - she’s surprised he
didn’t pick up any extra dishware on Conjunction, but she’s not complaining either. So far, he
hasn’t told her to get the fuck away from him, which is nice.

Plus, he only seems to want to strangle her three-fourths of the time now. Progress, Jolie
thinks with a dry half-smile.
At some point, while she’s sleeping or flying or showering, he’s even replaced the igniter on
the second stove burner, and fixed the electric kettle he’d dismantled days earlier. She smiles
when she finds them returned and functioning.

“Thanks for taking pity on me,” she says mildly. “Another day of having to cook and make
coffee on one burner was gonna do me in.”

The corner of his mouth twitches. She thinks his sneers and snarls are turning more into
smirks, though - maybe, sometimes, more mirthful than bitter - and that does something to
her.

“I was just tired of not having decent coffee,” he retorts. “When you make it on the stovetop,
it tastes like shit.”

She doesn’t believe that’s the only reason - not for a second - but she only winks at him.
“Then thanks for saving us both from that particular fate-worse-than-death.”

You’re stuck with me and my irrepressible gratitude now, buddy.

When he’s the one in the pilot’s chair, she tries to ration out their interactions to make sure he
doesn’t get annoyed or feel trapped. She distracts herself: usually by sketching on her datapad
or reading one of the four books she’s managed to find on junk planets. The first is an
electroscreen Kree informational manual for some kind of engine. Dry as hell, but she’d
effectively used it to teach herself to read the language when she’d first arrived in these far-
reaches of the galaxy. Her translator chip is great for spoken word, but pretty useless when it
comes to text.

She muddles through the second two: a handwritten epic on a Shi’ar scroll, and a trashy
Skrull novella on a miniature datapad, respectively. A few times, she knows Rocket has
glanced in her direction and watched her bent over them: a curtain of hair around her as she
tries to parse through the characters and words, tries to grasp how each written sentence
changes with tense and context, and scrawls notes in the little book of recycled scratch-paper
she’s made for herself.

She’s waited for him to make some crack about her not knowing how to read, but to her
surprise, it never comes.

The last book is a treasure: an old Terran paperback, in English, by Stephen King.
Copyrighted in ‘84, before she was even born. She’d never read it on Earth but it still feels
weirdly nostalgic: to see something in her own language and to know it had been popular at
some point. Maybe they’ve even made it into a movie by now.

And sometimes, she just watches Rocket. She tries not to act like a fuckin’ creep, but it’s
honestly a challenge.

He seems more at home in the pilot’s chair than anywhere else she's seen him, and he’s such
a natural with the yoke cradled loosely - almost gently - in his hands. It’s like the Gemma
Lynn isn’t a ship at all, but an animal he’s convincing to love him. Sometimes he glides his
fingers over the control screens: sleek, confident, almost tender - all without looking because
he’s somehow already memorized where each dial and button is on the interface. His eyes are
rarely on the route in front of them. Instead, he tracks passing nebulae and star systems,
constellations and asterisms, planets and clouds of stardust. The way his eyes scan the sky
around them - like he’s always trying to find the edge of eternity - resonates with something
in her. Evokes something in her.

He’s still prone to indecipherable, shifting moods, and raised hackles. His sharp little
comments are hilarious, but they also remind her that underneath it all, he’s insightful -
person couldn’t make such cutting, incisive remarks if they weren’t. She’s careful to make
sure she stays in the range of playfulness that he can tolerate, and not step over that edge into
actually irritating him. She can tell, though, that he’s sometimes trying to stretch his limited
patience for her, or strangle back some mean little comment he thinks might be too cruel -
even if he’s only occasionally successful.

It’s the way he cares that moves her the most. Deeply, and begrudgingly. Like he’d rather
throw himself out the airlock than be that vulnerable. It’s the care of someone who’s lost way
too much: people, yes, certainly - and autonomy. And peace. And hope.

And even then, he can’t help himself but to try to be just a little bit nicer to the annoying
Terran he’s currently stuck with.

All of it fucking melts her.

“I’m so glad you can talk,” she tells him frankly one day, sinking into one seat and handing
him some zargnuts while he flies.

He snickers. “Pretty sure that’s a thing no-one’s ever said before.”

She clucks her tongue. “Knowing what I’d be missing out on is devastating,” she tells him,
only half-teasing, and he slants her a dubious glance. “I like hearing what you think,” she
adds immediately, and a little more earnestly. “I like hearing your opinions. And - “ she
winks “-I like how fucking rude you are.”

He scoffs. “That makes you the idiot then,” he says, but his eyes flick from her to anywhere
else in the room, then back again. To her surprise, she wonders if he’s blushing beneath that
fur of his. She hadn’t intended to elicit that kind of reaction but it’s kind of a delicious
thought. Plus - and she’d never admit it directly because she’s sure it would result in him
immediately dumping her on the nearest hospitable planet - but yeah, the thought of that
crude commentary turning intimate makes her lower abdomen warm and fluttery.

She asks him questions when he seems like he’s in the mood to answer them, or at least won’t
be annoyed by her prying. What do you like to eat? Which planet has been your favorite? Is
there somewhere you want to go?

What do you like best about flying?

Normally she judges the situation well enough that he’s willing to indulge her - sometimes,
he's even hiding a smirk or a flicker of a smile. But with this question, he falters. For a
minute he looks lost, and then morose, and then resentful.
“I dunno,” he says at last, scowling. “What do you like best about breathing? It’s a thing you
gotta do.”

That’s a lie, she thinks - but she suspects it’s one he believes. So she decides to indulge him,
tilting her head back against her chair while he guides the Gemma Lynn through a jump-
point. If her seat was any higher, she knows she’d be swinging her legs like a little kid.

“I like the way it feels.”

“Flying?” he asks flatly, like it’s the most boring answer he’s ever heard. But she shakes her
head.

“Breathing. When I was a kid, and things would get too... intense... I’d, like, disconnect. I’d
get high on panic, in the worst fucking way, and I'd feel like I didn't have anything to hold
onto. So at some point, I learned to hold onto my breath. I'd try to really feel my lungs. I’d
breathe in and picture all the little alveoli expanding - blooming like flowers. I’d imagine I
could feel them. And it would bring me back into my body and make me feel like I was
something real.”

He’s quiet for a long moment. The Gemma Lynn purrs softly as it continues its path through
the galaxy. Somehow - surprisingly - the space between them loses tension, rather than
gaining it. His hands loosen further on the yoke.

“When I fly," he admits slowly, almost unwillingly, "I can go wherever I frickin’ want.”

The silence curls up around them, and lingers. Escape, she considers. And choice.

"What're you thinking about?" he asks, and he sounds wary, almost nervous.

She hums, then breathes out softly and chooses each word as thoughtfully and precisely as if
they were seashells on the beach. "I'm thinking about cages," she admits softly. "And ghosts."
She pauses, hesitates, grimaces. Because if this is a step too far, he very well might toss her
out the airlock anyway. "I'm thinking about how bodies can be prisons as much as they can be
homes."

She feels his eyes snap sideways to her and sees his fingers flinch on the yoke. She doesn't
move - just lets the words rest between them, tenuous and silvery in the dark. Slowly, slowly,
he relaxes - maybe even moreso than before.

“What about you? What do you like about flyin’?”

She blinks. She hadn't expected the sudden question. “Me?”

He rolls his eyes. “Who else would I be talking to?”

She snorts. "You'll think it's stupid."

"Prob'ly."

A laugh tumbles out of her. “Jump-points,” she confesses.
He raises a brow and snickers. “Jump-points?”

She shrugs and grins at him, recklessly. “I’m just a dumb Terran. The first time I saw one, it
changed my fuckin’ life.”

He’s practically cackling at her outright, but she kinda loves it.

“Jump-points aren’t even special. They’re frickin’ everywhere.”

She shakes her head, chuckling herself. “Things don’t get less amazing because they’re
common. I still get excited every time I go through one.” She lifts her hands and frames up
the sky in front of them between her forefingers and thumbs. “You go through this golden
honeycomb-door, and - “ she makes a soft popping sound with her mouth “ - you’ve stepped
past a million years.”

She can feel him looking at her sideways, but she just closes one eye, still studying the sky
between the rectangle of her fingers.

“Jumps aren’t just little hexagons on a star-map. They’re windows through space and time.”
She drops her hands in her lap and feels the corner of her mouth tilt up wistfully. “Impossible
connections made possible. Reach through and maybe you can grab a handful of hope.”

At some point while she was on her little soapbox, he’s stopped laughing, and she can’t read
his expression anymore. It could be pensive, or thoughtful, or bored. Self-consciousness
crawls over her skin.

“Anyway, thanks for coming to my TEDtalk,” she says lightly.

He blinks. “I don’t know what that means.”

“Stupid Terran shit,” she explains mildly. “I’m making fun of myself.”

His face does something, but she still can’t read it. She waits, and he says nothing, so she lets
go and allows the quiet to envelope them again. The ship continues its smooth course through
the galaxy: a little silver marble rolling through dark, glistening water.

She’s surprised by how much time he spends in the cockpit with her even when he’s not
flying. When they switch out and she’s back behind the yoke, he’ll tinker with whatever
brilliant gadget he’s currently working on. Grenades mostly, she thinks, but one time she asks
him about some sort of enormous, double-gripped cannon he’s been messing with, and he just
casually says - this one’s for blowing up moons - and goes back to his work.

Sometimes they sit in the relative silence for hours, broken up only by the soft waves of
music sprinkled with a couple old Terran songs from Pete. She’s noticed how drawn Rocket
is to the tunes. Even though she only has a few handfuls of recordings, he’s played them
more in the past rotations than she has in years. He even hums along while he builds things,
and if she had to choose a most-endearing-trait of his, this might be it. At least, it would rank
in the top five.
Everything seems to rest increasingly easily between them, like an old quilt loved into
softness. She could wrap herself in it.

At some point, Jolie asks him about the friend they’re going to break out of the Kyln. The
friend’s name is Groot, he tells her, and he’s a Flora Colossus - kind of a big tree.

“He don’t talk great,” Rocket explains. “Vocal cords aren’t built for it. So his vocabulistics is
limited to I and am and Groot . Exclusively in that order.”

Rocket can’t help some of the affection that creeps into his voice when he talks about his
friend, and that melts her too. She can’t wait to meet the guy, to see the two of them together,
even if it makes her a little nervous at the same time.

But maybe her favorite rotation is the one where he gets drunk on a giant bottle of Angargal’s
limited batch that he’d picked up while he'd been grabbing supplies on Conjunction. He’s
nowhere near as far gone as he was that night she found him blowing holes in bar walls and
threatening to shoot her in the face - he hasn’t been that drunk since, though she supposes
there hasn’t been much of an opportunity. But he’s buzzed enough to be a little more
gregarious than usual, and he starts telling her stories of his own accord while she flies.
Somewhere halfway through the second tale he even offers her a drink, which she declines
with a rueful little grin.

"I've had Angargal’s before, and frankly, there’s no accounting for your poor taste," she
teases, and he rolls his eyes dramatically, muttering something about the unrefined palates of
humans. Besides, the alcohol content in that shit is high enough for her to probably poison
herself by the second shot.

“Love Angargal’s,” he’s telling her tipsily. “Last time I had it was on Contraxia. You ever
been to Contraxia?” His voice is lilting in a way she’s unused to. He sounds almost playful.

“Once or twice,” she admits with a small smile, watching from the corner of her eye as he
leans back into the copilot’s chair and takes another swig from the bottle.

“You know the pleasure-bots?”

She grins. Even if she hadn’t been to Contraxia, she’d seen plenty of models - both
functioning and in storage - on Ravager ships. “Sure do. Sounds like you're familiar with
them?”

He snorts and gestures vaguely to himself. “Who else is gonna let me touch ‘em?”

She winces. Something in her chest cracks open a little at that, but she doesn’t speak. She’s
pretty sure he wouldn’t believe anything she’d want to tell him, and based on past
interactions, it seems like it wouldn’t take much to tip him from companionable storytelling
to defensive, derisive irritation.

Apparently the question was rhetorical anyway, because he’s already going on.

“But you know, they’re AI - do Terrans know what AI is?” he interrupts himself, curious.
Jolie can feel her expression going dry as she tilts the yoke to the left, then up, steering them
toward their next jump. “More or less.”

“So they’re AI. Usually, their programming is so that they can pick up on customer’s cues
and, ya know, give ‘em their fantasy. That’s all it’s supposed to be."

She nods, keeping her eyes on the sky.

“So I’m sitting at this bar, on like my third gargleblaster - with Angargal’s, of course. And
you know, the Contraxian bars are generous with their pours. So I’m on my third or fourth
gargleblaster, an’ this woman walks in. Comes right up to me. She’s gorgeous. Wide. Plush.
Big, dreamy fuckin’ eyes.”

He sounds almost whimsical in his recollection and it charms Jolie, though she’s wondering
if she should change the subject to spare him any embarrassment in the morning.

“An’ she orders a drink - some kind of ginsky sour or something - and starts talking to me.
An’ I’m annoyed about it - “

Of course you are, Jolie thinks affectionately.

“ - because that’s how I am,” he continues breezily, as if he’s just read her mind, “and she’s
asking all these questions. Why am I planetside? ‘Cause I’m chasin’ a bounty. Do I make use
of the sex-dolls? Sure, all the frickin' time. And visit the sex-workers? Yeah, some of 'em.
They're literally the only people on this damn planet I don't try to steal from. Blah blah blah.

“And then at some point, she starts tellin’ me her sob story, like she thinks I’m gonna care.”
He snorts. “She’s trapped on this planet, right? She’s got nobody. Nothing. She’s all alone in
the universe. Someone’s got power over her and they’re making her do things she doesn’t
wanna do. She won’t say what, but she doesn’t feel like she has any options, you know?
She’s got hopes and dreams. She wants to have friends and lovers and family. She just
doesn’t wanna be alone. So she’s trying to get off-planet, and can I take her? And I figure - I
know this broad’s using me. I’m not so drunk I can’t tell when I’m being used.”

He snorts again and lifts the bottle in a vague toast, and Jolie stays still and quiet, eyes
carefully averted. She locks them on the stars to be safe.

“But I am drunk enough that I figure - what the hell. Let her use me. I can get her somewhere
safe, easy. No problem. Won’t even break a sweat. Won’t even hafta go out of my way.
Plenty of planets and systems that don’t allow trafficking of higher lifeforms. Xandar, maybe.
Belua. Atraxia. She’ll be fine. And she’s so fuckin relieved about it. As soon as we get
starside, she’s telling me how happy she is, how she’ll never go back, how I’ve made her
wildest dreams come true, how I'll always have a friend in her, blah blah blah…” He trails
off, and chuckles dryly into his bottle.

Jolie waits, then asks carefully, “So…what happened?”

Rocket smirks up at her, then abruptly tilts back in the chair and cackles.
“Then I get a transmission from the Golden Peony, and they’re offering me seventy-five
thousand units to pretty-please bring back their newest model of pleasure-bot, who just
wandered off their compound. She ain’t sentient, they say. She’s just really good at fakin’ it.”

Jolie feels her hands tighten on the yoke, even while the rest of her goes soft.

“Ah,” she says.

He’s shaking his head, smirking at the memory. “Could kinda tell, once I sobered up. Frickin’
gargleblasters. Frickin’ Angargal’s, in particular. Maybe shoulda known I’d be the last thing
a woman like that would come to for help. But it was funny, and it taught those dickheads on
Contraxia a lesson or two.”

She tries not to openly flinch at the casual way he dismisses himself. Instead, she asks slowly,
cautiously, "Did you end up taking her back?”

For the first time in his buzzed storytelling, he falters, looking up at her with big, whiskey-
colored eyes. “Well,” he hedges, looking trapped. “I don’t know where the threshold is for
sentience. Who’m I to decide? Those Contraxian bastards in suits say oh it’s just
programming, but everyone runs on programming. What, it’s more real because it’s
biologicalistic? We’re all just frickin’ meat computers.” He scowls. “Plenty of people think
I’m a lower lifeform. And she still seemed sentient, even when I wasn’t drunk anymore.
Weird, but sentient. Kinda felt like I knew her by then.”

God, her heart. This fucking guy. Fuck me, she thinks flatly. I’m so fucked.

“So you dropped her somewhere safe,” she only says.

He grips the neck of the large bottle and studies the label, then nods distractedly. “Little
planet in the Tayo system. Far as I know, she’s still there. She an’ I filed off her serial
numbers and removed her tracker-chip, once we found ‘em.” He sneers. “Whatever. Fuck
those Contraxian bastards. Nobody’s got any business making somethin’ that close to
thinking and feeling, an’ then keepin’ it locked up for no reason.”

She tilts her head toward him so she can look at him more directly as he broods for a minute.
Then he’s shaking himself, and squinting one eye into his bottle to figure out how much of
the dark liquor is left.

“Yeah,” he says, chuckling again - like he’s remembered why he's telling the story in the first
place. “So, uh, that’s how I accidentally stole a pleasure-bot from Contraxia.” And he doesn’t
wait for a response, snickering and moving onto another tale. Maybe, come morning, he’ll
forget he even told it.

But Jolie won’t forget. She’s carved it on her heart. Because here’s what she knows:

That if this advanced AI courtesan was not sentient, then she was taking all her cues from
Rocket’s behavior, and the result was just a person who wanted to be freed from a cage and
have a friend. And, whether she was sentient or not, Rocket - in the absence of concrete
evidence to the contrary - decided it was better to treat that AI like a sentient lifeform and
help her emancipate herself, in spite of the reckless amount of units he could have collected
and the excuses he could’ve made.

Jolie tries to breathe evenly and sit with the shallow ache in her chest, behind her ribs. She
focuses on her breathing and just tries to listen as Rocket talks, because there’s nothing to do
about it now. it’s too fucking late. She’s a fucking goner.

She definitely fucking loves him.

The feelings have been growing since that night on Conjunction - maybe earlier, if she’s
being honest - but there’s definitely no denying them anymore. Later, when she tries to
convince him to go to bed, he refuses - you need constant frickin’ supervision, he tells her, as
if she hasn’t been flying this thing alone for years, as if he hadn’t hidden away in his bunk a
few times before Conjunction, as if they hadn't been taking turns for rotations now - and
stubbornly stays in the cockpit till he falls into a drunken doze in the copilot’s chair. She just
knows it’s going to fuck with his back and neck.

So she peels off her sweatshirt, grateful she wore a tanktop underneath today. Studying him,
she carefully rolls and bundles the soft fabric in her hands.

“Rocket,” she murmurs softly to him. His eyes snap open, hunted, but she was expecting that.
She waits till he looks at her, then keeps her voice small and low. “Your neck's gonna hurt.
Use this.”

She leans across the cockpit to hand him the makeshift pillow and he must still be half-
asleep, because he takes it without a single sneer and tucks it between his cheek and shoulder,
folding his arms across his chest and leaning into it. He's asleep again within moments.

The cockpit is a little chilly without the sweatshirt, but it’s a small price to pay.

She doesn’t even notice when he first wakes up - she’s too busy keeping her eyes on the stars.
It’s been hours, and she’s covered in goosebumps, dancing one finger on the yoke in time to
the alien orchestra playing softly over the speakers.

His voice rumbles through the cockpit like a quiet, incoming storm. “You’re cold.”

She startles a little - jumps - and turns her head to look at him. He’s just watching her, cheek
pressed into the sweatshirt and the edge of the chair: expressionless, and alert enough that she
knows he must've been observing her for a while. His eyes flick over her, then jerk back up to
her face. “You’re cold,” he repeats, but this time there’s an intensity to it, a warning.

“Did you sleep all right?” Jolie asks, and frowns. “Is your neck okay?”

He scoffs, and straightens, catching the sweatshirt in one quick hand and chucking it at her
face. She yelps, batting the soft fabric into her lap, and he says only, “You’re a frickin'
moron.” Then he slides out of the copilot’s seat, stretches, and heads off the bridge for some
water and a shower, muttering something like “gotta stop givin’ fuckin’ reprobates the
clothes right off 'er back.”
It’s toward the end of the second cycle, with Xandar just a rotation away and a plate of
rehydrated fruit between them in the cockpit, that Jolie finally asks what his plan is for
getting into the Kyln. Rocket has been making off-handed comments throughout the entire
journey, and she knows he’s been plotting. She's tried to be patient, watching as he pours over
blueprints and old security records. She's pretended not to notice when he'd started eyeing her
consideringly, even though it had brought relief sweeping through her. Finally, Jolie thinks.
She knows he’s still weighing out whether he should try to leave her on Xandar - good luck,
my dude - or take her with him and Groot. She’s been trying to figure out how to convince
him not to leave her behind, but if she’s reading his carnelian eyes right, maybe she won’t
have to do much convincing after all.

However, she’s more than a little alarmed when he mentions that he’s planning on getting
arrested. He must see it in her face, because his ears flicker in an expression she hasn’t quite
figured out how to place yet.

“That seems counterintuitive,” she ventures tentatively, and he smirks. She likes seeing him
smug and satisfied with himself, so she hates that she’s skeptical and knows it’s showing on
her face. It doesn’t seem to phase him though - like he’s used to people doubting him. The
thought alone makes her wince.

“I figure - why waste time breaking in, grabbing Groot, and breaking back out?” he reasons
with her, then snickers. “If I do this right, I can get the Nova Corps to do half the work for
me. Besides, I have more experience organizing escapes from the inside than the outside.
Inside, I can get a clearer idea of what we’re dealing with, and I’ll get to talk directly with
Groot. Trust me, it’s better.”

“You’re not worried they’ll turn you over to the High Evolutionary?” she asks quietly. His
eyes do tighten up at that, but he waves a clawed hand carelessly.

“The Nova Corps are a bunch of goodie-goodies. Even the eviler bastards who guard the
Kyln are too loyal to their stupid code to ship me off somewhere else.”

“Good and loyal,” she echoes grimly. “So naturally they want to throw you into their own
cage, rather than someone else’s. Sounds fashy as hell.”

He grins a little at that - sharp-toothed and mean, but it’s not directed at her. If anything, he
seems like he’s excited for the whole thing.

She sighs. “Okay. So - how are we getting arrested?”

His eyes widen at that, and then he’s bursting out in that loud cackle, brimming with ridicule.

“We? Please,” he says scornfully. “You ain’t exactly suited for a mission like this, princess.”

“Should I be insulted?”

“You’re gonna take some cute little short-term art-gig in Xandar -”

“Oh, there it is. There’s the insulting part.”
He huffs a breath of air, rolling his eyes as he reaches for the screens and pulls up a starmap
that shows both Xandar and, further out, the Kyln. The difficulty he’s run into, he explains,
is making sure the Gemma Lynn doesn’t get impounded. If he could drop it somewhere
secure, with someone he trusts, and hitch a ride back to Xandar for the first stage of his plan,
he feels certain he and Groot could steal a Nova Corps starblaster once they actually escape,
and ride that out to wherever the Gemma Lynn is stored. But Rocket doesn’t have any allies
or friends, and he doesn’t currently have enough units to buy the kind of loyalty he wants
right now.

She can see where he’s going with this, just like she can see his shoulders and jaw tighten as
he goes. His hands grip the air as he gestures along with his explanations. She steps in easily
as the tension creeps into his voice.

“Luckily for you, my loyalty comes extraordinarily cheap,” she interjects cheekily, and
winks.

For a moment, he looks utterly nonplussed, ears falling flat and palms falling open. Then he
drops his hands, eyelids lowering to half-mast.

“Yeah?” he asks drily, his eyes hooded and unreadable. “What d'you charge?”

She shrugs and reaches for the first thing she can think of. “Make sure you get out and come
back to me.”

He blinks and something ripples through him, but then he shakes himself, crosses his arms,
and raises a brow. “You always undercharge for your services, sweetheart?”

She shrugs again and hazards a grin at him. “Depends on who’s buying.”

He sighs. “We’ll land in Xandar. You’re gonna go do whatever art-shit you normally do while
I make my way to the Kyln. Then, in two rotations, you’re gonna set coordinates for this little
rock.” He pulls in on the star map and taps a tiny satellite caught in the Kyln’s orbit - or
maybe the Kyln is in its orbit. Hard to tell. “We’ll meet you there, probably in a starblaster.
You’re not gonna wait longer than six hours. If you don’t see us by then, you leave. No need
to get caught snoopin.’”

“Rocket,” she says.

He takes one look at her and shakes his head. She can tell he’s already at the edge of his
patience. “This is too touchy for me to be babysittin’ you. You probably don’t even have
enough of a record to land you in the Kyln anyway, no matter what you do to get yourself

“Rocket.”

He bares all his teeth, sharp and hard. “I said no.”

And it doesn’t bother her. Well, it does, but she’s pretty sure she’s got a lock on him. She
makes her voice as soft as she can. “Rocket,” she coaxes. “Look at me.”
He scowls, still studying the map. “What ?”

She reaches out very slowly, so he can see her coming, and drops her fingers, quick and light,
onto the back of his forearm before floating them away. He whips his face to hers, but -
surprisingly - he doesn’t snap his teeth at her. His eyes shutter, and his expression goes flat.

“Rocket,” she says again, solemnly. “If you don’t meet me on that rock, I’m coming in for
you. I’m not leaving you. I won’t do it.”

She waits for her words - the seriousness of her tone - to sink in. When they do, there’s just
the tiniest flicker of something in that locked-down expression of his.

“I mean it. Nothing’s gonna stop me.”

He opens his mouth.

“Nothing , Rocket.”

His mouth closes.

“And,” she adds gently, conspiratorially, “it’ll probably be a lot harder to babysit me at that
point.”

He snorts derisively then, and she counts it as a win.

“So let’s not find out, okay?”

“Yeah, yeah,” he says drily, but his voice sounds a little different this time. Abruptly, it turns -
smug. Show-offy. If voices could swagger, his does now. “I’m gonna be fine. I’ve broke outta
prison more’n twenty times.”

“Horrifying,” she replies pleasantly, and changes the subject as she maneuvers them toward
the Xandaran docking field. “You think Groot’s gonna like me?”

Rocket rolls his eyes. “Probably too much,” he tells her, muttering something about “a tree
with a bleeding heart” and “a frickin’ soft-touch.”

++++

Rocket sends her off before he does… whatever he does to get his ass arrested.

“Don’t trust you not to get in the frickin’ way,” he tells her with a scowl. So she heads to the
location of her first job - an assessment on the sale of a small collection of Indigarran
statuettes between two private collectors.

She puts on a pair of gloves to examine the pieces, noting each place where the stone has
been cut, chipped, grazed, and smoothed. She feels the weight of them, scrutinizes the
patterns in the sculpting, the crystal intrusions. Back on Terra, she would have needed a lab to
assess constituent material, mineral alteration, internal structure and homogeneity - but out
here in the more technologically-advanced regions of the galaxy, she can do all these things
with a few scanners and tools from the bags on her thighs. Painfully expensive tools, but the
convenience is unparalleled.

When she lifts the statues in her hands, though - that’s the real payout. The whole reason she
does this kind of work: the connection. Approximately two-million, thirty-thousand years ago
- give or take - some ancient Indigarran held this chunk of translucent jade in their hands, and
they used a cloth crusted with crushed diamond to sand it into shape. That person had a
family - a village - a place where they belonged. People who celebrated their lives and ate
meals together and mourned with them. They had a favorite food, and a best friend, and a
certain kind of weather they liked to be outside in. Maybe they were a morning person, or a
night owl. Maybe they had a favorite song or story. They were just a normal person, with
petty annoyances and heartbreaks and joys - and nothing is left of them but this perfect piece
of art, far from the home in which it was created.

For a moment, Jolie’s hands are holding the same stone that their hands held, with only some
thin cloth gloves and a couple million years between them.

She feels her eyes go glossy with the beauty of it, and she blinks back discreet tears.

“These are authentic,” she tells her employers, “and in impeccable condition. Can I ask what
your plans are for them?”

“Just an addition to my private collection,” the buyer says, waving one hand airily.

Jolie smiles her best dead-eyed, customer-service smile at both of them. “Have you ever
considered surrendering them to the Indigarran Council? They really should be back in
Indigarran hands, in order to be properly maintained, both physically and contextually.”

Both Xandarans chuckle like she has said the cutest thing, and she smiles sweetly and she
collects her payment and she also gouges them remorselessly on fees. And when she's back
on the Gemma Lynn, she sends a private transmission to an Indigarran colleague with some
significant political pull. She suspects that there will be a very public interplanetary lawsuit,
and the statuettes she’s just held in her gloved palms will be back where they belong in a
dozen cycles or less.

But then the transmission is sent, and the Gemma Lynn is painfully quiet, and Jolie has time
to wish she’d never agreed to any of Rocket’s plan.

That isn’t strictly true. She’s touched that he’s so dedicated to getting his friend out of the
Kyln - that place is a nightmare that only the most happily and willfully ignorant can support.
But… she wishes she’d gone with him. She wishes she knew if he was okay, if he’d been
injured, how he’s faring. If he found Groot and has a plan.

Of course she knows he’s capable. He’s brilliant and clever. But the act of not physically
being there with him - the act of just leaving him to fend for himself, alone - it gets under her
skin. She hasn’t torn her cuticles in years now, but anxiety brings her back to the old habits
she’d thought she’d killed. She chews her lip till it feels bruised, and peels the skin around
her nails till her fingertips go raw. She has to bandage one of them before she pulls up her
screens to place bids on other jobs.
The thing about Xandar is that there’s plenty of money to be had. There’s a lot of high-gloss
wealth on this planet, and a lot of people who fancy themselves some kind of art collector.
She’s able to pick up over a dozen other appraisals for single items and small collections, and
since these people are overwhelmingly rich, she has no issues with charging on the higher
end of her sliding scale. With individual households and galleries, she doesn’t generally take
a haul, but she will run up the pricetag in units. Her name is known well enough in these
circles that, if she says a piece is worth forty thousand units, it’s accepted pretty
intergalactically that it’s worth forty thousand units, barring further degradation or damage.

She’s learned to do some basic restoration in some of the more common mediums out here -
and some more extensive restoration with the Collector’s weird shit that no-one in their right
mind would touch. Unfortunately, the currently-available restoration gigs all take more time
than she feels comfortable spending while she waits - biting her lips raw and tearing her
cuticles - to take the Gemma Lynn out to the Kyln.

She banks forty-k pretty easily in one-and-a-half rotations. Unfortunately, a lot of that will go
into refueling and restocking the ship, probably some minor repairs. She may need to replace
parts on some of her scanners soon, too. That night, she tosses and turns. She knows the ship
isn't really any quieter than usual, but it feels quieter. Emptier. Sleep is a distant memory, so
she retreats to the cockpit after a few restless hours in her bunk.

Perched in the pilot’s chair in the cockpit, Jolie attempts to distract herself with a sketch on
her datapad: a perfect procyon profile, with a sloping valley curving from forehead to slender
nose. Streaks of teal and purple stardust, magenta nebulae and foreign constellations. Dark
eyes, fastened to the endless sky. Bitterness, but also curiosity, wonder, regret, awe, and a
kind of grief-strangled desperation. She paints in the sense of urgency she’d felt when she’d
first seen that cage and those scars. She paints in the feeling of each shared plate of eggs, the
crusted moonfish at midnight, the snarky cleverness and rough edges, the look on his face
when he’s plotting or piloting. She paints in escape and choice and flying. She paints in
everything she’s felt in the last few cycles she's shared with him.

Right down to each scrap of her heart that had been wrung out in the darkness when she'd
carried Rocket back to the Gemma Lynn and realized that he was just waiting for her to hurt
him.

Her whole heart still buckles when she thinks about it.

And finally - for now, anyway - she paints in a golden, hexagonal window: a jump-point to
somewhere he can be happy. And safe.

And loved.

Of course he’s okay. Of course he’s okay. He’s too smart, too quick, too creative and violent
to not be. He clearly knows how to take care of himself. Over twenty prisons. Christ. And
this one will be no exception.

“Unless he pisses off the wrong person,” she mumbles to herself, frowning. “Or the wrong
people.”
The sun rises on day two and she showers, rehydrates food she has no appetite to eat, and
sits, ripping at the skin on her fingers while she waits to leave. Her index finger starts
bleeding around the nailbed, and she sucks on it anxiously. She checks the clock, checks the
coordinates, checks the time he gave her.

The minute the clock ticks over, she’s undocking, hitting the air and slicing through each
layer of Xandar’s atmosphere, and then beyond. She navigates smoothly, trying not to rush.

“I know where I’m going,” she tells herself aloud, striving for calmness, “and I have every
right to be there.”

She’s less nervous about getting caught right now - she can play “dumb tourist” well enough;
has had plenty of practice, in fact - but she’s just on the edge of the seat to know her friend is
okay, and to do everything in her power to help however she might be able.

It takes half-a-rotation to get to the Kyln - can’t possibly have a prison in Xandar’s pristine
backyard, she thinks cynically - but eventually, she lands on the satellite Rocket had indicated
on the starmap.

Jolie watches the sky. She watches the Kyln. She waits. She waits. She chews her lips. She
chews the cuticles on her fingers too, until another one starts bleeding.

Her eyes narrow as she squints. Twin buttons of light rise: two small spacecraft. She suspects
they’re Nova Corps starblasters, and she only hopes they’re Rocket and his friend - not jailers
and Corpsmen.

“Right here,” she urges under her breath. “Come to me.”

The two craft hover, unmoving, for long moments. Just as she starts to get anxious - well,
more anxious - a third rises.

“Shit,” she curses, firing up the flight engines. Is it Rocket and Groot? Are they in trouble,
and should she go to them? How will she know?

Something in the Kyln explodes.

The third craft joins almost lazily, and then - amidst the billowing, slow-moving fire - all
three are darting in her direction.

She tenses, wrist resting on the yoke and fingertips on the throttle, chewing her lip. Torn.

And then, over comms, she hears, “Incoming, Jo.” A pause. “Unfortunately, Groot adopted
some strays.”

He sounds so aggrieved - so absolutely himself, annoyed and inconvenienced and vaguely
disgusted - that the relief floods through her palpably, and she laughs. She’s almost dizzy
with it.

“Roger, love,” she murmurs to the empty cockpit. Into comms, she says, “Got it. I’m ready
and waiting.”
She sits with practiced patience, trying not to jump out of her seat when the first starblaster
fastens onto the airlock. She slides the lever allowing admittance, and hears the soft tones and
whirs that mean someone is accessing the control panel.

And then she can hear Rocket’s voice, muffled clanks, and a deep rumble of words she can’t
make out. She lets out a breath. Apparently there have been layers to her anxiety that she
didn’t even know were there.

More clanking, and she watches on the screens as the empty starblaster is released while the
second one nudges it out of the way. The lack of gravity on this little rock provides
assistance, allowing the first ship to shift and topple with minimal effort.

The second starblaster locks in. Presumably, its passengers disembark - more voices,
snappish and annoyed, and the second little fightership is also forcibly undocked.

And finally, the third.

Jolie is tapping the yoke anxiously.The minute she hears the airlock seal up and the third
starblaster is disconnected from the dock, she calls over her shoulder, “Good to go?”

Rocket’s already there on the bridge, just behind her, so close she startles.

“Take off,” he orders, and she does so without thinking, maneuvering the Gemma Lynn
upward, gliding between a bit of rock debris, and heading - well, it doesn’t matter where right
now, just away.

When he slides into the copilot seat next to her and she can breathe, she tells him under her
breath, “I’m so hugging you as soon as I get the chance.”

To her surprise, he doesn’t respond to that - not even with a lip-curl of disdain - and when she
casts a sideways glance at him, she can see the tension around his eyes.

“What’s wrong, Rocket?”

“We need to set a course for Knowhere,” he tells her, reaching over to pull up one of the
screens and set coordinates. “Next jump’s in 12 clicks.”

“Okay,” she says cautiously, watching from the corner of her eye as he types furiously. Her
screen pops up with the coordinates and route, but he’s still entering information she can’t
see. She’d intended to throttle down once they got away from the immediate range of the
Nova Corps patrols, but his tension is renewing her anxiety. She pushes the thrusters forward
instead, adding a little extra speed. “Everything all right?”

“I am Groot,” a voice rumbles from the bridge, and she half-turns.

Rocket had told her his friend was a Flora Colossus, but she hadn’t really known what to
expect. Groot is majestic: hunched under the archway to the bridge, too tall to properly stand
in the cockpit.
  “He says hello,” Rocket offers distractedly, brow furrowed as he reads something on the
  datapad.

  “Hello,” she says to the tree warmly. “I’m Jolie. Rocket told me I might have a hard time
  understanding you at first - I’m sorry about that. I hope to learn quickly.”

  There’s a crackling noise, like the creaking of old trees in the wind, and she looks down to
  find Groot has stretched one long limb toward her. In his branchlike fingers, he’s delicately
  holding the tiniest little flower: white-petalled, with a golden heart.

  Oh, yep. She’s head over heels already.

  “For me?” she asks, smiling over her shoulder at him as she takes the tiny blossom in one
  hand. “That’s very sweet. Thank you - so much.”

  “I am Groot.”

  “Yeah, yeah; she’s a doll,” Rocket mutters under his breath. Something flutters in her chest at
  that, but she ignores it in favor of not pissing him off. He’s too focused on whatever he’s
  doing right now to interrupt him with teasing and frankly, she doesn’t want to sour whatever
  slim charitable feelings he’s having toward her right now. She sniffs the little daisy-like
  flower, and it smells sweet and clean. Jolie slides another sideways smile at Groot and tucks
  the tiny blossom into her hair.

  Still - “I did notice you didn’t answer me,” she murmurs, but doesn’t press it.

  “- you’re not the only one unhappy with this set-up,” she hears someone saying from just
  beyond Groot, where he stands half-hunched on the bridge. “Once we get this thing to
  Knowhere and get paid out, I’m getting my ship back.”

  Jolie starts. She knows that voice. She turns her head to peer sideways over her shoulder.

  “Pete?”

Yeah. Never mind leaving her on Xandar. He could just go. If she told him to.



There’s a long silence, and he gets more and more tense. But she hums her little data-
processor noise for a moment, then breaks into the quiet gently. “Pete is a good friend, in a
kind of…endearingly obnoxious way. He’s been with me in… very bad times. He’s the
annoying, surprisingly supportive brother who I love a lot and always wished I had.” She
slants a glance at Rocket from the corner of her eye, then carefully looks away. “But he’s not
anything other than that.”



He swallows, and just lets himself sit in the ambiguity of her words. Before he can think
better of it, he blurts out, “All I’m saying is, we get this payout, and I’ll get gone if you want.
Just tell me to go an’ I will.”



She whips around to face him so sharply he jumps. Her eyes are big - alarmed - and her
ragged fingers clutch the yoke. “What? No.”



The immediacy of her response - the urgency in it - makes something strange and soothing
flicker in his chest, but he stifles it as quick as he can, and looks away. He knows he still
hasn’t apologized for being a dick to her the night before they landed on Conjunction. She
might’ve forgotten, or maybe she’s just pretending to - but he hasn’t. The stars stream past
them. Minutes spill over the edges. His throat tightens. It’s good to have friends.



Unless, of course, the friend is him.



“I’m selfish,” he says at last, his voice so low he can barely hear it himself. Still, it echoes in
the dim cockpit. “And mean.” He hesitates, and the words rasp in his throat. He forces them
out like ground-up glass. “An' I get all my friends killed.”



He doesn’t know if it’s an apology or a warning, but it’s as close as he’s ever gotten to saying
any of it out loud. He keeps his eyes on the galaxy ahead and the endless night, but he can see
in his periphery that she doesn’t move her head at all - doesn’t turn, doesn’t look at him.



And then her right hand slips from the yoke and reaches out to him, palm up, across the
narrow space between their seats, where his cage had once sat.



“There are a lot of things I want to say to you right now, but you’re not going to believe any
of them.”



The words are so soft when they fall on him. Little wisps of cloud. Warm, fluffy snowflakes.



“So for now, I’m just going to tell you that I’m selfish too, and because of that, I don’t want
you going anywhere I can’t follow.”



His heart thuds once, painfully.



He can’t take her hand. He won’t.



But he does let the fur of his forearm ghost over her palm as he reaches across for the audio
and presses play on her clones of music, keeping the volume low.
++++



A few hours later, Rocket can tell she’s getting tired. He kind of suspects she didn’t sleep at
all the night before, and that means she might even be about as exhausted as he is. Maybe
more.



He’s been staring at her fingertips, bloody and raw around the base of her nails.



“What happened to your hands?” he asks finally, and she just looks at him blankly. “They’re
frickin’ mangled, Jo.”



She glances down at them on the yoke.



“Looks like an orloni stowed away on the ship and gnawed on ‘em while you were sleeping.”



“Oh,” she says vaguely. “When I get anxious, I have a bad habit of…well. I told you. I was
worried about you.”



He makes a little, disbelieving sound. “You did that to yourself?” he asks incredulously.
Because of me?



She flickers a self-conscious smile in his direction, and his voice turns sardonic. “You gotta
get a better coping mechanism.”



She hums noncommittally, with a little smile and one eyebrow slightly raised like she’s
thinking, Who are you to talk? But with, like, affection or something.



He flicks his gaze from her hands to her face and back again. Words are easy to dismiss, but
now he’s looking at what might be evidence of her concern, and he doesn’t like it.
He’s also suddenly, uncomfortably certain that if it were his hands, all chewed-looking and
freshly torn-up, she’d be acting all stupid and fretful. She’d probably insist on washing and
bandaging them herself. And that thought brings a hoard of others on its heels that he does
not want to consider or deal with, so he just closes the door on the whole line of thinking.



Nope.



He distracts himself by leaning over and using one clawed finger to bring up her music files
again, and then selects a new temporary playlist. The sounds quietly thrum into existence
around them.



She makes her little humming noise. “I’m excited for you to hear Pete’s old Terran music,
hopefully tomorrow. I think you’ll like it.” She keeps her eyes on the stars and preps them for
another series of jumps. “I personally think they’re better than this stuff, but I admit I’m
biased.”



Pop-pop-pop. The ship bounces through hexagon windows.



Music recordings are hard to find, and he’s surprised she has as many songs as she already
does. But the promise of something different and new is intriguing, even if he’s a little
conflicted about the possibility of enjoying anything related to Quill. For now, he just listens
to the deep thrum of the Gemma Lynn and the soft, undulating vocals in the speakers.



The quiet between them spreads out just like it had on the way to the Kyln - companionable,
and weirdly comforting.

“What?” he asks when she doesn’t say anything.
She casts him a sidewise look, and her lopsided smile grows wistful and distracted. “I was
just thinking.”



“‘Bout what?”



She’s visibly backpedaling. “Nothing. Nothing. Sorry.”



His eyes narrow. “Liar.”



She hesitates, purses her lips in vague distress, and then admits, “About one of the things I
worked on while you were gone.”



His ears twitch forward in interest. “Yeah? Another holovid?”



“Nope.” She hesitates again. “Just a portrait. And before you ask, it was for fun, not for units.
Though I did make about forty-k out there. If I were the sitting-still type, Xandar might be
the place to do it.”



He snorts, trying to imagine her tolerating Xandaran snobs for more than a cycle without
fleeing the planet.



“No trying to change the subject, " he tells her, and then orders without thinking, "Lemme see

finds himself wondering what kinds of things she makes for fun. Abruptly, he remembers the
holovid of the golden girl in the amber field, all knobby-kneed and freckled. He remembers
the way Jo had cried while she watched it.



She sucks her teeth, something like nervousness on her face. “You can pull it up on the
datapad there.” She nods her chin toward the pad lodged in a shelf on the console. “Just…”
she chews her lip, and looks like she regrets saying anything.
That’s what happens when you don’t play it close to the chest, he thinks remorselessly. “File

She actually flinches. He’s not sure if he’s seen her do that, not even that night he practically

He searches, pulls it open. The datapad isn’t currently synced to the screens, so instead the

He peers through a three-dimensional expanse of painted blue-purple sky, glittering with an
overabundance of stars. Clouds of sparkling cosmic dust and nebulae spin past, and a single
jump-point is open: the view through it leads somewhere else, somewhere golden and warm
and - he can feel it - happy. The universe spins lazily, every glowing pinprick of light rotating
around a smallish lifeform in the center. Its head is in profile, tipped upward, like it can’t get
enough of the open sky.



Rocket is aware that he’s not an art-person. He doesn’t know anything about painting and -
other than being kind of fascinated when watching her work on that holovid of the
Luphomoid kid - he doesn’t really care. Not unless he can make some money from it.



But the first thing he sees in this portrait is that every stroke was put into the screen almost
reverently, like she loved it into existence.



The line of the lifeform’s nose is sweeping and gracefully curved; its jaw is narrow and
sharp. The fur looks soft enough to touch, even though he knows it’s just a projection. The
ears are attentive and forward-facing, and its eyes - when he pulls in close to see the detail -
are full of the reflections of stars. They’re brilliant and shrewd and clever and lost and also,
somehow, full of a sharp and relentless curiosity that verges on insatiable. He recognizes that
cocktail of emotion all too well, and it tugs something in him.



It takes another long minute to recognize the face, though. As a rule, Rocket generally has no
interest in mirrors unless they’re the size of his fingertip and can redirect a laser or channel a
plasma blast. He can’t remember the last time he looked in one, especially not on purpose.



So it takes him a minute to place the pieces together: the dark mask. The bronze-and-
gunmetal fur, reflecting shards of starlight. The sloping, triangular face.



When he does recognize it - when he sees himself - he feels his eyes widen, because he’s
already admitted to himself that there’s no way this was created with anything but sheer,
unadulterated tenderness. It’s practically a lovesong.



And it’s not… there’s not a shred of ugliness in it.



He actually drops the pad in his lap and, before he thinks better of it, his clawed hands
instinctively rise to tentatively map the shape of his own nose. One reaches up further to
check the feel of his ear, almost against his will.



“It doesn’t do you justice,” she says softly, and her voice is all apology, like she’s
embarrassed and worried and maybe a little afraid. “But I like it anyway.”



He looks up at her slowly. She’s flushed from the tip of her nose all the way to the ends of her
ears, down her throat and into the gaping neckline of that Terran tunic. No fur to hide behind,
he thinks fleetingly, but he’d bet she’d hide in the curtain of her hair if she could get away
with it. Her gaze is firmly locked on the route in front of them. She must feel his eyes on her
though, because she gives herself a small shake and quirks an anxious, self-conscious little
grin at him and says,



“I think I’m going to call it, My Copilot When He’s Not Actively Planning to Slit My Throat.”




He looks back at the painting, then back up at her, and he can feel his ears flatten and droop -
not in anger, but under some sort of vast weight : every untapped thing he’s buried deep under
concrete since CounterEarth. It’s a cousin - distant, but related nonetheless - of something
like being seen but maybe also being so afraid of ruining shit. And it’s terrifying and he hates
it and for just a second he’s completely fuckin’ lost and hunted.
She looks stricken then, her eyes turning toward him and widening at whatever she’s reading
in his face and eyes and ears. She takes one hand off the yoke and reaches between their
chairs, toward him. “Hey now, Rocket,” she breathes, “there’s no reason for that.”



Her fingers flutter through the fur on his cheek, and he flinches. She snatches her hand back
like she’s been burned, or maybe like she’s afraid she’s burned him.



He wrangles it all in - this mess of unspooled feelings, all tangled together, that he has
absolutely no name or frame of reference for. Then he coughs a little, ignoring her as well as
he can, and taps the image to close it before he has the chance to look at it any further, to give
it any additional thought.



“M’not gonna slit your throat,” he mumbles, because it’s the only thing he can think of.



She hums. “But sometimes you want to,” she teases, offering him an escape hatch.



Like always.



He takes it anyway, and glowers.



“Don’t I have enough to deal with right now, without your heckling?” he asks, and she yawns
in response. When he glares at her, her smile turns gentle.



“I suppose you do,” she concedes softly. “I know you said Groot brought in the strays, but I
think that you’re secretly a leader.”



He scoffs, but she’s scrubbing at her eyes, and she switches out a hand on the yoke so she can
roll her other wrist. His eyes narrow.
“Time for my shift,” he says, and then cocks his head at her. “Where were you gonna sleep,
anyway?” He tsks. “Givin’ up your bunk for Drax -“



“Oh. I figured I’d probably just sleep up here,” she offers apologetically.



He winces. “In the chair?” He knows firsthand that’s the path to a major backache.



She looks around, at a loss. “I mean, I was gonna sleep on the couch, but - “



He grimaces. “Don’t think that’ll be much better.”



She shrugs and slants him that stupid wink. “Limited options, my dude.”



“Better option would’ve been to - I dunno - not give up your bunk,” he can’t help but point

“No,” he says drily, flicking the piloting controls over to his side of the console. “Get outta

She chuckles. She doesn’t just leave, though. When she gets up, she maneuvers the scant

He surprises himself by freezing instead of flinching this time, and her hand draws away,
reluctantly.
“I’m glad you made it,” she says again, lightly enough, “and that I didn’t have to come in

He snorts, but she doesn’t move. He doesn’t move either, his eyes on her reflection in the
glass ahead of him. She’s superimposed on the windshield like a ghost on the stars.



“You’re important to me. Do you know that, Rocket?”



“You’re gettin’ sappy,” he manages to grumble after a moment, and almost immediately

She backs up.



“I’ll be out in six hours, but send Groot or someone to get me if you need a break sooner. Do

He suddenly doesn’t want her to go after all. If she didn’t look so tired…well, the Gemma
Lynn is full of strangers and idiots, and Groot’s probably asleep. It wouldn’t have been bad to
have her stay with him for a while longer.



“Uh, I do have a question, actually,” he says, and then grimaces. Idiot, he berates himself.



“Mmm,” she hums, and turns back to him. “What is it?” He feels her leaning on the back of
his chair, her forearms draped over the headrest right above him. It’s tension-inducing - to

emptied out her entire bank account for him, waited on an abandoned satellite for him, gave
him the literal shirt off her stupid back, shared her food with him - right on the same frickin’
plate.



The likelihood that she’s gonna stick a blaster in his back is probably low.
He hesitates. “Quill called me a raccoon,” he says to the windshield in front of him. He can

“Mmmhmm.”

“It’s not - “ he scowls at her reflection. “M’not a raccoon.”



“Okay,” she says easily, stifling another yawn with the back of one hand.

He watches the faint outline of her shrug. “It’s hard to really think of you as…any kind of

I don’t know - look like ducks or something.”



“How do I remind you of a raccoon, though?” he asks, persistent.



“Mm, I don’t remember what I said before, but you look kinda like one. Big differences in

She gives a tired, lopsided smile into the windshield.
He mulls over that for a minute. “You like them? Raccoons? It’s not…it’s not a bad thing?”
He hates that his voice sounds uncertain, and he bares his teeth to make up for it.

He snorts. “What, and let Quill fly? Unlikely.” He pauses, though, because he can see she’s

  And as for her - well, he bets she’s given away dozens, maybe hundreds in her life.

  More like I’m his.
