Chapter Summary



      in which we visit Knowhere.



Chapter Notes
See the end of the chapter for notes



   Jolie and Rocket trade off a few times, overlapping a few hours in the cockpit and snagging
   meals together. Once in a while, they’re able to set the ship to auto-pilot, and that gives Jolie
   the opportunity to check in with Pete and really meet the rest of the new, temporary crew
   once they wake up.



   Drax seems stoic, perhaps, but - she suspects - ultimately soft. There are an abundance of
   miscommunications at first, since Rocket seems far too entertained by the chaos to fill her in.
   Luckily, it doesn’t take her too long to figure out Drax’s literal interpretation of language, and
   she does her best to shift her style of speaking to something more precise. When she’s in the
   kitchenette, quickly rehydrating some fish for her and Rocket to eat before she takes over the
   next shift of flying, the Kylosian leans over the breakfast bar to tell her - for the third time -
   of the deaths of his wife and daughter, and his intention to kill Ronan.




   Maybe it’s the repetition, or something in his tone - quiet, firm, unmoving - but she suddenly
   finds herself overwhelmed by a sense of recognition. She pauses, hand hovering over the
   buttons on the rehydrator, and blinks up at him.



   She’s seen this before. She’s been this before. So fixated on a thing that feels like an answer,
   but isn’t. Her hand floats across space and time before she even feels it move, and she lays
   her fingers on top of Drax’s where his hands grip the countertop.



   To her surprise, Drax breaks off in the middle of his sentence, looks down at her touch, up to
   her face, and then closes his mouth. There’s a moment where they both stand, unmoving and
   unspeaking, and then Drax simply covers her hand with his opposite palm.
He must’ve seen something he recognized in her too, then.



Gamora is - as Pete has described - smart, and intense. She’s practical, righteous, and
focused. She’s also immensely intimidating.



Jolie instantly wants to be her friend.



Jolie’s gotten too good at reading people over the years. It’s a defense mechanism, in a way.
Oldest child syndrome, she’s half-jokingly told people over the course of her life. So when
Jolie looks at Gamora, it takes less than a minute to see a woman who has never had a friend
in her life.



But, Jolie thinks, I bet she wants one.



Gamora is also startlingly slender. You’d think, in a galaxy full of all different, desirable body
types, right down to invertebrates and exoskeletons, a Terran girl could be spared some weird
body-image issues. Nope, Jolie realizes with a grimace: her Terran conditioning remains alive
and well. That’s a me-problem, she tells herself.



Not that it matters anyway. The only person Jolie has had any inclination to flirt with in
almost a decade is sitting across from her in the cockpit and they’re probably only really
friends because she’s been a near-constant and relentlessly-affectionate presence in his life
for a small handful cycles now.



It’s like exposure therapy, she suspects. Or acquiring a taste for mediocre beer.



She’s grown on him in spite of himself.



Jolie tries to piece together what happened in the Kyln, though everyone’s recounting varies
wildly. She’s able to gather that Pete and Gamora were incarcerated at the same time, while
he was trying to sell off the orb to a dealer of fine artifacts and she was trying to steal it from
him. Once in the Kyln, they met Drax - who had attempted to murder Gamora before Quill
had intervened - and Groot, who had decided to defend Quill from a particularly vile fellow
prisoner for some reason unknown to any of them.



Quill and Drax and Gamora might not have known the reason why Groot had decided to
intervene, but Jolie thinks she can guess. It’s simple, really - so simple that none of his
newest companions have realized it yet. It’s only this:



the Flora Colossus is kind.



He is, at his heart, generous, with an abundant softness for things he perceives as smaller and
more vulnerable than himself. Of course, she’s certain that Rocket has recognized this
tendency in his best friend by now, but just in case he hasn’t realized yet that Groot counts
him as one of those vulnerable things, she’ll never say it aloud.



Sleeping in Rocket’s bunk has been an unnerving experience. The first time she’d gone in on
her own, she’d perused his desk with her eyes, keeping her hands to herself. She’d smiled
fondly, fiddling with the ends of her too-long sweatshirt sleeves as she gazed around,
clocking the stock of bagged drinking water on his makeshift workbench, the neat stack of
clean hand- and shower-towels he’d stacked on the shelf by the door, and his makeshift
hammock in one high corner. He’d had a whole arsenal in the honeycomb-shelves lining the
far wall. The room had been cluttered - but shockingly and meticulously organized - and the
desktop had been liberally strewn with creations and machines cobbled together from parts
she often recognized, but whose whole was a mystery to her.



She’d known since the moment she’d met him that he was clever, and soon after she’d
figured he was something of a genius.



But his creativity - that is something special.



Wistfully, she’d imagined the two of them making things side-by-side - imagined getting to
see his quick fingers and quicker mind at work. She makes a mental note to suggest that they
make one of the walls in the common area into a workbench - something at a more
convenient height for him. It’s so well-suited for the purpose - run through with a low shelf,
and plenty of outlets and programmable screens - that it probably originally had been
intended as something of one, and it will give him room to spread out.
Now, her third time in the bunk alone, it still feels strange. To be here, in his space, without
him. She perches on the edge of the shelf-bed, unwinding a couple blankets from the nest
he’s crafted for himself, plumping a pillow and slipping out of her leggings and sweatshirt,
into the old button-down she uses to sleep in.



She's worried.



Because this…this could become habit-forming.



There’s a comfort to sharing your sleeping quarters with someone, to closing your eyes in the
darkness and knowing there’s another warm, breathing, trusted person just a few feet away.
She’d spent most of her remembered-childhood sharing a bed, or at least a room.



Every night now, though - even though he isn’t in the bunk - she can still feel that it’s still his
space. She knows he’s just spent time curled in the hammock. His belongings are shifted and
moved: evidence of another person in these tiny shared quarters.



Her friend.



Her very dear friend.



His bunk has some kind of scent: thick and musky, but not unpleasant. Woodsy. Blue spruce
and fallen maple leaves, mossy logs forgotten in an autumn forest. It’s layered with other
things, too: iron and copper, whatever other deep-space metals he’s been working with. The
syrup of engine fuel. Something thin and bright and clear that reminds her of ozone after a
Terran rainstorm: lightning and electricity.



She curls up in his bed each time it’s her turn to nap, and she sleeps better than she has since
she was a kid.
++++



Knowhere is a mess, but in a sort of comforting and weird way that reminds her of the
seedier and livelier parts of her hometown on Terra. Similar to Conjunction - neon signs,
outdoor bars, string lights swinging over the dusty streets - but not quite as desperate. Not
quite.



She perches on a barstool and watches Rocket, Drax, and Groot gamble on orloni fights.
She’s pretty sure Rocket knows almost exactly when she comes in, because his ears twitch,
and one swivels to follow her movements. She’s not sure how it’s possible he can hear so
well in this noisy place, but eventually he looks up and his eyes zero in on her without ever
having to glance around. He pauses, then turns his attention back to Drax, who is shouting at
the orloni.



The bar serves something that comes in steins as big and wide as her head, and the brown
liquor smells like a blend of old molasses, NyQuil, and nail polish remover. One sip tells her
that trying to drink more than a quarter of the cup will knock her flat on her ass and possibly
corrode her esophagus. Her shoulders spasm as it burns down her throat and she scrapes her
teeth over her tongue, almost gagging on the rotten-sweet-and-acetone flavor.



When she glances up, Rocket is looking straight at her, smirking. He mutters something to
Groot, and then makes his way over to sit beside her at the bar.



“Too strong, sweetheart?” he jeers.



“Too something,” she shoots back. “What is this - rotting syrup and fermented gasoline?”



He gestures to the bartender and soon has his own full stein. He takes a gulp with seemingly
no ill-effects, and Jolie shakes her head in mock dismay.



“Your shirt’s a choice for today,” Rocket says, gesturing to the white lettering on heather
gray, which modestly claims she is microdosing hell by going to work. “Didn’t you say you
work for the Collector sometimes?”
She leans toward him conspiratorially and bumps her shoulder against his, pleased as hell
when he doesn’t even flinch away this time. “And I wear it every time I do,” she confesses,
and winks.



He snorts, shaking his head and rolling his eyes before he takes another gulp from his stein.
But she’s pretty sure there’s something of a smirk in the corner of his mouth.



The excitement at the orloni table dies down, and it isn’t long before Groot joins them, a stem
on his forearm already twisting into a tiny snowflake of a flower. He plucks it and hands it to
her, and she smiles at him fondly as she adds the little blossom to the other three clustered
over her right ear. Groot hunches his bulk daintily on the barstool next to Rocket just as Drax
meanders over to join them on her other side.



Rocket seems to pace his drinks better than she would have expected, and she wonders if it’s
still due to everything that happened when he’d gotten wasted on Conjunction. Conversely,
Drax is on his third stein. As big he is, that’s still a lot of paint-thinner for even his
constitution. He’s a little fuzzy on the edges. His already questionable capacity for
diplomacy seems to be on the fritz, because while he’s talking to anyone who will listen
about Ronan and vengeance and cowardice and honor, he also chooses that moment to say, “I
would not have believed I would be on this journey and that my only companions would be
two useless Terrans, Ronan’s lackey, a tree, and vermin, but - “



Her hackles are up, high and fast. She’s already turning, even as she senses Rocket opening
his mouth to say something incendiary beside her, and then -



The entire contents of her enormous stein find their way into Drax’s lap. He breaks off mid-
sentence, staring at her with a dumbfounded expression, and she can practically feel Rocket
freeze in complete bafflement from her other side.



“Why would you do this?” Drax asks, and he sounds like a wounded puppy.



“Because you’re too tall for me to pour it on your head,” she replies politely. And because it’s
better than Rocket shooting you in the face, she thinks. She leans up to him, pats his cheek,
and lowers her voice to a whisper. “Listen to me. C’mere. Listen.”
He leans into her hushed voice, still stunned.



“Insulting those who have committed to being your allies is dishonorable.”



He gapes. “Insulting allies? I would not.”



“Drax,” she whispers, and pats his cheek again like he’s a puppy. “People generally consider
terms like vermin and lackey to be insults.”



“Oh,” he says, and now he leans back, looking perplexed. “What should I call them, then?
She is, objectively, Ronan’s lackey, and he - ” Drax gestures to Rocket, who’s already
growling warningly, his fur bristling.



“She’s just Gamora,” Jolie interrupts firmly. “Your former enemy, a woman on a mission, and
your current friend. And Rocket is just Rocket, a technical and creative genius, and also -
maybe - your current friend.” She leans in again. “I’m going to give you a little trick , Drax.
A tip. For free, because I like you, and because I know - very intimately - what losing the
people you love can do to a person. This trick is gonna make you happier, and it’s gonna
make you smarter, and it’s gonna make your alliances stronger. You ready?”



He nods, the booze still dripping off his thighs. She braces one hand on the counter and leans
up, balancing precariously on the footrest to buy herself an extra twelve inches of height so
she can press her cheek against his and whisper into his ear.



“Focus on the best aspects of the people around you,” she murmurs. “They’re just as much a
part of them as the things you think are bad. And more importantly, they’re the parts that they
usually need to be reminded of, too.”



He seems utterly nonplussed, but he pats her hand when she drops back into her seat. She can
almost see his brain turning over what she has said. “Thank you, Jolie. Ultimately you are
still weak and useless in a fight, but I appreciate the effort you put into contributing
something of value.” He meets her gaze solemnly. “Did I do it that time?”
She blinks at him, and then the snickers bubble up and she’s laughing and shaking her head.
Drax is still waiting for feedback, apparently, so she trades her empty stein for the full one in
his hand. “Progress,” she tells him, still chuckling. “Yes. And all future lessons will cost you
a drink apiece.” She takes a sip, half-convulses with her entire body, and pulls a face.
“Christ.”



It’s Drax’s turn to laugh then - big and booming - and he pats her hand again. Rising, he
meanders away toward the gambling tables.



“Once again under-changing for your services,” Rocket grunts from next to her, but he’s
watching her with curiosity in those bright eyes. “Why’d you do that?”



“I am Groot,” says the Flora Colossus from just beyond him.



She raises her stein in cheers toward Groot, then shrugs.



“Don’t like to hear the people I love referred to as pests and undesirables, I guess,” she says
mildly, and she notices something flicker in Rocket’s eyes. “What?” she asks, but before he
can answer, she’s taken another sip and is shuddering at the taste of burnt plastic and
something like brown sugar. Her eyes tear up. “Good god, why ?” she asks the galaxy at
large.



He snorts. “Why do you keep drinkin’ it?” He’s clearly entertained.



She stares into the stein forlornly. “I was hoping I’d get drunk enough for it to taste better.
Now I’m thinking that no amount of commitment is going to improve the flavor.” Her eyes
narrow on the tarry brown liquid. “Honestly, I’m starting to take it personally.”



“I am Groot.”
“Yeah, I agree,” Rocket says drily. “That’s probably enough for you, sweetheart.”



She tilts her head sideways and winks at him again. “You know I can’t refuse you anything
when you call me that,” she says, and she could almost swear he gets flustered for a minute.



“I am Groot.”



“Guys!”



The three of them turn. It’s Pete, and he’s beckoning them.



“The Collector sent someone to bring us to him,” he says.



++++



“Nope, don’t like this,” Jolie murmurs when Carina leads them into the main hall of the
Collector’s museum.



Nothing like a horror show to kill your hard-won, foul-tasting buzz.



Rocket leans toward her. “Thought you’d been here before,” he mutters from the corner of his
mouth.



She glances down at her copilot. “Not in the museum,” she says grimly. “He has me come to
a lab - empty except for whatever he wants me to work on - and he provides any of the
materials I need. It’s a pretty sterile environment. This though - “ she pauses as they pass a
glass column with a dog in a spacesuit, and her heart stutters. “This gives me the fuckin’
spooky-ookies.”
Rocket looks up at her, and his eyes narrow. She wonders if he can tell she’s already
considering trying to use her eight-hundred million to buy anything in the Collector’s cages
she can afford that might still be alive. But then he sighs, and turns his eyes back to the path
in front of them. “Yeah.”



She’s wound tight, but his tone and agreement soften her. “Sorry. I’m sure it’s fuckin’...weird
for you too.” Frightening, she thinks. Because it scares her - all these creatures in cages like
glass vials and sarcophagi - and she’s not even anything unique or special. And she hasn’t
been caged before.



Not like this. Not like Rocket has.



Carina is ushering them through the grand room, giving the tour-guide speech, Jolie guesses.
“We house the galaxy's largest collection of fauna, relics, and species of all manner.”



She likes Carina - the rosy-skinned assistant has always been sweet when Jolie has come to
work in the lab before, and Jolie suspects the Krylorian is underappreciated and perhaps even
abused. Jolie has offered to take Carina off Knowhere before, but it’s clear that her boss holds
some power over her.



“Now, may I present to you: Taneleer Tivan, the Collector.”



The Collector is sweeping up, pushing Carina aside and fawning over Gamora’s hand. Jolie
cringes. The Elder believes himself to be a gentleman but he’s uncomfortably handsy, on top
of his weird possessiveness toward literally anyone he encounters - a weird possessiveness
which, Jolie notices, seems to be an extension of whatever makes him feel entitled to cage all
the living things in here. Jolie wishes she’d thought to give Gamora a head’s up - not that the
woman can’t defend herself just fine, but it’s always nice to be prepared for creepy old men
ahead of time.



“Why, I never thought I'd meet a Groot!” The Elder’s eyes light on Groot, greedily, and he
immediately starts haggling for the tree’s corpse. “Sir, you must allow me to pay you now, so
that I may own your carcass. At the moment of your death, of course.”
“I am Groot.”



Rockets looks horrified and offended. “Why? So he can turn you into a chair?”



“Mmm,” Jolie interrupts with a pseudo-thoughtful hum, stepping smoothly in front of her
copilot to face the Collector. “Perhaps we can set down a contract once our business with the
orb is concluded, so both you and Mr Groot can be sure of the benefits you’ll be receiving.”
She makes the mental note to take Groot aside and let him know that she suspects the
Collector is not above orchestrating the deaths of creatures whose corpses he desires.



She can tell Rocket’s already suspected it from the way he tenses further.



“Why, My Little Jolie!” The Collector’s greeting is dramatic, expansive, as if she hadn’t just
interrupted him in the middle of a deal. “How good to see you! I did not expect you to be
involved in these proceedings!” He approaches, arms wide, and embraces her.



She stiffens up, just like she always does, and the Collector pins her arms to her sides like
she’s already wrapped in one of those glass coffins. To Jolie, Taneleer Tivan always smells
like old wine and the dusty wings of dead moths. She catches a glimpse of Rocket from just
around the Collector’s embrace, and he’s looking at her with a half-dumbfounded, half-
disgusted look on his face.



My Little Jolie? Rocket mouths up at her incredulously: ears down flattened, lip curled.
Repulsed, she thinks, but not half as repulsed as she is herself.



She shrugs helplessly from where she’s trapped against the Elder’s chest, and tries to send her
most pained expression back.



Something shifts and hardens in Rocket’s expression. “As touching as this is, whitey,” Rocket
interrupts, half-growling, “we’d really like to get paid.”
The Collector releases her and looks down at Rocket with an intrigued expression she does
not like at all. “Charming,” he utters thoughtfully, and glances at Jolie. “Is this your pet, Little
One?”



She can feel the snarl rising in Rocket as he reaches back and grapples for his gun. She
reaches out, mouth opening - I’m his, I’m his, she thinks frantically - but thankfully, Gamora
intervenes first.



“Tivan, we have been halfway around the galaxy, retrieving this orb,” the Zen-Whoberian
interjects, somehow still sounding gracious and dignified around her urgency, and the tension
eases - just a little.



“What is this thing, anyway?” Pete asks, tossing the orb up in the air and nearly fumbling the
catch. The Collector winces and takes it from him.



“Oh, my new friends,” he oozes, leading them toward some monstrous, mechanized device.
Jolie winces, trying to discreetly brush the feel of him from off her upper arms and
collarbone. Rocket’s watching her, an unreadable look in his eye, and she offers a crooked,
questioning little smile back.



“Before creation itself, there were six singularities,” the Collector says, and sets the orb into
the machine. It appears to be some kind of vice, clamping onto both halves of the orb.
“Then…the universe exploded into existence, and the remnants of these systems were forged
into concentrated ingots.” He breathes heavily, almost lustfully as the machine begins to
leverage apart the halves of the metal sphere. “The Infinity Stones.”



They all watch, listening to the Collector describe the thing’s origins with what Jolie assumes
is a shared and growing horror.



“These stones, it seems, can only be brandished by beings of extraordinary strength.
Observe.” The Collector pulls up a holovid, and in front of their eyes, they watch as giant
creatures brandish the stones, destroying entire planets. “These carriers can use the stone to
mow down entire civilizations…like wheat in a field.”
Pete seems to be on the same page as Jolie, because he immediately says, “I think I might be
peeing myself right now.”



“Once, for a moment, a group was able to share the energy amongst themselves, but even
they were quickly destroyed by it.”



The metal, apparently, is just a shell to be peeled back. Inside, something glows - violently,
blindingly, offensively purple. Looking at it makes Jolie’s brain feel like it’s being squeezed
in her skull. She’s immediately nauseous, till she can rip her gaze away.



“Ahh,” the Collector sighs. “It’s as beautiful as I imagined. Beautiful beyond compare.”



The light shimmers out in sickening, pulsing waves. Even with her eyes averted, Jolie thinks
her head is going to split open, or she’s going to hurl. Maybe both.



“Blah, blah, blah. We still wanna get paid.”



“Rocket,” she murmurs, and her mouth feels hot and sick, “I don’t think -“



“And how would you like to be paid?” the Collector speaks over her.



Jolie looks at Gamora, desperate to make eye contact with the one person who might see her
rising panic and recognize it as a very reasonable physiological reaction to giving this man
such a powerful, destructive object.



“In units, fancy man,” Rocket snaps, and then there is a noise from behind them, from behind
the vice and the stone.



“Carina, stand back,” the Collector snaps, with something as close to urgency as Jolie’s ever
heard in his voice. Her head snaps around to catch a glimpse of the Krylorian woman as she
reaches for the pulsing purple gem.
“I won’t let you hurt me anymore,” Carina says. Her voice trembles, but her eyes are
resolute. “And I won’t be your slave any longer.”



Before Jolie can reach out - can say anything at all, if it would even matter - Groot snaps a
winding branch around her and another around Rocket, and they are all three hurtling through
the air amidst an explosion of purple fire and the smell of hot coals and iron. Jolie lands on
one hip and slides, crushed between Flora Colossus and shards of stone floor - but even in
the chaos, some part of her brain dimly registers that it’s better than being in the path of that
scalding, sickening purple blaze. The momentum carries her forward, dragging her out of
Groot’s grasp, and she collides with the base of one glass cage, her body snapping around it.
Gravel and shrapnel rain down bitingly - she curls and covers her head instinctively.



Her ears are ringing. Someone is hoisting her up - Pete, his fingers anchored bruisingly into
the skin of her upper arm. Her eyes skitter over the wreckage. Where is Rocket? Her heart
stutters, thudding in her ears, but Pete’s yanking her after him and where is Rocket? She
thinks she might be telling Pete that she’s not leaving, can’t leave -



“M’here,” she hears her copilot say raggedly, and she lurches in Pete’s grip, eyes wide and
wild until she sets them on her friend. He’s got dust and debris in his fur, but there’s no blood,
and he seems whole. Her knees almost give out in relief - Pete curses and then Drax is there,
sweeping her up with a disapproving cluck of his tongue and tossing her over his shoulder in
a very undignified way, and muttering something about the frailty of Terrans.



She doesn’t care. She doesn’t care because it seems like they’re all okay, and when they get
to The Gemma Lynn , her own personal autopilot kicks in. She slides into the cockpit, sets
coordinates for somewhere deep and desolate and empty in space, and maneuvers them off of
Knowhere so quickly and deftly that she might as well be a magician.



They’re all piled onto the bridge. They don’t fit, but for once, Rocket isn’t complaining about
it.



“How could I think Tivan could contain whatever was within the orb?” Gamora is saying
from behind her. The Zen-Whoberian’s voice is hushed and horrified.
Jolie does not say I told you so, and she thinks maybe she deserves a medal for that.



“What do you even still have it for?” Rocket demands, and if his voice is a bit more shrill
than usual, she can’t blame him.



As for herself, she already knows she won’t sleep easily tonight. Not even with the coziness
of Rocket’s scent all around her.



“Well, what did you want us to do, leave it there?” Pete snaps.



“Yes!” Rocket shoots back. “Yes, leave it there.”



“We have to bring this to Asgard or the Nova Corps,” Gamora insists. “They’re the only ones
we know of who can contain this, right?”



“We’re wanted by Nova Corps,” Rocket’s reminding her, his voice furious. When Jolie flicks
a glance over at him, he’s not looking at Gamora though - he’s staring at her, looking pissed.



What the fuck did I do? she thinks, and giggles nervously. It’s not a typical sound for her, and
she swallows it in case she sounds panicked.



“Maybe the distance of Asgard is a plus,” she offers up. “If we take it to Xandar, it’s basically
right where Ronan wants it - he just has to get to it.”



“Or,” her copilot snaps, “we just frickin’ give it to Ronan and see if we can trade it for our
lives.” His glare is still so intent on her that she feels it when they slide downward, from her
eyes to her torso, then her chair. “Jo - “



“We can’t give it to Ronan,” she reasons, in what she thinks is a perfectly calm tone of voice.
“Yeah, what are you thinking ?” Pete adds. “He wants to destroy the whole galaxy!”



“Then let him,” Rocket snarls. “What’s the galaxy ever done for you, huh? For any of you?
Why would you want to save it?”



Brought me to you, Jolie thinks, but she’s not so deep into shock that she says it. She can
already imagine Rocket actually fully apoplectic, steam rising out of his ears like some sort
of old Terran cartoon. Instead, she offers up a little shrug.



“We live in it!” Pete’s practically exploding.



Her shoulder’s stinging a little, and her side, but she ignores it. “We can’t just abandon it.
Them. Whatever.” She looks at Rocket helplessly.



“Hear me out,” Pete reasons, turning to Gamora. “Forget Nova Corps. Forget Asgard. I’m
sure if we try, we can find someone nice to give it to, who can protect it, and who’s willing to
pay us a lot of money instead of throwing us back in the Kyln.”



“I hate sayin’ this, but I guess out of the available options, I’m once again with Quill,”
Rocket interjects.



“I am Groot.”



“So’s Groot.”



“I am Groot!” Groot says, with an appalled tone that clearly indicates his friend is lying. Jolie
snorts.



“We cannot allow the stone to fall into Ronan's hands,” Gamora replies sharply. “We have to
take the Gemma Lynn and deliver the orb somewhere we know it will be safe. We don’t have
the time to find that kind of buyer. It must go to Asgard or the Nova Corps.”
  “It’s settled,” Jolie says. “This ship is half-mine -” she cuts a sideways glance at Rocket,
  daring him to argue the point right now “- and I’m picking the flight path this time.”


  She taps in the coordinates, redirects the Gemma Lynn, and banks sharply down and to the
  right.



Chapter End Notes



    Finally, some plot development!

    I'm playing fast and loose with a lot of the travel times, friends. My thought is that
    maybe sometimes one pilot knows a shortcut that another one doesn't, and that different
    ships may travel at different speeds when they're not going through a jump, and that you
    can push your speed by going through jumps more quickly. I know MCU canon says 50
    jumps, but it doesn't give us the timeframe in which that 50 should ideally occur, so I'm
    playing with that - like, there's probably a minimum amount of time (I'm saying
    50/hour) and an ideal timeframe (50/12 hours). Or something. I don't know, I did the
    math back when I originally drafted this but I made up the rules and I'm not sure I kept it
    and also I am bad at math.

            Chapter 8: The Care &amp; Feeding of Human Pets.
Chapter Summary



      in which our heroes practice breathing and we lean into a new trope: “there was
      (technically) one bed.”



Chapter Notes
See the end of the chapter for notes



   Jolie refuses to let Rocket take over the flight controls, even after it’s been hours and she
   should really be in bed. And to her credit, she’s not shaking or making bad judgment calls on
   their route or anything - not unless you count trying to run to Asgard with this purple bomb
   as a bad judgment call, which he does - but she is kinda bleeding on the chair. Rocket’s not
   sure she’s even noticed that the right side of her tunic’s been torn clean off from the rib
   downward and along one shoulder, held together by threads on that side and sagging halfway
   off her body. He’s also not sure she’s noticed that her leggings are shredded at the right hip
   from waistband to halfway down her thigh. He can see the skin beneath - on both hip and
   shoulder- and it’s raw and oozing, glittering with chips of stone and glass. Some of her too-
   much, too-shiny hair is getting stuck in the congealing wounds.



   Meanwhile, as her blood dries, Gamora and Quill are tending to their bruises and scrapes in
   the common area, Drax is sulking somewhere, and Groot is hovering like a worried mother
   hen on the bridge. All the flowers have been blasted out of Jo’s hair, and Groot is offering her
   new ones faster than she can accept them while she flies.



   “I am Groot.”



   “I’m trying,” he snaps at his friend.



   “I am Groot.”



   “I said I’m trying!” Rocket snarls. “She won’t listen.”
“What did he say?” Jolie asks mildly, and he hesitates. Because she sounds all right but again,
she doesn’t seem to notice she’s sporting a gravel-burn across a fifth of her body.



I’m not leaving without Rocket, I won’t, he’d heard her say when his ears had come back
online. It wasn’t like she’d screamed it, exactly - but her tone had been so ragged and
breathless and bloody-sounding that for a second he’d thought her throat or lungs had taken
damage, and that had scared him more than he’d like to admit.



Throats and lungs are delicate. Especially on humies without metal ribcages to protect them.



Then, when he’d managed to tell her he was there - the look on her face had scared him even
more, albeit in other ways. No-one had ever looked at him with such bone-crushing relief
before, like they didn’t even trust their own eyes and ears.



It had reminded him of someone else, gazing at him with hope and fear and wonder and
again, mostly hope, all in a second before the first gunshot rang out. It had reminded him that
he didn’t deserve anything good at all.



“He says you should let me fly and get yourself cleaned up,” Rocket says flatly, and if he’s
taken some artistic liberties with the translation, who can blame him? No need for her to have
to be embarrassed too.



“I am Groot,” Groot admonishes.



Jolie smiles wryly. “I don’t need to know exactly what he’s saying to know he feels like
you’re misrepresenting him,” she says, and Rocket scowls. She flicks a sidewise glance at
him, and sighs, and says mildly, “I’m fine. Adrenaline is a solid painkiller, and I’m more
worried about you, anyway. You’re sure you’re okay?”



He’d been fully protected by Groot - sheltered from the fire, and the ground, by the branch-
like arms that hadn’t quite managed to cover Jolie the same way. He’s strained and scratched,
but all-in-all, he’d probably actually come out with the least injuries out of their whole crew,
and that kind of makes him feel like a jackass too.



Always the sole survivor, he thinks grimly, and then shuts the thought away.



“Not a bruise or a broken rib,” he says only.



“I don’t believe that,” she returns with a skeptical little moue of her lips. “You’re wincing.”



“Just sore,” he counters. “I ain’t the one actively oozing onto the upholstery - “



“We good now, captain?” Quill asks, squeezing past Groot on the bridge, and Rocket remains
unclear about who he’s referring to, but Jolie doesn’t answer. He clears his throat, but he’s
saved from making any assumptions by Quill’s exclamation of “Holy hell! Earthgirl, you
haven’t patched that up yet?!”

doin’ that.” He flexes his jaw uncomfortably, vaguely wishing he’d never said anything - not

Ravager cage, to keep his frickin’ mouth shut and never even let her know he can speak at all
in the first place.



And to maybe be a little nicer to her, while he’s at it.



Her brow is still furrowed and skeptical, and he has the sudden urge to reach out and smooth
it, and fuck an infinity stone because that is maybe the most horrifying thing to happen in the
last rotation. It makes him wriggle out from under the covers and off the bed as fast as he can.
  He grabs a clean jumpsuit, clutching it in front of himself at waist-level, and is halfway out
  the door before he pauses and looks back at her.



  She’s half-sitting, looking utterly perplexed at his sudden flurry of activity. Ribbons of shiny
  hair have fallen into her eyes and all around her shoulders.



  “Rocket?”



  The bewilderment in her tone does something to him.



  “I mean it,” he says, his voice harsher than he means it to be. “Call me - whatever you want.”



  And then he practically bolts to the showers.

   Jolie frowns as she tosses microdosing hell into the recycling compressor - but she supposes
   it’s a small price to pay for everything that has happened since they left Knowhere a few
   hours ago. Everyone is safe, and they’re headed to Asgard, and also, oh yeah, no big deal, but

   But.




   No promises.

God, she fucking loves looking at his hands. She’s never really been drawn to hands before -

Asgard is a long journey and will take nearly four more rotations of constant flight, if they

To make friends.

“It’s not a matter of faith,” Gamora starts.

I am Groot, he tells her kindly.

For taking care of all of us.

Fuck.

asked about pocket dimensions.



Stupid.

recognize?”



Another hum. “That’s a hexapull. We have something similar on Terra, but they’re shaped a
little differently - we call it a wrench. That’s what I use to get into the engine room when I
need to.”



He winces. “I’m not gonna ask why you gotta use a hexapull to get into your engine room,
but I’ll fix that later,” he says drily, before launching into a brief summary of the different
kinds of hexapulls and their sizes, and what they’re used for. He sees her nod in his periphery,
like she knows some of it and is committing the rest to memory, and she looks so pretty
peering over the roll of tools.



He grimaces into the pipes.



“I don’t recognize this one," she says, and he half-glances over.

“That’s a double-handed speed-drill. I’ll actually need that right at the end here, if you’re still
hangin’ around.”



“I will be,” she promises, crooked smile quirking up.



He swallows, harder than he should’ve had to. “D'you know what that thing that looks like a
little rotary blade is - uh, actually, do you know what a rotary blade is?”



“Yeah, but you’re talking about the glass cutter,” she says promptly. “On Terra, we call that
style with a swiveling head a Vigrue, but our wheels aren’t usually so big or so exposed, at
least not the ones that I use. We've also got grooved stems to make it easier to snap off
smaller pieces of glass after it's been scored. You’ve got a pistol-grip too.” She narrows her
eyes, which flick briefly to his hands and then back to the tools. She tilts her head. “Is your
wheel tungsten carbide or do you use something else out here?”



He blinks behind his goggles, pausing in his work to study her. “Usually diamond, but
sometimes you’ll find tungsten carbide in parts of the galaxy where diamond’s less
common.” Now he wonders about her shrewd glance at his paws. For a minute, he’s self-
conscious. He's got the pistol-grip for times when the metal pins in his hands are particularly
achy, his joints and tissues all inflamed. Did she figure that? And if she did, is she also
clocking some of the other modifications he’s made to his other tools - the ones that make it
easier for him to use them on bad days?



He doesn’t wanna fuckin' think about it. Instead, he just asks, “You used a glass cutter
before?”
But she only shrugs, cheeks turning pink. “Not on anything as useful as you do, I’m sure,”
she says lightly. “I used to fuck around with stained glass. Just - trying to make something
pretty to put into the universe, I guess.”



The confession scrapes over that rawness he's been carrying with him since this morning,
twisting something sharply in his gut. It's a reminder of what he’s not. Just to make something
pretty. He recalls the way she’d looked: painting in the cockpit, face golden and shining with
tears, or in the common area, surrounded by columns of blue light while she colored the air
with her fingertips.



Meanwhile, he’s over here, ripping open walls so he can cobble together water heaters and
explosive devices.



Just another ugly thing making more ugly things.



His lip curls in the ghost of snarl and he turns back to his work. “Well, we can’t all be
creator-types and artists,” he sneers, and he feels - more than sees - her head snap around to
stare up at him where he hangs in his little cave of pipe and cables.



Like some kind of frickin' gremlin, he thinks grimly.



“Some of us just like to destroy and ruin things,” he snarks, not looking at her.



She makes a little muffled noise he can’t identify - maybe a scoff, maybe a startled laugh.
Then she’s tilting her head, brow furrowed and eyes urgent, troubled. “You’re kidding,
right?”



Without meaning to, his mind lights up with the memory of her legs under the blankets this
morning. Even with the bandage, they’d been pretty: graceful, sloping, soft. He can’t believe
he’d thought, for even a millisecond, about putting his mangled paws all over her. Something
in his chest collapses inward at the thought.
His lip curls back further, because he never could stop when he was ahead. “You can leave
anytime, princess,” he tells her, the endearment turning venomous in his mouth. He
immediately regrets it, but doesn’t allow his face to do anything but snarl.



Through their shared time in the cockpit and the hours he’s spent in this frickin’ wall - alone -
he’s had time to think. And it’s all started to feel like it some sort of betrayal - the brief
moments of contentment. He peels back the scab on his memory of Lylla and Teefs and
Floor, and lets it hurt. He owes them after all, doesn’t he? He’s been turning the question over
in his mind all day and the only answer he comes to is yes, he owes them their lives back, and
since he can’t give them that, then he should pay for it himself.



I know what you’re doing, Jolie had said last night. Punishing yourself.



Well.



The silence feels like it goes on forever, broken only by the clinking of the pipes he’s
working on.



Then, gently:



“Rocket.”



A pause, which he’s starting to think might mean she’s only going to get more over-the-top
with her misplaced affection.



“Love. Darling. Light-of-my-life.”



Yep. There it is.



He points at her warningly with her skinny soldergun, not looking up. “You’re really takin’
this ‘call me whatever you want’ thing to an extreme.”
“I have to make up for lost time,” she teases, but her voice is so damn soft. Slowly, she goes
still and solemn, smile fading. “Rocket. Look at me. Look at what you’re doing. If there’s
anyone on this ship who’s an artist, it’s you.”



It’s his turn to scoff, and he can do it with a lot more venom than she'll ever be capable of.
“Don’t gimme that bullshit - I don’t need your fuckin’ pity - “



“Rocket.”



Something in her voice is so incredulous - and so quiet - that his own words strangle out of
his mouth like a wisp of smoke. He wrangles an inhalation - he hadn’t realized his chest was
heaving for air, like his body thought he was already fighting for his life. Or running for it.



He surprises himself, in that it only takes two breaths to drag his lungs down into some
rhythm resembling normal.



And she’s waiting for him. Just waiting for him to come down.



Slowly, slowly, he turns his gaze to her. Her face is patient and sad and clear - like she’s
about to explain the simplest, most self-evident truth in the galaxy - and she’s looking at him
with those big earnest eyes that he knows, now, aren’t lying. Her voice is all soft disbelief.



“Rocket. You can make a…a gun from a paper clip, a bomb from a wet shoelace, and a hot
shower from a tin can. You can make a frisbee - that makes people fly - from…what, exactly?
Some scrap metal and a dream?”



He can’t help the snort that escapes him then, and he’s surprised by how much of it is made
up of harsh tatters of a laugh, surprised out of him against his will. But her voice persists. It’s
the softest, most stubborn fuckin’ cloud to ever float across his fur.
“Here you are, putting all the pieces together to create a home for us.”



He sucks in a hitching breath after all. Because that doesn’t sound right. That doesn’t sound
like what he’s doing. It doesn’t sound like anything he’s capable of. But she leans back, the
urgency in her gaze melting into something misty. She shrugs one shoulder dismissively, as if
it doesn’t matter to her. But the little, lopsided smile tugging at her mouth is bemused, and
her eyes are still sad, and clearly, clearly, it does matter to her.



“I just draw pictures, Rocket,” she says softly, spreading her palms wide. “What you do is
art.”



He wants to reject that. It’s almost a compulsion. It’s almost involuntary. Everything under
his ribs pushes it away. He wants to sneer, and to say what do you know?



But he also wants to say, you don’t just draw pictures - you see people, and he’s not even sure
what he means by that.



So he just swallows it all down, packing it tight between his left lung and his heart, and just
tries to ignore her for the next ten minutes till he trusts himself to think, to breathe, to blink,
to speak.



And then, still tangled up, he just quietly asks for the lightcutter back like it’s some kind of
shitty apology, and takes it when she hands it over.



She helps him finish up in the next forty minutes or so, and holds the wall panel while he
screws it back in place. He follows her back to their bunk - hesitant, his guts still knotted -
and they pass Quill on the way in. Rocket expects some snide comment from Star-Dork, but
Quill just nods distractedly and wishes them both a good night.



When they get inside and the door slides shut behind him, Rocket rubs the back of his neck
awkwardly before hazarding a glance up at Jo. She’s pulling her sleepshirt out of the little
box she’s tucked under the bed, and he immediately turns his back to her and looks at the
floor, unmoving. He can hear her, though - the whisper of fabric, the sound of her kicking off
her stupidly-flimsy boots.
“I’m done,” she says softly, and when he turns back and looks up, she’s carefully placing her
sensored glove and her black glass on an empty corner of his workbench for the night. He
pats the metal key plate in his own pocket absently, staring at them as she peels back the
blankets on the shelf-bed.



And then, so casually he can’t believe how easy the words come to her, she asks, “Are you
joining me?”



Maybe, if he weren’t caught up in feeling his own body flinch at her words, he'd have noticed
the flush of red in her cheeks - but he doesn’t.



“Uh,” he says, “I’m gonna take the hammock tonight.”



She pauses, almost imperceptibly, and then slides into bed, lying on her side to look at him.
“Is it more comfortable for you?” she asks, her voice ringing with genuine, soft curiosity.
“Do you sleep better in the hammock?”



“Than the bed?” He shrugs. “Sometimes.”



Than with you? Probably not.



He notices that she hasn’t bothered to take her hair down - it’s falling out of the oversized
bun, little shining rivulets on the pillow, but her neck is still bare above the gaping collar of
the sleep shirt. He wonders if she’s keeping her hair up because of what he’d said in his
stupid, unguarded moment - you should wear it like that more often - or because she thinks he
still might join her, and doesn’t want him touching it the way he had this morning. The
thought makes him just a little nervy, almost-borderline-regretful, almost-borderline-angry
and defensive. She almost always wears it loose, so he’s pretty sure it’s not just a
coincidence.



He shouldn’t’ve touched it, dammit. He’d known he should’ve kept his frickin’ hands to
himself.
She only hums, pulling the covers up and around her, one hand curled up next to her cheek.
“Okay,” she says mildly. “Well, the offer remains open.” She chews her lip. “Good night
then? I guess?”



“Uh, yeah,” he says, moving for the first time and sliding the dimmer for the overhead light
down. “Good night.” He doesn’t need the light of the plasma orb to see, so he gets changed in
the dark and then leaps up to the overhead hammock.



He spends the first few - minutes? hours? - replaying her little speech in the utility closet. His
mind tries to reconsider that she might be lying, she might be mocking him, but at this point
he’d have to tie himself in knots to believe that. She’s too stupid-sincere. She means
everything she says, even if he doesn’t understand how or why. For whatever reason, she
seems to continue remaining stubbornly unaware of just how much of a selfish frickin’
lowlife he is.



But if he hasn’t come to any reconciliation with his own degeneracy since escaping
CounterEarth, he isn’t going to now. In all likelihood, he knows better than anyone that he’s
gonna continue cycling between stealing fragments of conflicted almost-happiness, and then
spiraling into guilt and anxiety and probably - but hopefully not - that mean smallness he
retreats into when he’s trying to protect himself and everyone else around him.



He rolls over, and tries to quiet his mind.



And rolls over again.



Her breathing has slowed. When he glances over, he’s pretty sure she’s fallen asleep. He tries
to match his breathing to hers like she’d made him do the night before, but his brain keeps
churning and that pit behind his sternum keeps aching. He loses track of the breaths,
distracting himself with the knot of his own thoughts. He considers just getting up and going
back to the utility closet, or heading up to the common room and working on the Aero-Rig
while Groot and Drax play cards, or maybe bothering Quill. Reluctantly - because it feels
weird, it feels vulnerable - he puts a hand on his own chest and taps his clawed fingers
against his shoulder, trying to pace his lungs the way Jo had done.
Nope.



He rolls over. Again.



He could get up and take over the flying. Quill would let him, and then Rocket could come
back to bed after Jo was already up, and he’d barely have to see her.



He’s not sure if that would be better or worse.



After taking too long - too frickin’ long - to decide, he finally slides out of the hammock,
landing softly on the thin throw-rug beneath him. When he lifts his head, he’s on eye-level
with her - and yeah, she’s asleep, her dark lashes making crescents on her cheeks, hair still
messily piled at the crown of her head and rapidly losing its valiant fight with the artificial
gravity.



He hesitates. For a long time, he hesitates. He’d intended to quietly grab a bundle of jeweler’s
tools and the vial he’d stolen from the Collector, maybe screw around with pocket-dimension
tech in the cockpit or the common room, but -



She shifts and rolls; her back is to him now, and she’s utterly oblivious. He remembers that
first night, searching her bunk for weapons and anything else of use, hating her, staring at the
delicate butterfly-bones of her wrist and wanting to bite her - and something gnaws at his
insides. Still, he stays frozen - just a moment longer. The offer remains open, she’d said. And
he is a selfish lowlife, after all.



Carefully, he climbs onto the shelf-bed behind her, burrows under the covers, and curls up
against the small of her back.



He’s asleep in moments.

Jolie says nothing the next morning - he’s not even sure when she gets up. Somehow, she’s
managed to crawl out of the bed without waking him, and has left him buried in the warm
blankets, all of which smell like her. That powdery, honey-scented soap, and her stupid
curlflower tea. He blinks slowly, taking in the plasma orb’s half-light through the veil of
sheets. He’s pretty sure he’s never slept through someone else moving around so close.



By the time he heads up the ladder, Groot is waiting for him.



“I am Groot.”



“Whaddaya mean?”



The Flora Colossus shrugs emphatically and spreads his hands. “I am Groot.”



Rocket’s brow furrows, already half-furious, when Gamora storms out of the cockpit,
followed by Quill.



“Oh, good,” Gamora says. “Maybe you can talk some sense into him.”



Rocket blinks. “Quill?”



“No, stupid,” the Terran man scoffs, and Rocket bristles. “Drax.”



“I am Groot.”



As if on cue, the Kylosian storms out of the cockpit as well.
“Speak of the devil,” Quill grumbles. “Decided to stop bothering Jolie?”



“Jolie says I am not a bother,” Drax says firmly. “But she also says you are not cowards, so
perhaps she is not a good judge of character.”



“Unbelievable,” Rocket mutters, watching as the three of them begin arguing. He hoists

Groot anticipates him, passing him a handled, wide-mouthed mug full to the brim with

bitterness right now. He tosses it back - too hot. His tongue feels scraped and raw.



“I am Groot.”



“Little late on the warning, buddy.”



“- need to stop being so selfish,” Gamora is snapping, and it sets Rocket’s teeth on edge. “We

Rocket feels his ears twitch toward his friend in spite of himself. “She did?”



“I am Groot.” The Flora Colossus slides him a plate piled high with rehydrated eggs,

“Lay off, Conan,” Quill’s snapping. “We all need to take a breath. I’m not a fan of the

“I don’t need you defending me,” Gamora hisses at Quill.

“ENOUGH!” Rocket bellows, lurching up to stand on the stool. “I’m about two seconds

He points a clawed finger at Drax, who is gaping in sudden silence. “This ship - my ship - is
headin' to Asgard. Get that through your thick head, asshole.”



Drax looks startled, and lifts both hands as if he’s trying to measure the width of his skull.



Rocket points at Gamora. “You’re supposed to be the reasonable one of this bunch of
baldbodies,” he snarls. “If you been lettin’ them two idiots scream like this over Jolie’s head

“And you,” Rocket drops his hand, but he’s fully glowering at Quill, eye-level with the

“Are you children?” he asks softly, borrowing from Jolie’s habit of unnervingly hostile
