anything bad - and you find out that the worst has already happened to them. It makes you
feel powerless. And mad. And all sorts of other things.” Quill pauses meaningfully. “I know,
okay? And I’m with you.”

Rocket had thought he was prepared for anything, but the words still make him flinch.
There’s a softening in Quill’s voice, similar to Jo’s. Rocket wonders if this is a Terran thing:
to go all quiet and tender at a moment’s notice. It had been unnerving when Jolie had done it
at the beginning of their friendship, but it’s even worse coming from Quill, who’s normally
such an ass.

Terrans aren’t good at much, but it seems like they’re exceptionally talented at making
Rocket like them. Even against his better judgment.

He hesitates.

Quill, in his typically-annoying fashion, notices.

“We can’t go back and fix things for each other. No matter how much we might want to. All
we can do is try to make today better.”

Rocket sighs, then snorts, but the sound isn’t as derisive as he’d been hoping for. He just
sounds tired. “You always give the most useless pep talks, Quill. I know better’n any of you
morons that I don’t get to go back.”
“Have a drink with me later,” Quill urges. “Once you’re done… you know, taking care our
Earthgirl. It can be good just to sit with someone who gets it, Rocket.”

Our. The word sounds good in Rocket’s ears, and he hates it.

He clears his throat. “Everybody’s got dead people,” he says instead, breaking the silence
with a callousness that borders on brutal. It’s the same thing he’d yelled at Drax after Asgard,
but it feels crueler - to shatter this rare moment of camaraderie with it, to dismiss what Jo had
shared.

“Yeah, okay, sure,” Quill replies flatly. His expression, looking down at Rocket, is
surprisingly shrewd. “Wanna know what I think?”

“Abso-frickin-lutely not.”

“I think you tell yourself that whenever someone’s got a story that makes you feel something,
or that reminds you that you still have a heart. I think you say it to try to remind yourself not
to care.”

Rocket feels his lips peel away from his teeth. “Shut the fuck up, Quill.”

The idiot in question raises his hands, palm out. “Look, I’m just saying - “

“I mean it,” Rocket interrupts, and he’s glad that he can shape his voice into such a threat,
such a warning.

The blond hesitates.

“You’re remindin’ me of all the reasons we’d be better off without each other.”

“Dude,” Quill says incredulously. “D’you really think that? After what the six of us were able
to do together?”

Rocket’s lip curls back in a silent snarl, but he can’t think of anything to say that isn’t the
spilling out of a story he himself isn’t ready to tell.

“...No,” Quill answers himself slowly, blue eyes widening in disbelief. “No, you think we’d
be better off without you.”

Rocket’s stomach twists and his heart thuds against his metal ribs. When did this frickin’
jackass get so insightful?

“You really think that,” Quill repeats, and leans forward to peer at Rocket. “That’s not - you
know we couldn’t do any of this without you, right? You’re our…our weapons specialist and
our mechanic and our tactician. Half of our captain. And you’re…you. We like you - even
when you’re being a pain in the ass. We care about you.”

Rocket wants to vomit. Not in a sarcastic, this-is-too-sappy-for-words way, either: he is
legitimately concerned that he’s gonna hurl on the airlock floor. Nausea and anxiety suddenly
swirl high in his belly. “I’m gonna puke on your boots.”
Quill, of course, interprets this as hyperbole and ignores him. “And Jolie…Jolie would not be
okay without you.”

Rocket tries to quell the rebellion in his stomach and snorts derisively instead. There’s a long
silence - the longest so far - between them. And then Quill breaks it, his voice quiet.

“She’s happy with you,” the Terran says softly. “She trusts you to look out for her. I mean,
she knows you always have her back in a fight, but…she told me once you found her crying
one night, and you just sat with her. She said she was pretty sure you ‘hated her guts’ - a
direct quote - but you sat with her anyway.”

Quill pauses - hesitates. Then plunges onward.

“She loves you a lot, you know. The things she says about you - I don’t know if I’ve ever
heard someone talk about another person like that. I don’t know what I’d give to hear
someone talk about me that way.”

“No-one said she was smart,” Rocket sneers, and immediately regrets it. But Quill eyes him
measuringly, as if Rocket has just confirmed whatever the Terran thinks he’s figured out.

“What - you really believe that, buddy?”

Rocket grimaces. Of course not. Or at any rate, it had been an oversimplification. Jo is
frickin’ brilliant when it comes to certain things, and a moron when it comes to others, just
like Rocket himself. She at least seems to know how to be a person better than he does.

He looks over his shoulder again, out the airlock bay, in the direction of the bridge and the
cockpit. He really needs to -

“Things don’t mean the same to Jo that they do to other people,” Quill’s saying. For fuck’s
sake, the Terran does not shut up. “I’m gonna tell you a secret.”

“Oh perfect,” Rocket mutters drily. “Then can I leave?”

Quill ignores him, of course. “When her sister was born, Jolie was still like - a little kid. I
think their parents were…hard people, and she’d always wished she’d had someone to look
out for her. And so, the baby came along, and Jolie said, I’m going to be everything I wanted
in an older sister.

“And then, you know - everything happened. I won’t share the details - that’s her story to tell.
I just - I don’t think she realizes it, but I don’t think she ever stopped… trying to do that thing
she’d done for her kid sister. I don’t think she ever stopped saying, I’m going to be the person
I needed. I’m gonna find every lost, lonely sonuvabitch out there in the cold universe, and I’m
gonna take care of ‘em.”

Rocket swallows, and glances over his shoulder again.

“Which makes the two of us into lucky bastards,” Quill continues, “but, uh, you know. She’s
not always good at being the things she needs for herself. No,” Quill corrects himself, “I take
that back. She’s consistently shit at it. So, when I say she trusts you to look out for her - it’s a
big deal. And it’s not something she lets just anyone do. Not unless they’ve earned it.”

It makes Rocket’s throat tighten, and he has to swallow around the lump there. I ain’t earned
anything, he thinks bitterly. But Quill’s looking at him curiously, like even he doesn’t believe
that anymore. Like he thinks maybe Rocket deserves to be at her side, after all.

At their side. Part of the family.

And that’s new. That’s the first time he’s felt a kind of almost-belonging in ages. It would be,
hypothetically, the first time he’s allowed himself to have a family since he’d gotten the last
one killed.

It’s dangerous.

They’d all be better off, he thinks, if they’d just leave him behind somewhere.

++++

Once he manages to extricate himself from Quill’s annoying grasp, he heads directly to the
cockpit. Jo’s framed up against the beads of light, a silhouette with a bare throat and shoulder,
and a pile of ridiculous shiny hair on top of her head. Between the stars and the control panel,
her skin is slicked with silver. Now he remembers where he’s seen her wearing that
expression earlier. In the cockpit - that night he’d found her limned in gold, painting with
light, her cheeks and collarbone drenched in tears.

Right before he’d called her a sniveling, spoiled, entitled brat.

The memory punches him in the gut and he’s back to considering whether or not he’s gonna
vomit on the floor of his own damn ship.

Jo’s not crying now, though. Not yet, anyway.

His jaw works. What to say?

I came looking for you.

I was worried.

Do you want to come home?

He strides to the copilot’s chair, hesitates, and then leans against it, crossing one foot over the
other and folding his hands into his pockets. He eyes her for a long moment. She tucks her
fingertips against her lip like she wants to chew them off, but she says nothing.

“We gonna talk about this, sweetheart?”

She chuckles, eyes on the windshield before her. “Not with you looking at me like that.”
For a moment, he bristles. Breathes. Smooths it out. Remembers the hundred times she’d
opened her mouth last night and said nothing.

He slides into his seat, and trains his eyes on the stars too. “Now?”

She sighs - not heavily or dramatically. Not even reluctantly. It’s just a tired sort of
exhalation, like she’s so exhausted her lungs can’t hold onto air anymore.

“I’m sorry,” she says to the windshield.

Why does every word she says hurt so much lately?

“I should’ve told you,” she says placidly. “I promised you I would tell you, and even Pete
told me to tell you, and I kept putting it off. Because…it’s a long, dumb story.” A puff of a
cynical, self-deprecating laugh. “And because I didn’t want to tell it.”

He swallows. She doesn’t move, and he gropes for some question to ask, something
innocuous. “When’d you promise me that?”

“You asked why Pete knew I’d go with you, after Knowhere,” she says, her voice even and
controlled. “Why I’d followed you when you left the cockpit.” She clears her throat. “Pete
knows enough about me to know, in that moment, I couldn’t…I would not have let you out of
my sight, not if I could help it. Not right then, not right after the explosion, after I’d
thought...” She shifts apologetically, like she knows he didn’t ask for this and like she expects
him to be annoyed.

That hurts too.

Then she tries to drag some cheerfulness into her wrung-out voice. “He’s such a bastard.”

“Well, yeah,” he deadpans, and she starts to laugh, but it cuts off with a ragged sound and
she’s back to just staring out at the flight path to Sovereign.

“So,” he utters at last, “d’you wanna tell me now?”

The silence drags on for such a long time. She takes a breath like she’s going to start, and
then stops. Twice she opens her mouth, and nothing comes out. She exhales in frustration.
Her eyes flicker over to him for the first time, anxiously, like she’s looking for an escape, and
then she’s looking away again. “Are you sure you want to waste your time listening to this?”

“Yeah,” he says quietly.

Her teeth are embedded in her lip. He’s surprised it hasn’t started bleeding. She stares at the
stars and he wonders if she’s seeing them at all.

Something in her unravels abruptly, then pulls back. It’s like watching the collapse of a sun:
bright everywhere, and then crushed down into dense matter. He can feel the air change.
She’s usually an open book, and so when she draws up her defenses, it feels different.
“Short version,” she says, and her voice is determined and hard-edged and utterly unlike her.
“I had a sister. She died. I have a lot of feelings about it and I’m not trying to make them your
problem.” She shrugs like a corpse.

This idiot makes me breathe with her every other frickin’ night, Rocket says to himself, and
shakes his head in incredulous annoyance.

“I want the long version,” he tells her flatly. “Normally I can’t get you to shut up. Don’t
cheap out on me now, doll.”

Another startled, half-broken laugh. “I don’t - I can’t - “

He’s not good at gentle. He’s not good at making his voice all soft and comforting and
blanket-like, the way she does. Jo has a voice a person could build a nest in when he’s
hurting, a voice he could make a home in if he needed to, and Rocket doesn’t know how to
give that back to her. So he clears his throat again instead, and tries to just speak quiet and
slow. He gropes for the words as he goes, because he’s never, ever said them before. They
hurt in his mouth, stick in his teeth. He swipes at his lips, trying to cover anything that might
be scared and trembling.

“Ya know. I, uh. I had a sister once.”

It comes out raw and bloody. He should’ve known it would’ve.

For a second, everything roars in his ears: the vacuum of space, the rasp of his lungs, his
pulse in his veins. He swears, for a minute, that he can hear the infrasonic hum of the stars.
But he sees her hands soften on the yoke, and he hangs onto that: the light touch, and the
knuckles like pearls under her skin: slicked with the wet silver-gold of cockpit lights.

“Oh,” she whispers, and she’s already got that tender, aching tone in her voice. “Oh.”

He clenches his fists. The nails pierce the leathery dark skin there, and he holds onto that
feeling, too. “What - uh. What was your sister’s name?”

“Rocket,” she murmurs, in a tone that clearly says, you don’t have to do this. He can see her
gaze skate sideways to his hands. He forces his fingers to relax - presses his bleeding palms
to the thighs of his jumpsuit. He tries to scrape a snicker out of his throat.

“Princess. I know it wasn’t Rocket.”

That bruised little smile flickers at the corner of her mouth again. She lets out a slow,
shuddering breath: one, two, three, four. He’s reminded that she probably learned her little
counting and tapping trick for herself, long before she’d whispered it to him in the warmth of
their shared cocoon.

“Oh, love,” she says gently. Achingly. She smiles a little. “You already know it.”

He feels his ears flatten against his skull.

Stupid.
Of course.

“Gemma Lynn,” he says.

“I mostly just called her Gemma,” she admits. She shrugs and casts him a tentative, sideways
little smile. An invitation. “What was your sister’s name?” The words are so soft he knows he
could pretend not to hear them, and she’d forgive him for it, even though she'd know it was a
lie.

He opens his mouth, and chokes. Tries again.

“Her name was Floor.”

The words hover and float: little iridescent bubbles. Fragile. Full of reflected light.

The ghost of a sad smile haunts Jolie’s lips. “Pretty,” she says.

He blinks: baffled right out of his grief for a second. “What?”

She tilts her head, brows slanting slightly with confusion. “Flor? Like, flower? It’s pretty.”

He stares at her for a second, wondering if his translation chip is on the fritz.

And then - he feels it. Foreign and shocking and irrepressible, forcing its way upward from
under his chest. He laughs. Actually laughs, loud and long and hard. And yeah, sure, maybe
every feeling is getting caught on the next one till they’re just a tangled spiral of grief and
rage and shame and guilt, but at least one of those emotions is something like relief, like
release, like one good memory just got plucked up from the wasteland of his life and revived,
however briefly.

Exactly like a frickin’ flower.

Jo’s looking at him, all perplexed and worried and biting her lip. He wipes the tears from his
eyes and he’s not sure if they’re tears of loss or tears of laughter or tears of something else
entirely, but it feels like something in him has cracked open - and not in an entirely bad way.

“No,” he says at last, still chuckling. “Floor like floor.” He points.

Her eyes widen. “Oh,” she says, and then she’s smiling at him uncertainly, shrugging. “Well,
it’s… still pretty?”

“She’d like that,” he tells Jo without thinking, and he’s still grinning in spite of himself - still
crying, too. “She’d like that you thought that - all a’ that.”

It doesn’t feel weird when he says it - it just feels honest, and clean. But the reality sweeps in
just as quick and just as hard the moment the words are hovering in the air. Floor would like
you, if she was here. But she ain’t. And that’s my fault.

He looks at Jo in the dim light of the cockpit. Tilts his head and studies her. Yeah. Floor
would like Jo. Floor would love her, the way Floor loved everything. And then some.
“I never said,” he concedes to the shadows, to the light fluttering over her features. “Not even
- not even to Groot. I didn’t think - “ What? That he could speak a memory into existence
without bleeding from the mouth? That their names wouldn’t become broken teeth, spat on
the floor and lost to him forever? That he’d ever be able to say anything about any of them,
and laugh?

She waits, but he doesn’t know what comes next. The silence lays thick and heavy, but it
feels like it’s supposed to. They both let it.

Eventually, Jo makes her thoughtful little hum. “I think - for me, anyway. I, like, press all
these scraps of what happened - down into a singularity. Because even though it’s… too
much matter, it’s the only way to keep it all small enough to take with me wherever I go. And
if I… “ she lifts one hand off the yoke to make an opening gesture with her fingers, like she’s
releasing a bird or letting go of a butterfly. “…if I say one thing, all the rest of it is no
longer… under my control?” She tilts her head, gnawing that stupid lip of hers. “And yeah,
part of me is worried I’ll, like, lose it - “ she points an index finger to her temple and rolls her
eyes “ - but a bigger part of me is afraid I’ll, like, lose it.” She presses her fingers into her
sternum like she’s trying to dig her own heart out, and he can see her little oval nails sink into
the skin there, hard enough that he knows they’ll leave red crescent moons behind when she
drops them.

Rocket’s mouth is so dry he thinks his tongue might crack, and his eyes are so wet they might
overflow again. “Yeah,” he utters, and tries to make it sound casual. “How d’you know
they’re still there if it don’t hurt?”

Jo hums again, and the shadows fall long and quiet between them, nested in wreaths of
control panel lights. They sit: quiet. Tired. Not-alone, together.

“Yeah, but,” she whispers at last, into the wreath of cockpit lights. Her voice is soft and
regretful.

“But?”

Her lips twist apologetically. “I don’t want you to have to be hurting.”

He wants to scoff. Fuck, she’s so soft he could wrap himself up in her and call it home.
Instead, all that comes out is a kind of annoyed, groaning sigh. The feeling’s mutual,
sweetheart.

“Well,” he says slowly, “I’m still a nosy frickin’ jackass and I still wanna know what
happened.” He hazards a glance over at her, and she looks pale - but not horrified. He claws
the words out of his voicebox before he can rethink them. “Maybe we trade.”

Her eyes flick to him, then back to the stars. “It’s a lot to tell at once,” she cautions, like she
has experience. “It’s a lot to hear at once.”

He shrugs, and tries to act like it’s not a big deal. It is a big deal - a thing he’d never thought
he’d offer anyone - but he remembers Jo on the streets of Conjunction, and Jo sharing his
breath, and he thinks he can do it. Probably. Maybe.
“A memory for a memory,” he says. “From, you know. Before.”

She’s silent for a long time - so long he starts to get nervous.

“You’re sure?” she asks at last, voice like a little dove.

He snorts. “No.”

Then she’s laughing - soft and maybe a bit ragged, but it’s there and it’s real, and he can feel
something warm and flickering answer from his chest.

“I’ll try if you try,” she tells him, and the words are light and feathery. “Just a little bit at a
time.”

“Yeah. Yeah, okay.” Time to get away. For both of their sakes. “You need some frickin’
breakfast,” he tells her, and moves to slide from his seat.

“Wait,” she says urgently, and he freezes for a moment, still poised on the edge of the
copilot’s chair. “I… I owe you.”

He feels his brow furrow in confusion. “What?”

“You’ve… “ She chews her lips. “You’ve said things before. I know you think I’m an idiot
but I notice. I pay attention.”

He doesn’t think she’s an idiot. Not about most stuff. Not anymore. But she doesn’t need to
know that.

She lets out a shaky breath. “I know that, whatever happened, it’s more than just the loss of
them that…that hurts you.” Her mouth twists to one side, all concern. “There’s nothing you
can’t tell me, if you want to, Rocket. There’s nothing that’s going to change my mind about…
who you are.”

Some part of him disconnects for a minute and everything seems foamy and surreal.

My body ain’t my own, and it never has been. They marked me down to my guts. I’ll never be
really away from ‘em because they took some of my bones out of me and they might still have
‘em - these pieces of me - and sometimes that skeleton comes tapping on the bunk door at
night.

He thinks about telling her this - but she already knows, doesn’t she? Or something close to
it. She’s seen. He’s pretty sure she’d heard it shouted at her from the streets in Conjunction.

My whole family is dead because of me, he thinks instead, ‘cause I couldn’t keep a lid on my
impulses, on my teeth and my claws. Because I had to hurt Him. Because I was selfish.
Because I ain’t good at looking out for anything that isn’t my own skin.

But she kinda knows that too, doesn’t she? He’d said as much after the Kyln. And again, after
Xandar.
“Rocket,” she says, and he comes back into his mangled body to look at her, to hear her. It
sounds like she’s carving out a piece of herself to share with him, bloody and raw. Her voice
has to be cut from her ribs before it makes it into the air.

“The worst part of my sister’s death is all the things she’ll never get to do, all the happiness
she’ll never get to feel.” She breathes: one, two, three, four. “The second-worst part is that
I’m responsible for it.”

I don’t believe that.

The words punch up from his gut so quickly that he doesn’t know how he keeps ‘em behind
his teeth, but he does.

And it probably doesn’t matter what he believes, anyway - not right now.

Rocket’s particular brand of genius may not be at its strongest when it comes to matters of
emotionalistic intelligence, but he knows what this is. I owe you. A memory for a memory,
backdated. The very worst parts, already out in the open. Whatever you think of yourself, I
won’t judge you. ‘Cause I’m there too.

He finishes his slide out of the copilot’s chair, and when he passes between the seats, he
pauses. Hesitates. Reaches out and lays a hand on the skin of her shoulder where it slopes
above the sweatshirt-collar, never mind how his clawed fingers look against all that softness.
Her skin is cool from the air in the cockpit, and it warms under his touch.

He slides his hand away as he heads to the kitchen.

++++

Rocket brings her a mug of tea, and it’s perfect.

Jolie has had time to pick up stupid hobbies in the last four years, since she’d been left
suddenly purposeless in the wake of learning of her sister’s death. There had been one time -
god, before the Kyln? - she had been chattering endlessly to fill a begrudging copilot’s
silence: the water needs to be a certain temperature to avoid scalding the curlflower petals,
timing is essential to prevent bitterness or acidity, her personally-preferred proportions of
milk and honey, blah blah blah. Truthfully, she’d just been talking to talk - and despite their
tentative truce at the time, Rocket had looked like he was seriously contemplating strangling
her to get her to shut the fuck up.

But he must’ve remembered.

Unless he’s secretly a tea master, despite - she’s almost certain - never making a single damn
cup before in their entire time together. Christ, it might be better than she makes it herself,
and how is that fair?

She’s surprised herself over the last rotation. She hasn’t felt the urge to cry at all - she’s only
felt hollow, gutted, empty. Scared, sometimes - of what, exactly, she isn’t sure. Of putting it
all into words again, probably.
And especially of putting it into words for Rocket.

But something about this perfect, careful cup of tea and the ghost of his hand on her shoulder
- she’s gone from brittle and tight to soft and pliant in a span of minutes. This kindness - the
unconditional quality of it, the pervasiveness of it - might end up being what brings her to
tears after all.

He’s so damn good, and she loves him so damn much.

She keeps her eyes straight ahead or bowed into her mug, hoping he doesn’t notice if they’re
extra-shiny right now.

He leaves again - comes back with a single plate of moonfish and taro, and a bowl of
rehydrated fruit for them to share. Like the old days, she thinks, and everything in her feels
like a very soft sigh.

She drinks the tea, slowly and gratefully, but she can barely pick at the food. She feels like
she’s been scraped out and strung up in the garage like the deer her father used to hunt, and
she’s too tired to even go through the motions of survival if it means actually having to put
food in her mouth.

Of course Rocket’s sharp eyes don’t miss a thing, but he doesn’t say a word.

When he gathers up the dishes to cart them back to the kitchen, Jolie reaches out. Usually
she’s intentionally slow in her movements - not that she thinks she’s likely to take him by
surprise anyway. But her brain is so fried at this point that she doesn’t think: just sweeps her
hand out as he passes her. Her fingers hook gently into the inside of his elbow, almost like
she’s searching for a pulse, and he freezes with his arms balancing flatware and silverware
and mugs.

“Rocket,” she says, and for a second, she thinks he shivers. God, he makes her feel so much.
Her mouth tilts like a secret. “What did I do to deserve having a friend like you?”

“Must’ve been something awful,” he snarks immediately, and then flinches like he hit a
button he didn’t know was there. His ears flatten, and she sees his tail flick nervously against
his ankles. “I didn’t mean - “

She huffs a little laugh of her own, spiderweb-cracked, but real. “Relax. It’s fine. I’m fine.”
She chews her lip, though, and doesn’t let him go. “Since you seem to have a lot of good will
toward me right now, though, I’ll ask for a favor.”

His ears shift forward attentively. “What?”

“Stop being so fuckin’ mean to yourself.”

He breathes out: something a little too condescending to be a sigh, but too gentle to be a
snort. “You’re one to talk. Someday I’m gonna sit down and tell you just what - “ he cuts
himself off, clicks his tongue impatiently, and then shakes his head like he’s annoyed at
himself. When his voice comes back, it’s bent at the edges, like the words don’t fit well in his
mouth. He says them anyway. “How lucky I am.”

Then he slides a step sideways, out of reach of her light fingers, and past the bridge.

It doesn’t take him long to return. They sit quietly together, watching the star systems and
nebulae spiral by, for hours. They’ve tended to spend their spare time in the cockpit together
anyway - since always, Jolie supposes, even before he’d been able to stand her - but now he’s
sitting beside her with an almost preternatural stillness. No tinkering, no talking. No getting
up to stretch out the hips and back and arms she knows are sore - take a quick stroll around
the ship, annoy Pete if he’s still up, grab a shower or a nap or work on something in his bunk
or the utility closet. No, today Rocket isn’t doing so much as flexing his fingers.

“You don’t have to stay, you know,” she tries to offer up gently, halfway through her shift.
“Go rest. Move. Get a snack. Or at least get something to entertain yourself.”

“Nah,” Rocket says flatly, sounding utterly disinterested in the prospect.

“But - “

“Jo.” He only says her name, but it’s enough to bring her protests stuttering to a halt. Her
eyes travel from the windshield to his face. She can see the beginnings of a scowl there.

He’s got no intention of going anywhere.

There’s something so reassuring about his annoyance, like the thought of him leaving her for
even the few minutes to go get a gravi-grenade to fuck around with is so outrageous. Still -

“You really don’t have to stay, Rocket.”

His fingers do twitch then, claws tapping a staccato rhythm on the armrest between them. “If
I didn’t leave you on Asgard with Ronan, there’s no way I’m leavin’ you right now,” he
grumbles irritably, like she’s already annoying the fuck out of him.

Can’t fool me, she thinks. She knows he can tell she doesn’t want to be alone.

She flicks her eyelids shut again, never mind the starry road before them, because yeah, it’s
gonna be his kindness that fucks her up before the end of the rotation. She can see it coming
from a hundred jump-points away.

By the time he takes over, she’s yawning and achy, and why is this hitting her so hard,
anyway? Rocket seems - fine. Well, as fine as he ever is, which is arguably not fine at all. But
he’d probably slept almost as poorly as she had last night, and he’d shared just as much of
himself. And she knows how hard that had to be for him. But there he is, seemingly unfazed -
and here she is, bruised and emptied out on the cockpit floor.

She makes them both a mid-rotation meal, and she can see him watching her from the corner
of his eyes as she picks up a forkful of food, pauses, and then sets it back on the plate. Moves
it around a little. Tries again. Fails again.
She’s so tired. She just wants to shift herself down on the cold ground right now, and lean her
head against Rocket’s thigh, and sleep there tonight. She’d do it if she thought it wouldn’t
make him wildly uncomfortable. Instead, she closes her eyes again, props her elbow on the
armrest and her chin on her fist, and tries to lose herself in the hum of the engines and her
own heartbeat.

“You should go to bed, princess,” he tells her an hour later, but he already sounds
exasperated, like he knows it’s a lost cause. “Quill’ll be around soon anyway. Just tell him to
come up early. He said somethin’ about - he said somethin’ earlier. Maybe I can tolerate him
for a few hours now.”

She blinks at him placidly. “Nope.”

She curls up in the chair next to him, knees bent and feet tucked next to her ass. And yeah,
god - yeah, she can barely think at this point. But this is the rest of her bullshit, right? Let
someone she loves out of her line of sight for five minutes, and they’re gone forever. Never
mind that a few hours earlier she’d been trying to get him to go take care of himself.

Instead of making sense, she ends up slowly sinking into the pilot’s chair, becoming one with
it in a way that she hasn’t done since those first few years in space, when she’d worried that
taking her eyes off the windshield for a half-minute would result in her waking up back in her
apartment at home, the escape and pursuit all just a dream. Feet still tucked, she leans one
forearm on the armrest, then rolls the side of her cheek onto her fist. Eventually, her other
arm joins the first, and she shifts till she’s sitting on her hip - like this terrible bucket seat is
the galaxy’s worst chaise lounge. Eyes heavy-lidded, she sinks lower, quietly crumpling into
herself like a ball of paper: resigned and ready to be thrown away. She presses her temple
into her folded forearms - body draped over one armrest and under the other - and she tries to
keep her eyes open: watching the stars, watching his face, watching his hands.

They’re so gentle as they cradle the yoke.

She dozes drowsily, fading in and out. Tattered dreams flutter at the edges of her eyes: stars
and jump-points, stowaways and datapads, the narrow hands and bright eyes of her copilot,
the ghost of her sister flickering into a golden haze. It’s long minutes - maybe hours - and
then she feels a slight frisson along her scalp, so unexpected and intimate that it startles a
half-shiver out of her before the sensation turns to a sharp jerk. That wakes her up, and her
eyes fly wide open and she whips her head up to face her copilot. Gamora’s in his seat and
he’s standing beside her, a lock of her hair pinned between his fingers. Thanks to how she’s
fallen asleep across her chair, they’re eye level, and he raises a brow at her sardonically. His
other arm is cradling a supply of orloni sticks and dried seaweed packs.

Did he just pull my hair? Jolie thinks blankly. As she stares, he gives it another experimental
tug, and she yelps.

“What was that for?”

“Up, sweetheart,” he orders, and she doesn’t think twice, unfolding herself like a rumpled
quilt. The sudden shift has her light-headed, joints whining.
She imagines he feels it too. These days, she’s pretty sure she can tell when he’s in more pain
than usual - there’s something different about the way he carries himself. She’s overcome by
the fleeting, melancholic desire to massage away whatever aches she can, to ask if he’ll let
her tonight.

It would feel nice. To give him something back when he’s been so careful with her for these
last two rotations. To give him something back when he’s tried so hard to help her that he’d
given up a little piece of the story she knows he hasn’t told anyone else.

Without a word, though, he’s herding her back toward the bridge. She calls out a scattered do
you need anything? - good night! to Gamora right as Pete passes them to join the Zen-

bumping against the back of Jolie’s thighs, propelling her to the hatch and then down into the
lower levels of the Gemma Lynn before she can distract herself with her habitual caretaking.
As they pass the bathroom stalls, she makes an apologetic hum and ducks in.

She takes her time. Washes her hands, and rinses her face with cool water from the tap,
pressing her fingertips against her closed eyelids and trying to clean away some of her
exhaustion. When she looks in the mirror, she notes distantly that she looks haggard: ashen,
lips bruised from being bitten, purple shadows under hunted eyes. She cracks a grim, self-
deprecating smile, then steps out.

He’s waiting when she gets into the hallway, propped lazily against the wall: shoulders
leaning and hipbones jutting forward, half-lidded eyes, arms crossed over his chest and
snacks tucked into one loose fist.

He straightens when she exits, gesturing with his chin, and she falls into step beside him.

“I can get myself into bed, you know,” she says - trying for lightness as if her whole body
isn’t leaden with exhaustion, and as if she doesn’t melt over his brusque way of taking care of
her.

“I don’t trust you,” he says flatly. “Have you eaten or drank anything today?”

“You made me tea,” she reminds him, and he glares.

“Sit,” he directs, and she perches on the edge of the shelf bed. “Good girl,” he mutters under
his breath, and hops up on the edge of the workbench, sitting there so that they’re facing each
other at a diagonal. He grabs a waterbag from the stash he keeps on the desktop, stabs the
metal straw into it like it’s a Capri Sun from her childhood, and hands it to her so he can open
the snackfoods. She drinks obediently, and when he hands her an open orloni stick, she
passes the water back to him.

“Your turn,” she says evenly. “You’ve been with me all day, so I know you haven’t been
staying hydrated or eating much, either.”

His eyes flicker from the water and back to her. He hesitates, cocking his head in some kind
of unspoken question she doesn’t understand. For a second, he looks almost anxious, then
tucks the straw into the side of his mouth, clamps it there with his teeth, and drinks.
She leans back and takes a bite of the orloni before accepting the water back from him and
drinking deep. Something in him visibly relaxes when she does, and some distant part of her
thinks briefly that maybe he’d been nervous she wouldn’t want to share a straw with him. She
dismisses the thought as soon as it rises, thinking she must be mistaken - after all, they’d
been eating off the same plate since their first rotation together.

They sit for a moment, passing food and water between themselves until the makeshift meal
is completed. It’s mostly silent, other than the crinkle of wrappings, but it feels
companionable. Most silences between them do, these days.

With their little feast concluded, Rocket bundles up the wrappers and tucks them into the
empty water bag, setting them and the metal straw aside on a cleared edge of his workbench.

“I’ll get those in the compressor in the morning,” he tells her, watching her off-handedly as
he springs from his perch onto the shelf-bed. He’s sidling behind her, almost cautiously, like
he’s waiting for an indication that she doesn’t want him there.

Jolie couldn’t care less that he’s circling her. She trusts him implicitly. To be honest, if she
were feeling better, she might be having different feelings about it altogether - something
closer to excitement and heat, especially after his careless good girl comment a few moments
earlier.

And yeah, she knows that’s entirely fucked up, but she’ll berate herself for it later, when she
has more energy.

She stops caring when she feels him come up close behind her, and she sits very still, waiting
for whatever he’s doing. Nevertheless, she’s startled to feel a shaky exhalation on the back of
her neck, and then a tickle on her scalp at the crown of her head. There’s a gentle tug and he’s
unsnapped the fastener at the base of her bun. She sees the alien hair-tie, made of two pins
and a stretchy ribbon of fabric that buckles into place, get tossed onto the workbench too.
Then her hair is cascading down her back.

In the course of a normal day, she never notices the pressure of the enormous, messy
ballerina-buns she’s taken to wearing regularly. But she knows Rocket has watched her take it
down in the evenings: groaning at the sudden release of tension on her skull, sometimes
burrowing her fingers through her mane to massage the back of her head. Now, with the
loosening of her hair, she feels her shoulders instinctively relax. Her eyes flutter closed and
she bows her head, suddenly even more spent than before.

And then, more surprising still, she feels his hands mimic her own nighttime routine:
carefully working through the sheets of her hair, clawed fingers lightly skating over her scalp.

She tries to stifle her moan but she must make some sort of sound because he falters, and she
can feel his anxiety spike.

“Please don’t stop,” she murmurs instinctively.

The pause lasts just a second longer and then he resumes, not saying a word.
Tears prickle behind her eyelids again. She tries to remember a time in her life when anyone
has shown her this kind of tenderness, and she can’t. So she just holds herself very still,
letting him ease his fingers along the back of her head.

“You should get changed,” he says at last, gruffly, and she feels the thin mattress shift as he
steps back.

She doesn’t think twice. She just sits up and begins wriggling out of her sweatshirt - this one
reads I don’t have enough serotonin for this shit, and it feels particularly apt today - and she’s
in her sports bra before she hears the strangled sound Rocket’s making behind her.

Oops, she thinks blankly, and grabs up her button-down from where she’d tucked it under the
pillow this morning.

“Sorry, sorry,” she says hurriedly, flushing. She dives into the sleepshirt, bra and all. “Sorry.
I’m a fucking mess.”

“It’s fine,” he mutters distractedly, and if she’d been more alert, she might’ve noticed some
extra raspiness in his voice. He’s moved further away though, and when she looks over her
shoulder, she can see he’s retreated to the foot of the bed. “Just, uh, get comfortable.”

He jumps off the bed, rummaging in a drawer for his own extra pajama pants and making a
show of not looking at her while she wrestles herself out of bra and leggings.

She’s suddenly very grateful to have been so emotionally fucked-up that she hadn’t reacted to
his muttered good girl or his breath on the back of her neck. She knows now, beyond a
shadow of a doubt, that she would’ve given herself away and made her poor copilot so
fucking uncomfortable. She apologizes again.

“I’m sorry -“

“Shut it,” he snaps, and his voice is hard and harsh around the edges. Her brow dips
worriedly, but she climbs cautiously under the covers, making room for him on the shelf-bed.
He must be able to hear when she’s tucked in, because he turns around and sets the plasma
orbs to dim, changes quickly in the dark, and then climbs in after her.

She’s grateful he’s joined her, despite her weird-ass behavior tonight. However, there’s still
the possibility he’ll be too irritated to welcome her usual, casual stroking along his shoulders,
around the tender flesh of his scars, over his head - not that she could blame him.

In what must be the tenth shocking moment of the day, though, he doesn’t curl under the
covers at all like she’s used to.

He moves toward her, the same as last night, and reaches for her with one hand.

“C’mere,” he says, and before she can fully register what’s happening, he’s tucking her face
against the fur of his throat and shoulder again, his long chin and narrow jaw resting lightly
atop her head.
  Her eyes are leaking again, goddammit. Yeah. It was always going to be the kindness that
  undid her.

  She’s used to everything else.

  This time she’s too tired to fully blink the tears away. Her breath hitches unexpectedly, almost
  a sob, and she strangles it back.

  “Hey - what the hell - ?” He jerks back, looking down at her in the darkness. She imagines, if
  she could see him, that he’s looking alarmed and maybe even horrified. Now she has to
  fucking apologize again.

  “Sorry,” she says, trying not to sniffle. “It’s just - goddammit.” She can’t stop the crying now
  and she’s pulling back too, bringing her hands up to scrub at her wet face, hard.

  “Whoa. Whoa.” His clawed fingers snag her wrists, stilling them. “You’re so frickin’ rough

  She chokes back something like a laugh, something like a whimper. “You just take such good

  There’s a long silence, and she’s trying to hold back these stupid tears and she can’t, so she

  She hiccups, just once.

  “Fuck,” he says flatly, and he’s pulling her back in before she realizes it. Both arms are
  wound around her now: one pillowing her head and the other small, clawed hand pressing

  “I don’t want to get your fur wet,” she protests, her voice cracking. She wiggles against him,
  trying to make space, but he’s surprisingly strong and he holds her steady against him.

  “Knock it off,” he rumbles. “And get ready.”

  She stills. “For what?”

  He sighs, and she feels his claws comb through her hair delicately.

  “I’m gonna tell you about pocket-dimension tech, I guess.”

   Jolie wakes up later than usual. Rocket must’ve left at some point to relieve Pete, because the
   bunk is empty and lonely and dim.

   He’s taken up yesterday’s wrappers, and left her a glass of water in their place.

   God, why is he like this? She’s already in love; he doesn’t have to make it worse.

   She sits up on the edge of the bed, pressing the palms of her hands into her scratchy, tired
   eyes before she reaches for the glass and takes a grateful sip. She’s wrung out, but the sleep
   did her good. Nevertheless, when she scrapes herself out of bed, she still feels vaguely
   uncomfortable.

   Guilty.

   She’s gotten very used to telling her own story - at least the first half of it - and she knows
   how it can feel, to have the words forced out of you. He’d given her something unbelievably
   precious yesterday.

   Floor.

   She wonders if he’ll back out of this thing he’d proposed - a secret for a secret, a memory for
   a memory. She won’t blame him. She should tell him that. In this, at least, she has more
   experience than he does.

   He’d already told her about his sister - eyes ragged and haggard, nose and ears quivering.
   He’d given her that for - whatever reason. Because it would free her up to speak, maybe, or
   because it would obligate her. Either way, it was yet another kindness, shivering up inside her
   heart and glowing there.

   And then he’d trundled her messy self down to the bunk where she’d fucking cried on him
   before - exactly as he’d predicted - she’d fallen asleep during his explanation of pocket
   dimension tech.

   To be fair, he’d chosen the most exhausting night in recent memory to talk her through it, and
   his voice had been low and soothing and rhythmic. He’d done it on purpose, she’s sure. And
he’d been petting her hair the whole time, letting her breathe in the foresty, musky, electrical
scent of his fur.

For a second, Jolie wonders if this is what it feels like to be loved.

She groans and stares at the ceiling for a long minute, perched on the edge of the shelf-bed.
That’s a lot of feeling to project on someone else, she thinks. And what would Rocket say if
he’d known she’d wondered, for even a second, if he might…?

He’d either laugh in her face or not talk to her for days, depending on his mood, she tells
herself with a dry little smile. Maybe both. But either way, he’d start by being profoundly
uneasy.

Oh, Christ. Had she taken her sweatshirt off in front of him?

“I would like to die now,” she informs the ceiling.

By the time she gets to the upper level, Drax is finishing up clearing breakfast, and Gamora
and Pete have already gone to bed. She grabs some fruit, a roll, and a leftover sea-owl

“I am Groot,” says little Groot, peering around the chair he’s camped out in, just behind
Rocket.

“Groot thought you were never gonna wake up,” Rocket says drily, not turning around.

The tension rushes out of her in a whoosh. “Gotta wake up,” she says, balancing a plate in
one hand and plucking up the tiny Flora Colossus with her other. He nuzzles her cheek and
she nuzzles back. “Can’t miss seeing my favorite guy.”

“I am Groot,” he tells her seriously. She thinks she’s gathering most of what he says these

Groot’s words can sometimes be lost on her.

Which is why her copilot rolls his eyes from the pilot’s seat. “Don’t call her that.”

“Call me what?”

“I am Groot.”

“Don’t call me that!” Rocket snaps, much more sharply, almost frantically.

Jolie decides not to ask again. Instead, she shifts Groot to her shoulder. Then, to Rocket:
“You need anything, love?”

She almost flinches when she realizes what she’s called him - even though it’s not out of the
ordinary for them these days. He must’ve heard something in her voice, though, because he

“I’m set. You good, Jo?”
“Yes,” she says, too quickly. He raises a brow and she winces. “Sorry,” she says immediately,

“I am Groot.”

“He definitely won. You’d be impressed.”

“I am Groot.”

“I am Groot.”

“He only ate it because he could tell she was sad and he wanted to make her feel better.

Rocket is not sure how this new thing is going to unfold. New thing, of course, referring to
his brilliant idea of trading terrible frickin’ memories like some kind of fucked-up kid’s
playing-card game, or the worst bedtime stories in the history of the universe. But he wants to
know. And more than that, he wants Jo to feel -

Better. He just wants her to feel better.

Flor? Like flower?

It’s been almost a full rotation and the thought still makes the corner of his mouth twitch in a
bemused, perplexed little curl. He thinks it might be bittersweet. He’s never had anything
bittersweet before. He tries to imagine Floor’s response, if she’d heard it.

Pretty.

He’s been hoarding these memories for so long. The pain, the shame, yeah - but also, to
protect them. He knows he’s a monster - he knows he’s just a thing that’s been cobbled
together by fat-fingered children, so to frickin’ speak, because every word of that day is
tattooed on his bones just like his goddamn serial number. He knows because he’s heard it a
million times, so old it gets tiresome: Rodent. Vermin. Monster. Animal. Pet. Experiment.

Subject.

But his family had been - if someone were to say something like that, about them -

Were they like you? Were they fucked up? Were they fucked up like you?

Fuck, no. They’d been perfect. They had been, regardless of what He had thought.
That night, Jolie tucks Groot in, and they get changed in the dimmed light of the plasma orbs,

There are ten more rotations before they get to Sovereign. Ten bits of storied truth to spill
quietly to each other in the shadowed cockpit, or curled up together in the bunk like lovers.

And this is how Rocket slowly slides the first few interlocking pieces together, like bits of
scrapmetal that he supposes make their own kind of key.
She was five years younger than me - I was twelve, and she was seven. All I wanted to do for
the rest of my life was to look out for her. We were playing hide-and-seek in the field by the
river in early autumn. Do you know hide-and-seek?

It had sounded like a game Batch 89 had attempted, with limited success, in the cages. More
often, the four of them had played tag, or told stories, or talked about the shiny treasures
Rocket had brought back from the central chamber where he was encouraged to build little
machines and metal constructs.

Everything was gold and hazy. She asked me to get her a juicebox from the house. I
remember her running into the treeline to hide while I went to get it.

He remembers, again, the amber-misted holovid Jo had been painting in the cockpit, the night
before he’d bared his teeth and his claws and his stupid, jackass ability to open his mouth and
hurt everyone around him. Before he’d sunk all three deep into her grief, and had done his
damnedest to draw blood.

He tries to make it up to her now, with the memory of his first glimpse of blue, and the

traveling homes for adventurers. For him and his friends. He tries to make it up to her by
letting her connect the dots, by telling her the story of how they’d chosen their names.

Rocket, she murmurs once she’s collected up the implications - once she understands what

Another night, late in the dark shadows, with the blankets drawn up around her like a cocoon

The river? he’d asked.

You’d think, right? But no. When I came out, they were already taking her - right up into the

them. Twenty years ago, most Terrans didn’t believe in - in aliens. My family thought I was

Or - worse. That I’d - done something. On purpose. Or maybe - on accident, but out of anger.

He’d understood immediately what she hadn’t quite said. Rotations later, it still makes his

anyone would think she’d be anything but kind to a little vulnerable creature who she’d loved
most and best.

But he’d still been an idiot. He’d still asked her, in the hushed tones of instinctive horror -
and very much afraid of the answer -
What’d they do to you?

She’d given him her biggest eyes.

If you - she’d whispered in the dark like a little hunted animal - if you - if someone you loved
had died and you knew who was responsible, what would you do to them?

He thinks of the High Evolutionary’s face, like wet tissue paper beneath his claws. Rocket

him had recognized it even then.

But he’d gone for pain. He’d wanted to hurt Him. He’d never stopped wanting to hurt Him.

As far as Rocket has seen, the only significant scar Jo has is the one from Asgard, and maybe
in some ways that’s scarier. He doesn’t answer her question, and he’s sure she’ll still tell him

They’d torn her apart.

Not her face or her body, maybe. But everything else.

And yeah, he’d been mean as hell the day after that one. Not to Jo or Groot, but to pretty
much everyone else. Even Gamora had spent a good part of the rotation glaring at him

tries to channel the same energy she’d given him cycles and cycles ago, when she’d told him
to offer Yondu two-hundred-thirty-thousand units for a certain caged copilot on her behalf.
She slides the drink into his hand and taps his chest. “Let me just take care of you.”

His eyes nearly fall out of his head. She turns back to the bar, trying not to flinch – or shoot
him a glare over her shoulder – when she feels his stare on her ass. Instead, she grimaces and
pulls her sweatshirt down over her hips.

“Did ya hear that, men?” Taserface bellows from behind her, so abruptly and loudly that she
almost jumps “The lass wants t’take care a’ me!”

She swallows back a grimace and instead sends her most saccharine smile over her shoulder.
She imagines being empty and echoing, all her annoyance and apprehension seeping out of
the soles of her boots, sinking into the floor. Later, she promises. She’ll get this monster and
his lackeys so drunk they pass out in their own vomit, and then she’ll get the fin, and then
she’ll get Rocket.

And once she has him out of that fucking cage – again – she’ll be able to be herself. Even if
he’s mad about it.

Which isn’t something she can afford to think about. When she remembers the look in his
eyes – concern and fear, with the edges set fire and burning furiously – her bones feel like
hollow wind chimes, resonant with guilt and misery. She can feel her face fall, and right now
she needs to keep that mild, pleasant expression on her face.

She pours more drinks. As soon as Taserface finishes one, she’s pressing another into his
hand. He blinks at it, then manages to grab a fistful of her sweatshirt, tugging so hard she
nearly falls into him. The urge to pull away rises in her throat like bile but she swallows it
down and leans in, pressing into the side of his chair at just such an angle that he’d have to
twist in his seat to put his hands on her. He must be mollified by her closeness because he lets
the shirt slip from his massive grip.

“Sit, lass,” he says, gesturing again to his lap and taking another swallow of nearly-pure
ginsky.

“I will,” she promises again. “I just want to make sure you have everything you need.” She
tries to manufacture something doe-eyed, tries not to wince. “I want to be… attentive.”

He looks so fucking pleased and satisfied that it makes her want to hurl.

So she slips behind his chair, out of his reach, and heads back to the bar. Pours another round
for the room, another fake-cocktail of mostly-water for herself, raises a glass to the room
again. The Ravagers are starting to drop: sitting on the stairs and in corners, slamming back
drinks and resting their heads in their arms at the bar. From here, it looks like Taserface is
starting to wobble a bit, so she pours two more drinks for him – largely, straight ginsky. A
fight breaks out on the floor as she brings them to him, and she has to dodge a thrown body.
Luckily, the glasses remain unspilled, and when she gets to Taserface’s knee, his eyes are –
finally – bleary and unfocused.

“Hey,” she says lightly.

“Lass,” he slurs. “Sit in my lap. In front of my crew. I want them to see–”

She grits her teeth. “I don’t think I deserve to yet,” she says meekly. “I was so rude earlier,
and I haven’t been keeping your drinks coming.” She hands him the first drink, then takes his
empty glass and presses the second drink into his newly-emptied palm. This time, when he
gropes for her, she evades him easily and he nearly tumbles out of his chair.

“Let me get the boys one more round,” she tells him. “Then I’ll come back to you.”

Some part of her twinges with guilt. She’s drugging him. She’s absolutely drugging him. All
of them, really. And she’s not an idiot – she doubts either Rocket or Yondu are interested in a
stealthy escape at this point. All these people are going to die.

She stifles a sigh. A whole Ravager clan, gone up in smoke in the course of a single cycle.
Half of them by the others’ hands, and half of them done in by the captain they’d betrayed
and two outsiders. It’s disheartening, really.

But desperate times call for desperate measures. The pulsing ache in her shoulder reminds her
that Taserface is an irredeemable asshole, and she only has to think of Tullk and Phaedor
floating out into the infinite abyss to remind herself that none of these bastards have clean
hands.

And besides, she’s not taking her chances with Rocket’s safety.

She watches from the bar, pouring more drinks as Taserface slugs down one of the drinks and
tosses the glass to the floor. She flinches when it shatters, but it’s probably the twentieth
broken glass of the night. He tosses back the second, and sways, then leans back in his chair.
The remaining glass slides from his thick fingers and the thick bottom cracks when it hits the
ground.

She waits until his spine softens into a slump and his legs sprawl, and she pours another
round of drinks for the ten or so remaining Ravagers. The majority of the chamber has been
emptied out, and the last handful are so deep in their cups that Jolie could probably announce
her intentions from atop the bar, and they’d neither notice nor remember.

She slips away, and then strides down the hallway. If anyone is still awake and about, she’ll
tell them she’s retrieving something for Taserface. Stealth will probably do worse for her in
this situation than acting like she belongs here.

She’s seen the bunks before, and she’s able to navigate herself there without issue. A dozen
or so have apparently staggered their way to their beds after all, and the drunken snoring is
cacophonous. She finds the little bedstand, and the drawer squeaks when she slides it open.
Fortunately, these Ravagers are used to louder noises while they sleep – and tonight they’ve
been drugged by alcohol and hubris.
  Jolie finds the fin easily, and tucks it into the waistband of her leggings, hidden under her
  shirt.

  She hesitates, then peels back the loose, draping neckline of the sweatshirt to check the
  shoulder she’s been favoring since the mutineer had gripped it. Her skin there is blued and
  purpled, and her collarbone aches on that side.

  She’s probably lucky.

  When she looks up, someone’s silhouetted in the doorway, watching her. For a moment, her
  heart leaps into her mouth, but then she recognizes the lanky silhouette.

  Kraglin.

  She hesitates, then approaches him. “Sorry,” she whispers. “Taserface just asked me to bring
  -“

  The former second-mate sighs and steps back, letting her ease past him into the corridor.

  “Don’t lie to me, Earthgirl. I know what you were doin’.”

  She hesitates.

  “D’you got it?”

  She nods mutely. He looks so sad and lost, and she knows how much he admires and loves
  Yondu. There’s no way he anticipated…all this.

  She reaches out, grabs his hand, and squeezes.

  “S’been a long day, Jolie,” Kraglin mumbles, and then sniffles.

  She closes her eyes and pulls him in for a hug. “I know, Krags,” she whispers. “I’m sorry.”

  He hangs onto her for a second, and she feels tears falling onto her bruised shoulder. Then he
  pulls back and clears his throat.

  “Let’s go.”

   Having Kraglin at her side makes things easier. To start with, Jolie doesn’t have to wait for
   Yondu to kill someone with his arrow so she can raid their body for keys.

   Rocket’s already waiting when they arrive. His narrow, meticulous hands are wrapped around
   the bars, nose pressed between them, eyes on her before she even comes around the corner
   and onto the catwalk with Kraglin in tow. There’s something in his eyes when she walks up,
   but she can’t figure out what it is. Instead, she’s struck by how beautiful he is: the curved line
   of his narrow nose, his liquid-dark eyes. Her heart aches enough to match her shoulder:
   bruised and broken. She wishes he would believe her if she told him.

   Jolie swallows. Because she had told him, hadn’t she? Or to be more accurate, she’d told a
   chamber full of Ravagers. How much she wanted him, how much she—

   But Rocket hadn’t mentioned it other than to chastise her for angering Taserface. He's being
   gracious, she supposes — pretending it never happened.

   She should probably take his lead.

   Yondu’s also looking alert, she realizes as she draws closer. She wonders how they'd known
   to expect her right then, like they could see around corners or felt her coming. She supposes
   it doesn't matter, though — both of them are eyeing Kraglin suspiciously now. She wonders if
   she should step in and explain, but then the Ravager speaks.

   “I didn’t mean to do a mutiny,” he tells his captain. His voice wobbles. He swallows, and
   doesn’t bother trying to hide the tears in his voice when he says, “They killed all my friends.”
Her eyes prickle against her will. He sounds so bereft. She looks at Rocket, who’s got one
brow raised skeptically. Her copilot glances at her and he must see something beseeching in
her gaze. He pauses, rolls his eyes, and then huffs a half-bitter, half-incredulous laugh.

“Trust you to go looking for a weapon and come back with an ally, princess.”

She casts her copilot a crooked smile and a wink. “Why not both?” Then she peels up the
bottom edge of her sweatshirt and untucks the fin from her waistband, passing it through the
bars to Rocket so he can run his hands over it and figure out how to reconnect it for Yondu.

She can see her copilot try to muffle a chuckle behind a swiped paw, like he doesn’t want to
encourage her behavior too much. It fills her belly with that warm fluttering that almost
makes her forget the bruising ache deep inside her shoulder. She watches, entranced, as he
slides his fingers lingeringly over the prototype, learning it by touch alone. “Good girl,” he
admits grudgingly, and she tamps down on the frisson of eager delight that blossoms in her
abdomen and sparks through her brain.

“Get the Third Quadrant ready for release,” the Ravager captain says to his new first mate,
nodding his acceptance.

“Uh, one more thing,” Rocket interjects. “You got any clones of Quill’s old music on the
ship?”

Kraglin nods, unlocks the door, and eases it open, then heads off to do his captain’s bidding
while Rocket continues to examine the loose wiring on the old piece of tech. Yondu stays
patiently on the floor while her copilot prods through the docking station in his skull.

Jo watches him admiringly. How does it take him less than a minute to figure out how the fin
should connect to Yondu’s remaining hardware? Rocket gestures her over and positions her
hands on the apparatus, showing her how to hold it close to Yondu’s head so he can snake his
narrow fingers between them and adjust some wiring or terminals that neither of them can
see. He does it all by touch alone: light-fingered, quick. She watches what she can see: the
way the tendons flex in the backs of his hand as he curls his digits, as he grips and twists
wires. Jolie watches, and she thinks she can count the number of times Rocket has had his
hands on her. It’s definitely not a high enough number.

Unfortunately for her, the only person who’s wanted to touch her lately is Taserface. She
flinches.

“You all right?” Rocket murmurs under his breath. She suddenly realizes how tired she is,
how much she wants to curl up in his voice.

“I’m fine,” she says softly. It’s not a lie, she reasons.

He takes the fin from her and locks it onto the Centaurian’s head, then gives Yondu a little
slap on the back of his head, like he’s just closed the hood on a car. Jolie stifles a startled
laugh.

“All done, Old Man,” her copilot states dryly.
Yondu stands, and Rocket reaches for her – hand sliding between her thighs casually in a way
that makes her heart stammer against her ribs. He tugs, handling her, pulling her in front of
him as he strides past her on the other side. It takes a second for her to realize he’s effectively
tucked her between himself and Yondu. Then his fingers tap the back of her thigh and the
three of them stride onto the grated catwalk just as the opening notes of one of Quill’s songs
is humming into the ship’s speaker system. Jolie barely has time to deal with the hot flush of
warmth rising from her chest into her cheeks: too much lust again, yes – she’s too fuckin’
easy, apparently – but also the embarrassment of once again having to be protected.

She doesn’t have much time to be humiliated, though. Jolie has never seen Yondu’s arrow in
action before, but as it sings along a line of red laser-bright light, it reminds her of a dance – a
ballet, maybe. A ballet of murder, sure, but beautiful nonetheless.

Not that she’d tell him that.

The first bodies fall and Rocket’s already grinning gleefully, smugly pulling what she thinks
is a BN1 blaster and some kind of triple-barrel ion pistol from the carcasses. He has an
unerring instinct for firearms, Jolie thinks - if one is anywhere in his vicinity, it might as well
already be in his hands.

Maybe it’s fucked up - how much she admires his casual, flawless aim, the grin he wears
when he’s killing people. But she reminds herself that these bastards had killed Tullk and
Phaedor and a number of other Yondu clan Ravagers she’d liked, that they would’ve turned
her copilot and Yondu over to be killed by the people paying their bounties – and she decides
she doesn’t care if it’s fucked up after all.

And Rocket is fucking beautiful while he does it.

When they reach the chamber with the security screens, Rocket’s eyes narrow. He gets this
look of intense concentration she usually only sees when he’s trying to make something he’s
never made before - and it makes her grip her lip with her teeth.

He centers himself among the screens, then raises one hand, pointing his newly-acquired gun
to one side, almost experimentally.

He pulls the trigger, and a neat hole punches through the door.

Onscreen, a Ravager buckles on the catwalk.

The corner of Rocket’s mouth pulls back in a grin of pure, spiteful delight. He meets Jolie’s
gaze slowly.

“Get down, sweetheart,” he says, and she immediately crouches low.

Seeing him in action has always been a gift, Jolie thinks. From the very first moment she’d
wrapped up her job on the Dead Morrigan and had come home to find him stealing every
piece of tech he could get his hands on, she’d only wanted to watch him work. Countless
shared rotations in the cockpit, she’d borne witness from the corner of her eye as his quick
clever hands and unerring instincts made something new, and she’d treasured each moment.
Whenever he’s in his element, his confidence burns to the surface and everything moves so
quickly: his eyes, his mind, his fingers and palms.

Now he turns reflexively, tail swinging behind him, firing shots through walls and doors in
accordance with whatever he sees in the screens. His instincts are flawless, and the look of
satisfaction on his face makes her toes curl inside her boots.

Jolie has never really considered herself a lover of violence, but apparently she could watch
him kill people for hours.

He must notice something in the monitors because she sees his ears flick and his face shift
and he whirls toward Yondu. “No,” he snaps.

Yondu whistles once, sharply, and then says, “We’ll be fine. I got an escape plan for us.”

“Don’t care,” her copilot answers. “I want a chance at that hand first.”

Yondu stares at him, then sighs. “I don’t think that gesture’s gonna mean much to her–”

“Oh, it’s all for me, Old Man,” her copilot says bitterly.

“Wait,” Jolie says, brow furrowing. “What? What are you–”

“I’ll be right back, sweetheart,” Rocket’s telling her. He tosses her the BN1 blaster and she

minutes since they’d left the cell. “She’ll take care of you. Stay with Yondu.”

“But–”

He drops to all fours and sprints out the door, gone so quickly she can’t say anything. She

“We’ll wait right here,” the Centaurian says, sounding annoyed. “Shouldn’t take him that

She can see Rocket darting from camera to camera, catwalk to catwalk: legs a blur, tail

But in the blurred sights of the camera, it looks like Rocket takes advantage of Taserface’s

Jolie’s palm slaps against the screen – not on purpose, just instinctively. Her heart is gone —

“Yondu – Yondu–”

  And so this is how Rocket finds himself sitting behind the flight controls of the Fleetwood,

  The Fleetwood begins to rattle, lights flickering as it approaches the monstrous jump-point.

  “Brace yourselves, morons!” Rocket roars.



Chapter End Notes



    a note about jump-points! (we had a fun discussion on tumblr about them!). in the mcu
    they are described as being part of the Universal Neural Teleportation Network (UNTN),
    but they are also described as being made up of a network of wormholes (they don’t
    look to me the way I imagine either of these things looking but I have not yet traveled
by either means). now i’m just a lowly fanfic writer and not even a little bit of a
physicist but my understanding is that teleportation is the instantaneous transportation of
energy and matter (and the information about how they fit together) without having to
cross physical space — a process. but wormholes are bridges across two points in
space/time — structural. one seems to me like a thing that can be mobilized, and the
other seems like a thing that can be built? (at least hypothetically) maybe there’s some
overlap (or way to overlap both to make real-life application possible someday lol) but i
don’t think they’re the same.

so. i’ve sort of married the two concepts for our lil story. when i reference reconstitution
after going through a jump, that’s about teleportation and the breaking-down and
putting-back-together of energy/matter/information (maybe why our friends were
experienced such distortion when they tried to make 700 jumps). but visuals in the mcu
do seem to make jump points kinda look like wormholes so i’m also talking about wear-
and-tear of just – wormhole travel. i mean it looks mostly-smooth but it seems like
there’s a sort of pop (reconstitution? temporal turbulence? atmospheric displacement?
who knows. someone probably) — and it does seem like they generally “prepare” for
the jump based on how they talk about them.

SO this is the model i’m using for now. :) outside of this context i AM happy to talk
about other theories related to how jump-points work (‘cause it’s fun)

oh also, i know i’m playing fast-and-loose with loki’s illusion abilities but we’re also
(again) talking about teleportation and wormholes and talking raccoons who fuck
extremely well so let’s just suspend our disbelief a little



friends. friends. the last chapter is coming and. i have so many feelings. i really
hope it feels like as satisfying an ending for you as it does for me. i also know it is
going to leave some threads unsewn just because we all know what’s coming “next”
after our story ends. maybe i’ll come back someday and write a sequel or a handful
of oneshots to follow up on our friends but as of .... 2/6 I think? their story will be
concluded. ♡♡♡ i will cry. i will. i am already. thank you so much for being part
of this with me, and for all your support and kindness. it has meant the whole
galaxy to me.

   When Rocket wakes up, the sky is calm and blue and star-studded, and he can hear his family
   shifting behind him. He shakes the sound of exploding stars out of his head, and his mind
   immediately goes to Jo and Groot. He twists in the pilot’s seat, so fast that his spine crackles,
   and casts his eyes around like frantic red fireflies.

   Everyone but Pete and Loki are spilled on the floor, and for a moment, every bone in
   Rocket’s body is brittle and sharp, so heavy he’s pinned and stabbed by gravity itself. It’s the
   first time in ages that he’s found himself trapped back in the room of cages, Lylla and Teefs
   and Floor dead on the ground. He’s not prepared for the way it sucks the breath out of his
   lungs, for the way that black hole behind his sternum — dormant for so frickin’ long —
   suddenly becomes active again: empty and pulling, crumpling his whole damaged and
   fucked-up body into it.
Jo is stirring, and so is Groot — and Thor, and Loki in the chair behind him. But for just a

nothing fits in his crumpled-up lungs.

It’s surreal: some distant part of his brain registers Jolie’s eyes opening, seeking his like it’s
an instinct she’s had her whole life. He can see the relief in her features when she realizes
he’s okay — and then the flooding concern when she realizes he’s really, really not. She

shoulder: one, two, three, four, breathing deeply for him, steadying him.

“Groot’s fine,” she whispers into his downturned ear, flattened tight and protective against his
skull. “I’m fine. Pete’s gonna be fine. Gamora’s fine. Drax is fine and Mantis is fine and Thor

Loki clears his throat. “I am also fine.”

Rocket can feel Jolie lift her head and look at the younger Odinsson. There’s a pause and

Rocket breathes deep, and climbs around Jolie. She starts to move — to give him room —

You said you’d stay.

You said, if I wanted you to return the favor, you’d stay.

counts. He wonders if this is what she feels like everytime she gives some survivor a little
flicker of their lost loved ones back.

Jolie wraps both hands around his wrist, pulling his hand up to her mouth, pressing teary
kisses to all his knuckles and tugging him closer, over the datapad and through the projection,
cradling his face in her hands. Her soft lips and wet cheeks press all over his face, tucking
every droplet of love and loss and devotion into his fur, and he lets her.

“Jo,” he says, once her tears have slowed and her breathing’s shivered into little hiccups. “I
gotta —there’s something else. I —” His mouth is slick. Scared. “I told you earlier,” he says
quietly, wrapping his voice around the hoarseness in his throat, wrapping his fingers around
her wrists. “I think about how things coulda been different. I think — I think I shoulda been
falling for you the second you opened that cage-door. Or when you wouldn’t let ‘em put me
in the cargo hold. Or when you told Taserface you wanted my stuff back and demanded a
frickin’ floor in the cage. Hell, when I first saw you look through the damn bars. I shoulda
started falling in love with you any of those times.” The words fall out of his mouth now: fast
and spattering, like fat raindrops refracting sunlight, iridescent and splashing everything
around them. He doesn’t miss the way her eyes go wide. “I look back and there’s a hundred
different times I coulda loved you sooner.”

“Rocket — “

“But I think I always would’ve got here.” His voice cracks again, but he makes himself go
on: determined not to let those words slide back into his lungs, cowardly and unsaid. “I
would’ve loved you no matter what. I would’ve loved even if you never d— even if you
never. I would’ve.”

“Baby,” she says, her hands fluttering in the loose bracelets of his fingers like a bouquet
made of butterflies. Precious. He presses her knuckles against his teeth; he wants them buried
in his ribs, in his heart.

“I love you.” The words are ragged. “I do. An’ I know I — I don’t deserve this. What we’ve
got. I know this wasn’t meant for me. But I love you.”

You were never meant for the new world.

You could figure out the complex workings of cytoplasmic filtration systems, but you couldn't
figure out that?

But whenever Rocket is curled up against Jo — two crescent moons tangled together, his
clawed fingers knotted into the satin strands of her hair and locks of it wrapped around his
wrists while he tastes her, breathes her in, fucks into her, just lays beside her — in these
moments, even the High Evolutionary’s crackling, mimicky voice seems muted.

And like clockwork — so predictable — her words come, still softened by all her tears.

“Rocket,” Jo says, her voice weepy and sweet and always the softest little welcome in his
ears.

I was looking for you. I was worried. Do you want to come home?

He knows what she’s going to say, half a second before she says it, because this is what
happens when you spend too many rotations falling asleep to the lullaby of someone else’s
breathing. He lets the knowledge of her words curl up behind his breastbone, a little spiral
made of sky and certainty, a little golden jump-point he can carry behind his ribs: so bright,
so warm, and so whole that it lights him up on the inside, maybe shines out his eyes and the
points of his claws. He lets himself feel her words like that knock on his sternum — can I
come in? — waiting so patiently outside his door. Lets himself see the words like an open
hand waiting to be taken, or a bottle of shimmering Sovereign rum waiting to be shared. Lets
himself hear the words like a hundred unnecessary regrets, because what’s here and now is so
good in this moment, and so perfect.

Lets himself reach out and take the words in his hands, like so many palmfuls of warmth and
softness, freely given.
  Fuck me, my dude. I’ve always wanted a raccoon.

  “Rocket,” she says again, and they’re exactly the words he’d thought they’d be. “I was
  absolutely meant for you.”

  And this time, when he takes her face into his hands, he lets himself believe them.
